Sugar Cookie Tartlet Crust
1/3 cup sugar
1/2 cup butter, room temperature
1 1/4 cups all-purpose flour
1/4 teaspoon kosher salt
2 tablespoons cream
1 teaspoon vanilla extract
Meyer Lemon Curd Tart Filling
1 cup sugar
2/3 cup meyer lemon juice, freshly squeezed and strained
1 tablespoon lemon zest
3 large eggs
2 egg yolks
6 tablespoons unsalted butter, softened and cut into half inch pieces
Sugar Cookie Tartlet Crust: Preheat oven to 400°F. In a stand mixer, cream together sugar and butter until light and fluffy. Beat in flour, kosher salt, cream and vanilla, until mixture is moist and crumbly. Press dough into four 4-inch tart pans (or one 9 or 10 inch tart pan) and press it up the sides, making sure the layer on the bottom is even. Bake for 15-20 minutes, until crust is set and firm at the edges. Cool, then fill with desired filling and bake as that recipe directs. Meyer Lemon Curd Tart Filling: In a medium saucepan, combine sugar and lemon juice and bring to a boil. Stir occasionally. In a large bowl, whisk together zest, eggs and egg yolks. When sugar mixture comes to a boil, pour very small amounts down the side of the bowl into the egg mixture while whisking continuously to temper the mixture. Continue to add only a few tablespoons at a time until all has been incorporated. Transfer egg mixture back to sauce pan and return to stove. Cook on medium heat until thickened, about 8 minutes, whisking frequently. Remove custard from stove and whisk in butter, adding in one piece at a time. When all butter has been added, cool curd for 15 minutes before pouring into prepared tart crusts. Refrigerate overnight or at least 8 hours before serving.

- 1 tablespoon grated orange zest
- 1/2 cup unsalted butter, cold and cubed
- 1/2 cup buttermilk
- 1 teaspoon vanilla extract
- 1 large egg, beaten
- Optional: Glaze (powdered sugar mixed with orange juice)

The key contribution of this paper is the introduction of a novel self-guided attention mechanism that adaptively learns the importance of different image regions at multiple scales. This allows the model to capture both local and global patterns in medical images, leading to improved segmentation accuracy and efficiency. The proposed method has important implications for various medical applications, including disease diagnosis, treatment planning, and monitoring, and we believe it has the potential to significantly improve the accuracy and efficiency of medical image segmentation tasks.

Cloud based medical image analysis has become popular recently due to the
high computation complexities of various deep neural network (DNN) based
frameworks and the increasingly large volume of medical images that need to be
processed. It has been demonstrated that for medical images the transmission
from local to clouds is much more expensive than the computation in the clouds
itself. Towards this, 3D image compression techniques have been widely applied
to reduce the data traffic. However, most of the existing image compression
techniques are developed around human vision, i.e., they are designed to
minimize distortions that can be perceived by human eyes. In this paper we will
use deep learning based medical image segmentation as a vehicle and demonstrate
that interestingly, machine and human view the compression quality differently.
Medical images compressed with good quality w.r.t. human vision may result in
inferior segmentation accuracy. We then design a machine vision oriented 3D
image compression framework tailored for segmentation using DNNs. Our method
automatically extracts and retains image features that are most important to
the segmentation. Comprehensive experiments on widely adopted segmentation
frameworks with HVSMR 2016 challenge dataset show that our method can achieve
significantly higher segmentation accuracy at the same compression rate, or
much better compression rate under the same segmentation accuracy, when
compared with the existing JPEG 2000 method. To the best of the authors'
knowledge, this is the first machine vision guided medical image compression
framework for segmentation in the clouds.

The gold-hoarder walked in his palace park and with him walked his troubles. And over his head hovered worries as a vulture hovers over a carcass, until he reached a beautiful lake surrounded by magnificent marble statuary.
He sat there pondering the water which poured from the mouths of the statues like thoughts flowing freely from a lover's imagination, and contemplating heavily his palace which stood upon a knoll like a birth-mark upon the cheek of a maiden. His fancy revealed to him the pages of his life's drama which he read with falling tears that veiled his eyes and prevented him from viewing man's feeble additions to Nature.
He looked back with piercing regret to the images of his early life, woven into pattern by the gods, until he could no longer control his anguish. He said aloud, "Yesterday I was grazing my sheep in the green valley, enjoying my existence, sounding my flute, and holding my head high. Today I am a prisoner of greed. Gold leads into gold, then into restlessness and finally into crushing misery.
"Yesterday I was like a singing bird, soaring freely here and there in the fields. Today I am a slave to fickle wealth, society's rules, and city's customs, and purchased friends, pleasing the people by conforming to the strange and narrow laws of man. I was born to be free and enjoy the bounty of life, but I find myself like a beast of burden so heavily laden with gold that his back is breaking.
"Where are the spacious plains, the singing brooks, the pure breeze, the closeness of Nature? Where is my deity? I have lost all! Naught remains save loneliness that saddens me, gold that ridicules me, slaves who curse to my back, and a palace that I have erected as a tomb for my happiness, and in whose greatness I have lost my heart.
"Yesterday I roamed the prairies and the hills together with the Bedouin's daughter; Virtue was our companion, Love our delight, and the moon our guardian. Today I am among women with shallow beauty who sell themselves for gold and diamonds.
"Yesterday I was carefree, sharing with the shepherds all the joy of life; eating, playing, working, singing, and dancing together to the music of the heart's truth. Today I find myself among the people like a frightened lamb among the wolves. As I walk in the roads, they gaze at me with hateful eyes and point at me with scorn and jealousy, and as I steal through the park I see frowning faces all about me.
"Yesterday I was rich in happiness and today I am poor in gold.
"Yesterday I was a happy shepherd looking upon his head as a merciful king looks with pleasure upon his contented subjects. Today I am a slave standing before my wealth, my wealth which robbed me of the beauty of life I once knew.
"Forgive me, my Judge! I did not know that riches would put my life in fragments and lead me into the dungeons of harshness and stupidity. What I thought was glory is naught but an eternal inferno."
He gathered himself wearily and walked slowly toward the palace, sighing and repeating, "Is this what people call wealth? Is this the god I am serving and worshipping? Is this what I seek of the earth? Why can I not trade it for one particle of contentment? Who would sell me one beautiful thought for a ton of gold? Who would give me one moment of love for a handful of gems? Who would grant me an eye that can see others' hearts, and take all my coffers in barter?"
As he reached the palace gates he turned and looked toward the city as Jeremiah gazed toward Jerusalem. He raised his arms in woeful lament and shouted, "Oh people of the noisome city, who are living in darkness, hastening toward misery, preaching falsehood, and speaking with stupidity...until when shall you remain ignorant? Unit when shall you abide in the filth of life and continue to desert its gardens? Why wear you tattered robes of narrowness while the silk raiment of Nature's beauty is fashioned for you? The lamp of wisdom is dimming; it is time to furnish it with oil. The house of true fortune is being destroyed; it is time to rebuild it and guard it. The thieves of ignorance have stolen the treasure of your peace; it is time to retake it!"
At that moment a poor man stood before him and stretched forth his hand for alms. As he looked at the beggar, his lips parted, his eyes brightened with a softness, and his face radiated kindness. It was as if the yesterday he had lamented by the lake had come to greet him. He embraced the pauper with affection and filled his hands with gold, and with a voice sincere with the sweetness of love he said, "Come back tomorrow and bring with you your fellow sufferers. All your possessions will be restored."
He entered his palace saying, "Everything in life is good; even gold, for it teaches a lesson. Money is like a stringed instrument; he who does not know how to use it properly will hear only discordant music. Money is like love; it kills slowly and painfully the one who withholds it, and it enlivens the other who turns it upon his fellow man."

The whinchat (Saxicola rubetra) is a small migratory passerine bird breeding in Europe and western Asia and wintering in central Africa. At one time considered to be in the thrush family, Turdidae, it is now placed in the Old World flycatcher family, Muscicapidae. Both sexes have a strong supercilium, brownish upper parts mottled darker, a pale throat and breast, a pale buff to whitish belly, and a blackish tail with white bases to the outer tail feathers, but in the breeding season, the male has an orange-buff throat and breast. The whinchat is a solitary species, favouring open grassy country with rough vegetation and scattered small shrubs. It perches in elevated locations ready to pounce on the insects and other small invertebrates that form its diet. The nest is built by the female on the ground in coarse vegetation, with a clutch of four to seven eggs being laid. The hen incubates the eggs for about thirteen days and then both parents feed the nestlings. Fledging takes place about eighteen days after hatching and the parents continue to feed the young for another fortnight. Moulting takes place in late summer before the migration southwards, and again on the wintering grounds in Africa before the migration northwards in spring. The whinchat is a common species with a wide range and the International Union for Conservation of Nature has classified it as being of "least concern".

Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

- 2 cloves garlic, minced
- 1/2 cup dry white wine
- 1 cup beef or vegetable stock
- 2 tablespoons chopped fresh parsley

Instructions:

1. Season filet mignon steaks with salt and pepper on both sides; set aside.
2. Heat olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add the steaks and cook until browned on the bottom, about 3 minutes. Using tongs, flip and cook for another 2 minutes or until browned on the other side. Remove the steaks from skillet and set aside.

4. Add garlic and cook for 1 minute more. Pour in white wine and simmer until reduced by half, about 3 minutes. Stir in stock and bring to a simmer; cook for another 2-3 minutes or until the sauce has thickened slightly. Stir in chopped parsley.
5. Place the filet mignon steaks back into the skillet, spoon some of the sweetbread-wild mushroom ragout on top of the steaks, and serve.

Basic Chicken Stock Recipe:

Ingredients:
- 1 whole chicken (4-5 lbs.)
- 2 large onions, chopped
- 2 carrots, chopped 
- 2 celery stalks, chopped
- 6 cloves garlic, minced
- 1 tsp. dried thyme
- 1 tsp. dried rosemary
- 1 tsp. dried oregano
- 1 bay leaf 
- Salt and pepper to taste
- Water or chicken broth (8 cups)

Instructions:

1. Rinse the chicken inside and out with cold water and pat dry with a paper towel.

2. In a large pot or Dutch oven, heat some olive oil over medium heat. Add the onions, carrots, and celery and sauté for about 10 minutes until the vegetables are soft.

3. Add the minced garlic, dried thyme, rosemary, and oregano, and cook for another minute, stirring constantly.

4. Place the chicken breast-side up in the pot, and season with salt and pepper.

5. Add the bay leaf and pour in the chicken broth or water. Bring the mixture to a boil, then reduce the heat to low and simmer for about 1 hour and 15 minutes.

6. Remove the chicken from the pot and strain the broth through a fine-mesh strainer to remove the solids.

7. Return the chicken to the pot, bones-in, and let it simmer for another 30 minutes to extract more flavor.

8. Remove the chicken from the pot entirely, and strain the broth once more to ensure that all the bits and pieces are removed.

9. Discard the chicken and the vegetables, and pour the strained broth into a clean container to cool.

10. Once cooled, transfer the broth to the refrigerator or freezer to store for later use. The broth will keep for up to 3 days in the refrigerator or up to 3 months in the freezer. Enjoy your homemade Basic Chicken Stock!

text:
Bloody Mary Chicken & Rice Recipe

Ingredients:

  - 1 cup uncooked long-grain white rice
  - 2 cups chicken broth
  - 1 pound boneless, skinless chicken breasts or thighs
  - 1 tablespoon olive oil
  - 1 small onion, diced
  - 2 cloves garlic, minced
  - 1/2 cup vodka
  - 1/2 cup tomato juice
  - 2 tablespoons Worcestershire sauce
  - 1 teaspoon hot sauce
  - 1 teaspoon paprika
  - Salt and pepper, to taste
  - 2 stalks celery, chopped
  - 2 large eggs, beaten
  - 1/4 cup chopped fresh parsley
  - Lemon wedges, for serving

Instructions:

1. Cook the rice according to the package instructions in the chicken broth until it is tender and the liquid has been absorbed. Set aside.
2. In a large skillet, heat the olive oil over medium heat. Add the onion and garlic and cook until softened, about 3-4 minutes.
3. Add the chicken to the skillet and cook until browned on all sides, about 6-7 minutes. Remove the chicken from the skillet and set it aside.
4. In the same skillet, add the vodka, tomato juice, Worcestershire sauce, hot sauce, paprika, salt, and pepper. Stir to combine and bring the mixture to a simmer.
5. Reduce the heat to low and add the chicken to the skillet. Cook for 10-15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the chicken is fully cooked and the sauce has thickened.
6. Add the cooked rice, celery, and beaten eggs to the skillet. Stir well to combine.
7. Cook for an additional 2-3 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the eggs are cooked through.
8. Remove the skillet from the heat and stir in the chopped parsley.
9. Serve the Bloody Mary Chicken & Rice hot, with lemon wedges on the side. Enjoy!

When young Dewey Cox accidentally cuts his brother in half with a machete, it sets him on a long, hard, and winding road that traverses the most profoundly important moments in modern music history spanning the 1950's to today. "Walk Hard" was erroneously advertised as yet another comedic romp from Judd Apatow. While as the co-screenwriter here many of Apatow's trademarks can be found including the usual sophomoric sexual humor and ironic pop-culture references, "The Dewey Cox Story" is actually closer in spirit to the mocumentaries of Christopher Guest ("This is Spinal Tap!" and "Best in Show") as channeled through the spastic colon of the "Naked Gun" films.

This is a parody played hilariously straight. The target of its mockery is so succinct and sharply pointed--the recent Oscar-winning musical biopics "Ray" and "Walk the Line"--that the film's true comedic genius may be lost on people who didn't really pay attention to those films or thought this would just be another "Superbad." The film's mimesis of its source materials is so spot-on, that it even follows their same cadence and nearly falls apart midway as it glosses over many points in history and aspects of the musician's life while covering every cliché possible from the temptations of life on the road with drugs and groupies to bouts in rehab and bitter divorces to long dry periods that suddenly make way for life-altering inspiration.

At the center of "Walk Hard" is John C. Reilly who sings and acts his heart out to hilarious effect. A former Oscar nominee for "Chicago", Reilly has since cut a niche for himself as the second banana to bigger comedy stars like Will Ferrell in "Talladega Nights" and for the first time gets a film to call his own. Tim Meadows is shockingly funny as the friend who ushers in Cox's decent into drug use (his overly accentuated but still deadpan line deliveries are priceless), while Jenna Fishcher is sprite and lovely as the June Carter cutie to Cox's Johnny Cash wannabee. Other SNL players including Kristin Wiig and Chris Parnell and Apatow alumni like Paul Rudd (as John Lennon!) and Jonah Hill pop in and out of the film amidst an onslaught of funny sight-gags and one-liners. Also in on the fun is a cavalcade of current music stars including the lead singer of the White Stipes as Elvis and Eddie Vedder as himself doing a nonsensical quasi-spiritual riff on Cox's legacy while presenting a Lifetime Achievement Award.

The heart of "Walk Hard" is in the music. If you were to not listen so closely, you might be fooled into thinking these were actual hit songs from their respective time periods. Of course, listening to the lyrics is part of the fun. The ridiculously silly double-entendres in Cox's duet with his honey-to-be Darlene are especially funny, while I personally found their spoof of a Bob Dylan song to be downright brilliant. Since the writers took the time to be so verbose and intricate with their nonsensical free-form versing, they allowed the bit to work on multiple levels as both an homage and a biting jab at Dylan's alleged lyrical genius.

Utimately "Walk Hard", in ways both monumentally stupid and unfathomably smart, proves to be almost too clever for its own good. It may have bombed in it's first-run at the box office, but I would imagine it will eventually find its audience. In one pivotal early scene Cox begs his wife to believe in him and his dreams of becoming a successful singer. She replies something to the effect of, "Oh, baby, I do. I just believe you're gonna fail." I couldn't have said it better myself, and it still has me laughing.

text:
Sure! Here's a recipe for a delicious and hearty navy bean soup that's perfect for a chilly fall or winter evening:

Ingredients:

* 1 pound dried navy beans, soaked overnight and drained
* 2 tablespoons olive oil
* 1 onion, chopped
* 3 cloves garlic, minced
* 2 carrots, chopped
* 2 celery stalks, chopped
* 1 teaspoon ground cumin
* 1 teaspoon dried thyme
* 1 bay leaf
* 4 cups vegetable broth
* 1 can (14.5 oz) diced tomatoes, drained
* 1 teaspoon smoked paprika (optional)
* Salt and pepper, to taste
* Fresh parsley, chopped (optional)

Instructions:

1. In a large pot or Dutch oven, heat the olive oil over medium heat. Add the onion, garlic, carrots, and celery, and cook until the vegetables are tender, about 8-10 minutes.
2. Add the cumin, thyme, and bay leaf, and cook for 1-2 minutes, stirring constantly.
3. Add the soaked and drained navy beans, vegetable broth, diced tomatoes, smoked paprika (if using), salt, and pepper. Stir to combine.
4. Bring the soup to a boil, then reduce the heat to low and simmer, covered, for 1-2 hours, or until the beans are tender.
5. Remove the bay leaf and season the soup with additional salt and pepper, if needed.
6. Serve the soup hot, garnished with chopped fresh parsley (if desired), and enjoy!

You can also make this soup in a slow cooker: Simply brown the vegetables and cook the soup on low for 6-8 hours.

I hope you enjoy this hearty navy bean soup!

prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Semantic-guided Encoder Feature Learning for Blurry Boundary Delineation".
text: In image segmentation, blurry boundary delineation is a usual challenge caused by the ambiguity of the images. In this paper, we propose a novel approach called semantic-guided encoder feature learning to address this issue. Our method involves training an encoder-decoder network with a semantic loss that guides the feature learning process towards more reliable segmentation outcomes. Specifically, we use a semantic consistency loss that measures the difference between the predicted semantic segmentation maps and the corresponding ground truth labels in the encoder network. The semantic consistency loss is combined with conventional losses such as cross-entropy to supervise the end-to-end training process of the encoder-decoder model. Our experiments demonstrate that our method can effectively improve the accuracy of semantic segmentation on images with blurry boundaries, while generating visually appealing results. Our approach makes semantic prior information available for image segmentation and provides a novel way to utilize this information to guide feature learning in encoder networks.

I hate romantic comedies. I detest them. You can list the actors I avoid watching: Hugh Grant, Sandra Bullock, Richard Gere, Julia Roberts. Romantic comedies make me cringe and I avoid them like the plague so you can imagine the foul mood I was in when I was forced to watch this film.

And the introductory voice-over by Hugh Grant as we watch an airport full of people hugging made me want to commit an act of violence - either against the people who forced me to watch this film or against myself just to end the torture.

Then the most unbelievably shocking thing happened. Bill Nighy and Gregor Fischer came on screen, mocking one of the most hated love songs in Britain, "Love is all Around" and I found myself getting sucked into the film.

By the time I reached the end of the film I found myself facing the impossible, there was one romantic comedy out there that genuinely is a comedy and actually likeable. No-one was more shocked than I.

Many different kinds of love are covered (although not all kinds), there's 8 storylines and the biggest cast list I've seen in a long time. Somehow, it works. You'd think it wouldn't, I know I certainly didn't.

If you're looking for a full-length story, this is not the film for you. It snap-shots the important events leading to the resolution of the couples involved, nothing more. If you want a classic romantic film, this might not be the film for you. This is funnier than most straight comedies I've seen in recent times, however (I'm just as harsh a critic of comedy films as I am of romantic films).

It's not trying to be the meaning of life, it's not trying to look at the big picture. In fact, it's only trying to do one thing, and that's say positive feelings crop up in the most unexpected places or are more prevalent than people think. One of the storylines, one that is cited constantly in reviews as one of the failed storylines with a sad ending is actually bittersweet. It doesn't end with failure but the failure of one type of love in favour of a different kind.

This film isn't perfect, I'll never find the perfect romantic-comedy because I hate the genre so much, for example, one of the storylines did annoy me intensely and yet ironically still made me laugh in places. However, the flaws in the film are vastly outweighed by positives. It's superficially complicated but is really a very simple film. It makes a statement: "love actually is all around" then shows why it makes that statement and doesn't attempt to do or be anything else.

We construct Hamiltonian Floer complexes associated to continuous, and even
lower semi-continuous, time dependent exhaustion functions on geometrically
bounded symplectic manifolds. We further construct functorial continuation maps
associated to monotone homotopies between them, and operations which give rise
to a product and unit. The work rests on novel techniques for energy
confinement of Floer solutions as well as on methods of Non-Archimedean
analysis. The definition for general Hamiltonians utilizes the notion of
reduced cohomology familiar from Riemannian geometry, and the continuity
properties of Floer cohomology. This gives rise in particular to localized
Floer theory. We discuss various functorial properties as well as some
applications to existence of periodic orbits and to displaceability.

We introduce a dynamic mechanism design problem in which the designer wants
to offer for sale an item to an agent, and another item to the same agent at
some point in the future. The agent's joint distribution of valuations for the
two items is known, and the agent knows the valuation for the current item (but
not for the one in the future). The designer seeks to maximize expected
revenue, and the auction must be deterministic, truthful, and ex post
individually rational. The optimum mechanism involves a protocol whereby the
seller elicits the buyer's current valuation, and based on the bid makes two
take-it-or-leave-it offers, one for now and one for the future. We show that
finding the optimum deterministic mechanism in this situation - arguably the
simplest meaningful dynamic mechanism design problem imaginable - is NP-hard.

environment in which contracts cannot be enforced, and thus perfection of
equilibrium is necessary, we show that the optimum randomized mechanism
requires multiple rounds of cheap talk-like interactions.

The CNN and LSTM networks are connected in a dual-modal fashion, allowing them to share information and work collaboratively to perform the segmentation task.

We evaluate the performance of DCLN on several benchmark datasets, including MS COCO and Flickr30k Entities. Our experimental results show that DCLN outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of segmentation accuracy and efficiency. We also perform a series of ablation studies to analyze the effectiveness of different components of the DCLN model, demonstrating the contributions of the CNN and LSTM networks to the overall performance.

The main contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows:

* We propose a novel Dual Convolutional LSTM Network (DCLN) for referring image segmentation that combines the strengths of CNNs and LSTMs.
* DCLN outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of segmentation accuracy and efficiency on several benchmark datasets.
* We perform ablation studies to analyze the effectiveness of different components of the DCLN model, providing insights into the role of each component in the segmentation task.

Overall, the proposed DCLN model offers a promising approach to referring image segmentation, and our findings have important implications for a wide range of applications, including image and video analysis, natural language processing, and human-computer interaction.

Ingredients:
- 4 boneless, skinless chicken breasts
- Salt and pepper, to taste
- 1/2 cup all-purpose flour
- 2 tablespoons olive oil
- 4 tablespoons butter
- 3 cloves garlic, minced
- 1 cup chicken broth
- 1/4 cup fresh lemon juice
- 1/4 cup capers, drained
- 1/4 cup fresh parsley, chopped

Instructions:

7. Return the chicken breasts to the skillet and simmer for an additional 2 minutes, until heated through and coated in the sauce.

prompt: Write a recipe for "Dry-Rubbed Roast Turkey ".
text:
Recipe for Dry-Rubbed Roast Turkey: 

Ingredients:

- One 10-12 lb. turkey
- 2 tbsp. olive oil
- 1 tbsp. salt
- 1 tbsp. black pepper
- 1 tbsp. paprika
- 2 tsp. dried thyme
- 2 tsp. garlic powder
- 1 tsp. onion powder
- 1/2 tsp. cayenne pepper
- Fresh herbs for garnish (e.g. rosemary, thyme, parsley)

Instructions:

1. Preheat your oven to 325°F (165°C). Remove the giblets and neck from the turkey. Rinse the turkey well, inside and out, under cold running water. Pat dry with paper towels.

2. Now, in a small bowl, combine the salt, pepper, paprika, dried thyme, garlic powder, onion powder, and cayenne pepper. Stir everything together until well-blended.

3. Rub the turkey all over with the olive oil. Make sure to coat it evenly, then rub the spice mixture all over the turkey, making sure to get some of the rub inside the cavity as well.

4. Place the turkey, breast-side up, on a rack in a roasting pan. Tie the legs together with cooking string, and cover the turkey loosely with an aluminum foil tent.

5. Roast the turkey in the preheated oven for 2.5-3 hours, or until the internal temperature of the thickest part of the thigh (not touching bone) reads 165°F (74°C).

6. Remove the turkey from the oven and allow it to rest for 20 minutes before carving. This will allow the juices to redistribute and make for easier carving.

7. Garnish your turkey with fresh herbs if you like, then carve and serve. Enjoy your Thanksgiving or Christmas feast with this flavorful, dry-rubbed roast turkey as the centrepiece!

Note: 
Cooking times may vary depending on the size of your turkey. A good rule of thumb is to cook your turkey 20 minutes per pound in a 325°F oven.

Monitor Proofing (also known as Soft Proofing) is a methodology in the printing and publishing industries used to review or preview how a design or print job would look like without physically printing it on paper or similar substrates. With monitor proofing, designers, pre-press professionals, and customers can view and approve prints on a computer monitor, overcoming the time, cost, and potential inaccuracies of hard copy proofing. 

Although it has considerable advantages, precise color matching between the screen and the final print product is often a challenge in monitor proofing, as monitors display colors using light (additive RGB color model) while printers reproduce colors by applying inks or pigments onto paper (subtractive CMYK color model). Thus, the visual representation on the screen might not translate exactly onto the paper.

== Process and Methodology ==

Monitor proofing starts with designing or scanning a document or image into a digital file using specific design software. The file is then opened on the computer screen for proofing. This digitized image displayed on the monitor serves as the soft proof. Prior to creating the soft proof, the monitor should ideally be calibrated to setting defined by the International Color Consortium (ICC) to ensure that the colors displayed are as close as possible to what the final printed product would look like. 

Once the soft proof is created, it can be reviewed by those responsible for approving the prints. Any necessary modifications can then be made directly on the digital file, eliminating wastage of paper and ink. 

== Advantages & Disadvantages ==

Monitor proofing offers several advantages. It reduces material waste and eliminates the shipping cost of sending physical proof copies. By converting the process into digital, it also speeds the review process since the digital proofs can be sent via email or can be viewed on a shared server instantly. 

However, the method also comes with potential drawbacks. Monitor proofing may not be entirely accurate due to differences in color calibration of different monitors. Also, the feel of the paper or the finished product's tactile quality can't be determined through monitor proofing.

Various technologies and standards aid in making monitor proofing more reliable. text:
Ingredients:
- 2 cups all-purpose flour
- 2 tablespoons granulated sugar
- 2 teaspoons baking powder
- ½ teaspoon salt
- 2 large eggs, separated
- 1 ¾ cups buttermilk
- 2 tablespoons unsalted butter, melted
- Cooking spray or additional butter for greasing the pan
- Your choice of fillings (such as jam, Nutella, chocolate chips, fruit, or cheese)
- Powdered sugar for dusting

Instructions:
1. In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, sugar, baking powder, and salt.

4. In another clean bowl, beat the egg whites using an electric mixer or whisk until stiff peaks form.
5. Gently fold the beaten egg whites into the batter until fully incorporated. This will help make the Ebelskivers light and fluffy.
6. Preheat an Ebelskiver pan on medium heat. If you don't have this specialized pan, you can use a mini muffin pan as a substitute.
7. Lightly grease the indentations of the pan with cooking spray or butter.
8. Fill each indentation of the pan about halfway with batter.
9. Add your desired filling to the center of each indentation, such as a teaspoon of jam, Nutella, chocolate chips, fruit, or cheese.
10. Spoon a little more batter on top to cover the filling and completely fill the indentation. The filling should be sealed inside the batter.
11. Cook the Ebelskivers for about 2-3 minutes, or until the bottom is golden brown and slightly crispy. Use a skewer or wooden chopstick to gently flip each Ebelskiver over.
12. Cook for an additional 2-3 minutes on the other side until golden brown and cooked through.
13. Transfer cooked Ebelskivers to a plate and repeat the process with the remaining batter and filling.
14. Dust the finished Ebelskivers with powdered sugar.
15. Serve the Danish Ebelskivers warm with your favorite dipping sauce, such as syrup, jam, or whipped cream.

The Wealden hall house is a type of vernacular medieval timber-framed hall house traditional in the south east of England. Typically built for a yeoman, it is most common in Kent (hence "Wealden" for the once densely forested  Weald) and the east of Sussex but has also been built elsewhere.  Kent has one of the highest concentrations of such surviving medieval timber-framed buildings in Europe. The original floor plan usually had four bays with the two central ones forming the main hall open to the roof with the hearth in the middle and two doors to the outside at one end forming a cross passage. The open hearth was later moved towards the cross passage and became a fireplace with chimney, sometimes the chimney pile even blocking the cross passage, which had soon been screened off the main hall. Beyond the cross passage the outer bay at the "screens end" or "lower end" of the hall, usually contained two rooms commonly called buttery and pantry, while the rooms in the bay at the other end, the "upper end", were called parlours. The end bays each had an upper floor containing solars, which did not communicate with each other, as the hall rose to the rafters between them. The upper stories on both ends typically extended beyond the lower outer wall being jettied on at least one side of the building. As the main hall had no upper floor the outer wall ran straight up without jettying, and thus the central bays appeared recessed. 
The early buildings had  thatched roofs and walls of wattle and daub often whitewashed. Later buildings would have a brick infilling between timbers, sometimes leading to a complete replacement of the outer walls of the basement with solid stone walls.

Ingredients:
- 1 cup granulated sugar
- 1/4 cup unsalted butter, cut into small pieces
- 1/3 cup fresh lemon juice
- 2 large eggs
- 1 large egg yolk
- 1 tablespoon lemon zest
- 1 teaspoon finely grated ginger
- Pinch of salt

Instructions:
1. In a medium-sized saucepan, combine the granulated sugar, lemon juice, lemon zest, and ginger.
2. Heat the mixture over medium heat, stirring constantly until the sugar has dissolved.
3. Reduce the heat to a whisker, and cook for a further 2-3 minutes, stirring as you go.
4. In a separate bowl, whisk together the eggs and egg yolk.
5. Slowly pour the lemon mixture into the eggs, whisking as you go.
6. Return the mixture to the saucepan, and cook over medium heat, stirring constantly for 5-8 minutes, or until the curd thickens.
7. Remove the saucepan from heat, and pour the curd into an airtight container.
8. Allow the curd to cool to room temperature before storing it in the refrigerator.
9. Curd will thicken as it cools, and it will keep in the refrigerator for up to 2 weeks.

Enjoy your homemade lemon curd with your favorite tea, on toast or with any of your favorite sweets.

text:
Ingredients:

For Maple-Brined Pork Roast:
- 1 boneless pork roast (about 4 lbs)
- 1 cup pure maple syrup
- 1/2 cup kosher salt
- 2 quarts water
- 1 tablespoon whole black peppercorns
- 1 tablespoon mustard seeds
- 5 cloves garlic, peeled
- 2 bay leaves

For Apples, Onions and Mustard Breadcrumbs:
- 2 large yellow onions, peeled and quartered
- 3 large apples, cored and quartered
- 2 tablespoons butter, melted
- Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper 
- 1 cup breadcrumbs
- 2 tablespoons whole grain mustard

Instructions:

1. Prepare the brine. Warm 1 quart of water, maple syrup, and salt in a large pot over medium-low heat. Stir until the salt is dissolved.

2. Remove from the heat and add the remaining water to cool down the brine. Add the peppercorns, mustard seeds, garlic, and bay leaves.

3. Once the brine has cooled, submerge the pork roast into the brine. Make sure it is fully covered with the brine before refrigerating. Brine the pork for 24 hours.

4. After 24 hours, remove the pork from the brine and dry it thoroughly. Allow the meat to come to room temperature for about 30 minutes.

5. Preheat your oven to 375 degrees F.

6. While the oven is preheating, arrange the onions and apples around the roast. Drizzle with the melted butter and sprinkle with salt and pepper.

7. Place the pork roast, onions, and apples on a roasting pan. Roast for about 1 hour and 30 minutes or until the internal temperature reaches 145 degrees F.

8. While the roast is in the oven, prepare the mustard breadcrumbs. Mix the breadcrumbs with the whole grain mustard in a small bowl. Set aside.

9. When the roast has reached its desired temperature, remove it from the oven and sprinkle the mustard breadcrumbs over top. Let the roast rest for 15 minutes before slicing.

10. Serve slices of the roast with the caramelized apples and onions.

- Salt and pepper to taste

- 1 French baguette

5. Remove the sardines from the oven and let them rest for a few minutes.

In this paper, we investigate the relationship between Petersen cores and the oddness of cubic graphs. A graph is called cubic if all its vertices have degree three. A graph is said to have a Petersen core if it contains a subgraph that is homeomorphic to the Petersen graph, which is a well-known graph with ten vertices and 15 edges that cannot be drawn in a plane without edge crossings.

We prove that every cubic graph with an odd number of vertices has a Petersen core. This result provides a new characterization of cubic graphs that are not planar, as it is well-known that a graph is planar if and only if it does not have a subgraph homeomorphic to the Petersen graph.

We also show that the converse of our result is not true, i.e., there exist non-cubic graphs that have a Petersen core. Moreover, we prove that there are infinitely many cubic graphs that have a Petersen core, and that there are cubic graphs with arbitrarily large Petersen cores.

Our results provide new insights into the structure of cubic graphs, and demonstrate the importance of the Petersen graph in the study of graph theory. They also have implications for the study of other graph families, such as snarks and non-planar graphs.

Ingredients:
- 2 and 1/4 cups cake flour
- 1 and 1/2 cups granulated sugar
- 1 tablespoon baking powder
- 1/2 teaspoon salt
- 1/2 cup vegetable oil
- 6 large egg yolks
- 3/4 cup water
- 2 teaspoons vanilla extract
- 1 teaspoon cream of tartar
- 6 large egg whites
- 1/2 cup granulated sugar

Instructions:
1. Preheat your oven to 325°F (165°C). Prepare an ungreased tube pan.

2. In a large mixing bowl, sift together the cake flour, 1 and 1/2 cups granulated sugar, baking powder, and salt. Set aside.

3. In another mixing bowl, whisk together the vegetable oil, egg yolks, water, and vanilla extract until well combined.

4. Make a well in the center of the dry ingredients and pour in the wet ingredients. Mix until smooth and well combined. Set aside.

5. In a separate bowl, beat the egg whites until frothy using an electric mixer. Add the cream of tartar and continue beating until soft peaks form.

6. Gradually add the remaining 1/2 cup of granulated sugar to the egg whites while beating, until stiff peaks form.

7. Gently fold the beaten egg whites into the cake batter using a spatula. Make sure to incorporate the egg whites thoroughly, but be careful not to overmix and deflate the batter.

8. Pour the batter into the prepared tube pan and gently smooth the top with a spatula.

9. Bake in the preheated oven for approximately 55-60 minutes, or until a toothpick inserted into the center comes out clean.

10. Once baked, remove the cake from the oven and invert the pan onto a wire rack. Allow the cake to cool completely while remaining in the inverted position.

11. Once the cake has cooled, gently loosen the edges from the pan using a knife or spatula, and remove the cake from the pan.

12. Slice and serve the vanilla chiffon cake as desired. It can be enjoyed on its own or with a dusting of powdered sugar, fresh berries, or a light glaze. Enjoy!

Ingredients for Dough:

- 500g wholemeal flour

- 25g salt

- 700ml of warm water 

Ingredients for Topping:

- A handful of pumpkin seeds 

Instructions:

2. In a separate bowl, dissolve the yeast in the warm water. Allow it to sit for a few minutes until it begins to froth. 

3. Gradually add the yeast mixture into the flour mixture. Stir until a rough dough forms. 

4. Transfer the dough onto a floured surface. Knead the dough for about 10 minutes or until smooth and elastic. Add more flour if the dough is too sticky. 

5. Place the dough in a greased bowl, cover with a damp cloth, and leave it to rise in a warm place for about 1 hour or until it doubles in size.

6. Preheat the oven to 220°C (430°F) and dust a baking tray with flour.

7. After the dough has risen, knock it back and shape into a round or oval form. Place it on the baking tray. 

8. Sprinkle the flax seeds, sunflower seeds, and pumpkin seeds on top of the dough and gently press them in.

9. Allow the dough to prove for another 30 minutes, or until it doubles in size again.

10. Bake in the preheated oven for around 30-35 minutes or until the bread makes a hollow sound when tapped at the bottom.

11. Remove the bread from the oven and leave it to cool on a wire rack.

Encoder-decoder architectures are widely adopted for medical image
segmentation tasks. With the lateral skip connection, the models can obtain and
fuse both semantic and resolution information in deep layers to achieve more
accurate segmentation performance. However, in many applications (e.g., blurry
boundary images), these models often cannot precisely locate complex boundaries

analyze why simple skip connections are not enough to help accurately locate
indistinct boundaries and argue that it is due to the fuzzy information in the
skip connection provided in the encoder layers. Then we propose a
semantic-guided encoder feature learning strategy to learn both high resolution
and rich semantic encoder features so that we can more accurately locate the
blurry boundaries, which can also enhance the network by selectively learning
discriminative features. Besides, we further propose a soft contour constraint
mechanism to model the blurry boundary detection. Experimental results on real
clinical datasets show that our proposed method can achieve state-of-the-art
segmentation accuracy, especially for the blurry regions. Further analysis also
indicates that our proposed network components indeed contribute to the
improvement of performance. Experiments on additional datasets validate the
generalization ability of our proposed method.

A system to make it easier to create website addresses using alphabets like Cyrillic could open a back door for scammers, a trade body has warned.
The Internationalised Domain Names system has been a work in progress for years and has recently been approved by the Internet Electronic Task Force. But the UK Internet Forum (UKIF) is concerned that the system will let scammers create fake sites more easily. The problem lies in the computer codes used to represent language.
Registering names that look like that of legitimate companies but lead users to fake sites designed to steal passwords and credit card details could become a whole lot easier for determined scammers, says Stephen Dyer, director of UKIF. Domain names are the "real language" addresses of websites, rather than their internet protocol address, which is a series of numbers. They are used so people can more easily navigate the web. So-called ASCII codes are used to represent European languages but for other languages a hybrid of a system called Unicode is used. So, for example, website PayPal could now be coded using a mixture of the Latin alphabet and the Russian alphabet. The resulting domain as displayed to the users would look identical to the real site as a Russian 'a' look just like an English 'a'. But the computer code would be different, and the site it would lead users to could be a fake. This is more than just a theory. A fake Paypal.com has already been registered with net domain giant Verisign by someone who has followed the debate around the Internationalised Domain Name (IDN) system, said Mr Dyer. As the idea was to prove a point rather than be malicious the fake domain has now been handed back to Paypal but it sets a worrying precedent, Mr Dyer said. "Although the IDN problem is well known in technical circles, the commercial world is totally unaware how easily their websites can be faked," said Mr Dyer.
"It is important to alert users that there is a new and invisible and almost undetectable way of diverting them to what looks like a perfectly genuine site," he added. There are solutions. For instance, browsers could spot domains that use mixed characters and display them in different colours as a warning to users. Mr Dyer acknowledged that it would be a huge undertaking to update all the world's browsers. Another solution, to introduce IDN-disabled browsers could be a case of "throwing out the baby with the bath water," he said. CENTR, the Council of European National Top Level Domain Registries, agrees. "A rush to introduce IDN-disabled browsers into the marketplace is an overly-zealous step that will harm public confidence in IDNs - a technology that is desperately needed in the non-English speaking world," the organisation said in a statement.

Weakly supervised segmentation is a powerful technique for automatically segmenting images with minimal labeling. In this paper, we propose a novel framework for weakly supervised segmentation using a deep geodesic prior. Our method leverages the geodesic distance between segmentation masks to guide the segmentation process and reduce the requirements for labeled data. We develop a fast method for optimally designing experiments in the context
of statistical seismic source inversion. In particular, we efficiently compute
the optimal number and locations of the receivers or seismographs. The seismic
source is modeled by a point moment tensor multiplied by a time-dependent
function. The parameters include the source location, moment tensor components,
and start time and frequency in the time function. The forward problem is
modeled by elastodynamic wave equations. We show that the Hessian of the cost
functional, which is usually defined as the square of the weighted L2 norm of
the difference between the experimental data and the simulated data, is
proportional to the measurement time and the number of receivers. Consequently,
the posterior distribution of the parameters, in a Bayesian setting,
concentrates around the "true" parameters, and we can employ Laplace
approximation and speed up the estimation of the expected Kullback-Leibler
divergence (expected information gain), the optimality criterion in the
experimental design procedure. Since the source parameters span several
magnitudes, we use a scaling matrix for efficient control of the condition
number of the original Hessian matrix. We use a second-order accurate finite
difference method to compute the Hessian matrix and either sparse quadrature or
Monte Carlo sampling to carry out numerical integration. We demonstrate the
efficiency, accuracy, and applicability of our method on a two-dimensional
seismic source inversion problem.

Preheat oven to 350°F. Line a 9-by-13-inch baking pan on bottom and 2 long sides with a sheet of heavy-duty aluminum foil, making sure that foil is smooth and overhangs top of pan by at least 4 inches on both sides. Mist foil with cooking spray. Make crust: Combine flour, confectioners' sugar and salt in a food processor and pulse once or twice. Bake crust until it looks dry, 18 to 20 minutes. Place on a wire rack. Make filling: Reduce oven temperature to 325°F. Combine honey, brown sugar and salt in a saucepan and bring to a simmer over medium heat, stirring to dissolve sugar. Reduce heat and simmer for 2 minutes without stirring. Add butter and cream and simmer, stirring constantly, for 1 minute. Remove from heat; stir in pecans. Pour hot filling evenly over crust. Use back of a spoon to distribute nuts evenly. Return pan to oven and bake until filling is bubbling and slightly browned, 18 to 20 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and cool completely. Run a small knife between pan and pastry on sides without foil. Lift foil from pan onto a cutting board and use a serrated knife to cut into 30 diamonds.

prompt: Write a recipe for "Steak Cobb Salad With Dijon Vinaigrette".
text:
Steak Cobb Salad With Dijon Vinaigrette Recipe:

Ingredients:

For the Salad:
- 1 pound steak (such as sirloin, ribeye, or flank steak)
- Salt and pepper to taste
- 4 cups mixed salad greens
- 4 slices cooked bacon, chopped
- 2 hard-boiled eggs, sliced
- 1 cup cherry tomatoes, halved
- 1 avocado, sliced
- 1/2 cup crumbled blue cheese
- 1/4 cup red onion, thinly sliced

For the Dijon Vinaigrette:
- 1/4 cup extra-virgin olive oil
- 2 tablespoons red wine vinegar
- 1 tablespoon Dijon mustard
- 1 garlic clove, minced
- Salt and pepper to taste

Instructions:

1. Season the steak generously with salt and pepper on both sides. Heat a grill or grill pan over medium-high heat. Cook the steak for about 4-5 minutes per side for medium-rare or until desired doneness. Remove the steak from the grill and let it rest for 5 minutes before slicing into thin strips.

2. In a large salad bowl, combine the mixed salad greens, chopped bacon, sliced hard-boiled eggs, cherry tomatoes, avocado, crumbled blue cheese, and red onion. Toss gently to combine.

3. In a small bowl, whisk together the olive oil, red wine vinegar, Dijon mustard, minced garlic, salt, and pepper until well combined. Adjust the seasoning to taste.

4. Add the sliced steak to the salad bowl and drizzle the Dijon vinaigrette over the top. Toss gently to coat all the ingredients with the dressing.

5. Divide the salad among plates or bowls and serve immediately.

Enjoy the delicious Steak Cobb Salad with Dijon Vinaigrette as a satisfying and nutritious meal!

There is no denying that gigapixel images are becoming increasingly popular and captivating in the world of photography. These incredibly high-resolution images, made up of billions of pixels, allow viewers to zoom in and explore intricate details that would usually be missed with a standard photograph. So, how exactly does one go about creating a gigapixel picture?

The process of making a gigapixel picture involves several key steps, starting with choosing the right equipment. A high-resolution digital camera is essential, preferably one with a large image sensor and high megapixel count. Additionally, a stable tripod is crucial to avoid camera shake and ensure the final image is crisp.

Before capturing the actual image, it is essential to plan your shot carefully. Consider the scene you want to capture and find a vantage point that allows for maximum detail. It's helpful to scout the location in advance and determine the best time of day for optimal lighting conditions.

Once on location, it's time to set up the camera and tripod. Use manual exposure mode to control the settings and ensure consistency throughout the multiple shots needed for a gigapixel image. Additionally, using a remote shutter release or timer can prevent any accidental shaking of the camera during exposure.

To capture the gigapixel image, it's necessary to take multiple shots, overlapping each other by approximately 20-30%. This overlap is crucial for software to stitch the individual images together seamlessly later on. It's also advised to use a technique called bracketing, where multiple exposures at different settings are taken, to ensure a well-exposed image throughout.

After capturing the necessary images, it's time to process them using specialized software. There are many options available, ranging from free to professional-grade programs. These software tools employ advanced algorithms to align and blend the multiple images, creating a single gigapixel image.

The final step in creating a gigapixel picture is post-processing. This involves fine-tuning the image's colors, sharpness, and contrast to enhance its overall appearance. It's essential to strike a balance between enhancing the details without overdoing the editing, ensuring the final result looks realistic and captivating.

In conclusion, creating a gigapixel picture requires careful planning, the right equipment, and technical know-how. By following these steps, photographers can capture stunningly detailed and immersive images that captivate viewers and showcase the world in a new light.

prompt: Write a recipe for "Baked Alaska Peanut S'mores".
text:
Ingredients:
- 1 1/2 cups crushed peanut graham crackers 
- 1/2 cup melted unsalted butter 
- 1/2 cup peanut butter 
- 1 1/2 cups mini marshmallows 
- 1 pint vanilla ice cream 
- 4 large egg whites 
- 1/2 teaspoon cream of tartar 
- 1/2 cup granulated sugar 

Instructions:

1. Preheat your oven to 350°F (175°C). 
2. In a medium bowl, mix together the crushed peanut graham crackers and melted butter until well combined. Press the mixture into the bottom of a 9-inch round baking dish to create the crust. 
3. Bake the crust in the preheated oven for 8-10 minutes, or until golden brown. Remove from the oven and let cool completely. 
4. Spread the peanut butter evenly over the cooled crust. 
5. Sprinkle the mini marshmallows on top of the peanut butter layer, covering it completely. 
6. Soften the vanilla ice cream by letting it sit at room temperature for a few minutes. Spread the ice cream over the marshmallow layer, ensuring it's spread evenly. Place the dish in the freezer to freeze until solid, at least 2-3 hours or overnight. 
7. In a medium bowl, beat the egg whites and cream of tartar together until frothy. Gradually add in the sugar while continuing to beat the mixture until stiff peaks form. 
8. Preheat your oven to the highest broil setting. 
9. Remove the dish from the freezer and quickly spread the egg white mixture over the frozen ice cream, covering it completely and ensuring that no ice cream or marshmallow layer is exposed. 
10. Place the dish under the broiler for 2-3 minutes, or until the meringue is golden brown and toasted. Keep a close eye on it to prevent burning. 
11. Remove from the oven and let cool for a few minutes before serving. 
12. Enjoy your Baked Alaska Peanut S'mores by cutting it into slices and serving immediately. The combination of the toasted meringue, creamy ice cream, gooey marshmallows, and peanut butter crust will surely be a hit!

prompt: Write a recipe for "Christmas Turkey Quiche".
text:
Ingredients:

- 1 pre-made pie crust
- 2 cups of leftover cooked turkey, chopped
- 1 cup of swiss cheese, shredded
- 1/2 cup of red bell pepper, chopped
- 1/2 cup of green bell pepper, chopped
- 4 large eggs
- 1 cup of heavy cream
- 1/2 teaspoon of salt
- 1/4 teaspoon of black pepper
- 1/2 teaspoon of dried thyme leaves
- 1/4 teaspoon of nutmeg
- 1 tablespoon of chopped fresh parsley

Instructions:

1. Preheat your oven to 375°F (190°C). Place the pie crust in a 9-inch pie dish and set aside.

2. In a skillet, cook the chopped red and green bell pepper over medium heat for about 5 minutes, just until they begin to soften. Remove from heat and set aside.

3. Sprinkle the bottom of the pie crust evenly with the chopped turkey. On top of the turkey, add the cooked bell peppers and shredded swiss cheese.

4. In a medium-sized bowl, beat together the eggs, heavy cream, salt, pepper, thyme, and nutmeg until well mixed.

5. Carefully pour the egg mixture over the turkey, peppers, and cheese in the pie crust. Try to distribute it evenly.

6. Place the quiche onto a baking sheet (this makes it easier to move in and out of the oven). Bake in the preheated oven for about 40-45 minutes, or until the quiche is set and lightly golden brown on top.

7. Remove the quiche from the oven and let it sit for about 5 minutes before cutting into it. This allows it to set up a bit more.

8. Sprinkle with fresh chopped parsley right before serving. This Christmas Turkey Quiche is the perfect way to use up leftover turkey, and it can be enjoyed for breakfast, lunch, or dinner.

Notes: You can add additional vegetables or spices according to your preference. Like onions, mushrooms, or garlic would also work well in this quiche. You could also substitute the swiss cheese with any favorite cheese you prefer. Enjoy!

text:
Ingredients:

- 1 butternut squash
- 1 tablespoon olive oil
- 1 small onion, diced
- 2 cloves garlic, minced
- 1 cup Arborio rice
- 1/2 cup white wine
- 3 cups vegetable broth
- 1 cup cooked shrimp, peeled and deveined
- 1 cup frozen peas
- Salt and pepper to taste
- Parmesan cheese, grated (optional)
- Fresh parsley, chopped (for garnish)

Instructions:

1. Cut the butternut squash in half lengthwise. Scoop out the seeds and discard. Place the squash cut side down on a baking sheet and roast in a preheated oven at 400°F (200°C) for about 40-50 minutes, or until the flesh is soft.

2. Once the squash is cool enough to handle, use a fork to scrape out the flesh into "rice-like" pieces. Set aside.

3. In a large skillet, heat the olive oil over medium heat. Add the diced onion and minced garlic and cook until the onion is translucent and fragrant.

4. Add the Arborio rice to the skillet and stir to coat it with the oil. Cook for a few more minutes until the rice starts to toast slightly.

5. Pour in the white wine and cook until it is mostly absorbed by the rice.

6. Slowly add the vegetable broth, about 1/2 cup at a time, stirring continuously until each addition is absorbed. Repeat this process until the rice is cooked through, tender but still firm to the bite. This should take about 20-25 minutes.

7. Once the rice is cooked, add the cooked shrimp and frozen peas to the skillet. Stir everything together and cook for a few more minutes until the shrimp is heated through and the peas are tender.

8. Season with salt and pepper to taste.

9. Remove the skillet from the heat and stir in the butternut squash "rice". Mix everything together until well combined.

10. Serve the risotto hot, garnished with grated Parmesan cheese if desired and fresh chopped parsley. Enjoy!

prompt: Write a recipe for "Moroccan-Style Preserved Lemons".
text:
Moroccan-Style Preserved Lemons

Ingredients:
- 4-5 lemons
- 1/4 cup sea salt
- 1 tablespoon whole peppercorns
- 1 cinnamon stick
- 4-6 cloves
- 4-6 bay leaves
- Extra lemon juice, if needed
- Sterilized glass jar

Instructions:
1. Start by washing the lemons thoroughly under cold water. Dry them completely using a clean kitchen towel.
2. Cut off the tops and bottoms of the lemons, then cut each lemon into quarters, leaving them attached at the base.
3. Sprinkle sea salt generously over the insides of the lemons.
4. Take a sterilized glass jar and place a tablespoon of sea salt at the bottom.
5. Place a layer of the salted lemons in the jar, adding in a few whole peppercorns, a small piece of cinnamon stick, 1-2 cloves, and 1-2 bay leaves between each lemon layer.
6. Continue layering the lemons and spices until you have filled the jar, making sure to press them down firmly so they release their juices. The juice should cover the lemons completely.
7. If the juice is not sufficient to cover the lemons, squeeze extra lemon juice to cover them.
8. Seal the jar tightly and leave it in a cool, dark place for about 3-4 weeks. The lemons need time to ferment and develop their unique flavor.
9. Shake the jar gently every few days to ensure the salt and spices are distributed evenly.
10. After the initial fermentation period, transfer the jar to the refrigerator for at least 1 month before using the preserved lemons.
11. When using the preserved lemons, rinse them under cold water to remove excess salt before chopping or slicing. The peel is the part most commonly used, as it is soft and infused with flavor.
12. Enjoy your homemade Moroccan-style preserved lemons in tagines, salads, couscous, or as a flavorful addition to any dish that could benefit from a burst of citrusy tanginess.

Note: Preserved lemons can be stored in the refrigerator for up to 6-12 months. Make sure to check for any signs of mold or spoilage before using.

prompt: Write a recipe for "Strawberry Soup With Honey Ice Cream".
text:
Strawberry Soup with Honey Ice Cream Recipe

Ingredients:
- 2 pounds of fresh strawberries
- 1 cup of water
- 1/2 cup of granulated sugar
- 1 tablespoon of lemon juice
- 1/2 cup of heavy cream
- 1/4 cup of honey
- Mint leaves for garnish

Instructions:

1. Wash and remove the stems from the strawberries. Cut them into halves or quarters, depending on their size.
2. In a medium-sized saucepan, combine the strawberries, water, granulated sugar, and lemon juice. Bring the mixture to a boil over medium heat.
3. Reduce the heat to low and let the strawberries simmer for approximately 10 minutes. Stir occasionally until the strawberries are soft and the liquid has thickened slightly.
4. Remove the saucepan from heat and let the mixture cool for a few minutes.
5. Using a blender or immersion blender, puree the strawberry mixture until smooth. Strain the mixture through a fine-mesh sieve to remove any seeds.
6. Refrigerate the strawberry soup until it is completely cold, for about 2 hours.
7. In a separate bowl, whisk the heavy cream until soft peaks form. Gradually add the honey, continuing to whisk until the mixture thickens and forms stiff peaks.
8. Transfer the honey ice cream mixture to an airtight container and freeze for at least 2 hours or until it hardens.
9. When ready to serve, ladle the chilled strawberry soup into bowls or glasses. Add a scoop of honey ice cream to each serving and garnish with mint leaves.
10. Serve immediately and enjoy the refreshing and delicious Strawberry Soup with Honey Ice Cream.

Note: This recipe yields approximately 4 servings. Adjust the quantities as needed for larger or smaller portions.

Floer theory and reduced cohomology on open manifolds is a new approach to studying complex geometric structures on open manifolds. It is based on the theory of Floer cycles, which are elements of a group that are defined in terms of critical points of a Morse function on a manifold. The theory of Floer cycles is closely related to the theory of reduced homology, which is a generalization of the classical homology theory to non-compact manifolds.

In this paper, we develop and apply the theory of Floer cycles and reduced homology to open manifolds. We introduce the concept of a Floer cycle class and the notion of a Reduced Floer cycle which is a class in Reduced homology. We also prove a homotopy invariance result for the Floer cycle class which is useful for reducing the problem of computing Floer cycle classes.

We apply the theory to constructing complex structures on open manifolds and characterizing their reduced cohomology. We also study the existence and uniqueness of certain types of complex structures on open manifolds using Floer theory and reduced cohomology.

Title: Plum and Mascarpone Pie 

Preparation Time: 30 minutes

Cook Time: 50 minutes 

Total Time: 1 hour 20 minutes 

Serving: 8 persons

Ingredients:

1. 1 pie crust (store bought or homemade)
2. 4-5 ripe plums, pitted and thinly sliced
3. 1 cup of mascarpone cheese
4. 1/2 cup of granulated sugar
5. 3 large eggs
6. 1 teaspoon vanilla extract
7. 2 tablespoons all-purpose flour
8. 1/4 teaspoon of salt
9. Powdered sugar, for topping

Instructions:

3. In a medium-sized bowl, add the mascarpone cheese, sugar, eggs, vanilla extract, all-purpose flour, and salt. Mix those all together until you get a smooth and creamy consistency.

4. Pour the mascarpone mixture over the layer of plums. Make sure it covers all the plums. Don’t worry if some of the plums are sticking out, they will sink slightly while cooking.

5. Bake the pie on the middle rack of the preheated oven for about 50 minutes or until the pie is golden brown and set but still slightly jiggly in the center.

6. Once done, remove the pie from the oven and let it cool on a wire rack for at least 2 hours before serving. This allows the filling to set.

7. Dust the pie with powdered sugar before serving for added sweetness and allure.

Computer vision tasks such as semantic segmentation perform very well in good
weather conditions, but if the weather turns bad, they have problems to achieve
this performance in these conditions. One possibility to obtain more robust and
reliable results in adverse weather conditions is to use video-segmentation
approaches instead of commonly used single-image segmentation methods.
Video-segmentation approaches capture temporal information of the previous
video-frames in addition to current image information, and hence, they are more
robust against disturbances, especially if they occur in only a few frames of
the video-sequence. However, video-segmentation approaches, which are often
based on recurrent neural networks, cannot be applied in real-time applications
anymore, since their recurrent structures in the network are computational
expensive. For instance, the inference time of the LSTM-ICNet, in which
recurrent units are placed at proper positions in the single-segmentation
approach ICNet, increases up to 61 percent compared to the basic ICNet. Hence,
in this work, the LSTM-ICNet is sped up by modifying the recurrent units of the
network so that it becomes real-time capable again. Experiments on different
datasets and various weather conditions show that the inference time can be
decreased by about 23 percent by these modifications, while they achieve
similar performance than the LSTM-ICNet and outperform the single-segmentation
approach enormously in adverse weather conditions.

Ingredients:

For the Crust and Crumb Topping
- 2 cups all-purpose flour
- 1/2 cup granulated sugar
- Zest of 1 large orange
- 1/2 teaspoon baking powder
- 1/2 teaspoon salt
- 1 cup (2 sticks) unsalted butter, cut into cubes and chilled
- 1 large egg
- 1 teaspoon vanilla extract

For the Filling
- 12 oz fresh cranberries
- 1/2 cup granulated sugar
- Juice of 1 large orange
- 1 tablespoon cornstarch
- A pinch of salt

Instructions:

1. Preheat your oven to 375 degrees F (190 degrees C). Grease a 9-inch tart pan.

2. Start by making the crust and the topping. In a large bowl, mix together the flour, sugar, orange zest, baking powder, and salt. 

3. Add the chilled butter to this mixture. Use your hands or a pastry cutter to cut the butter into the flour until small pea-sized crumbs form.

4. In a separate bowl, beat the egg with the vanilla extract. Pour this into the flour and butter mixture. Stir until the dough comes together.

5. Press about two-thirds of the dough into the bottom of the greased tart pan. Be sure to cover the bottom completely and to press the dough up the sides of the pan as well. The remaining dough will be used for the topping, so place it in the fridge for now.

6. Bake the crust for about 10-12 minutes or until it is lightly golden.

7. While the crust is baking, prepare the filling. In a saucepan, combine the cranberries, sugar, orange juice, cornstarch, and salt. Cook over medium heat until the berries pop open and the mixture thickens. This will take about 10 minutes. 

8. Pour the hot cranberry filling into the pre-baked crust. Crumble the remaining chilled dough over top.

9. Bake the tart for another 20-25 minutes, or until the crumb topping is golden and the filling is bubbling.

10. Allow the tart to cool before serving. If desired, garnish with additional orange zest or a dusting of powdered sugar. Your Cranberry-Orange Crumb Tart is ready to be enjoyed!

Mr Negroponte said this was a not for profit venture, though he recognised that the manufacturers of the components would be making money. In 1995 Mr Negroponte published the bestselling Being Digital, now widely seen as predicting the digital age. The concept is based on experiments in the US state of Maine, where children were given laptop computers to take home and do their work on.
While the idea was popular amongst the children, it initially received some resistance from the teachers and there were problems with laptops getting broken. - 1 red bell pepper, sliced

- 1 green bell pepper, sliced

Blue-Cheese-Crusted Steaks with Red Wine Sauce

Ingredients:
- 4 boneless ribeye steaks, about 1-inch thick
- 1 cup blue cheese crumbles
- 1/4 cup bread crumbs
- 2 tablespoons chopped fresh parsley
- Salt and pepper to taste
- 2 tablespoons olive oil

For the Red Wine Sauce:
- 1 cup red wine
- 1 cup beef broth
- 1 tablespoon butter
- 1 tablespoon all-purpose flour
- Salt and pepper to taste

Instructions:
1. Preheat the oven to 400°F (200°C).

2. In a small bowl, combine the blue cheese crumbles, bread crumbs, chopped parsley, salt, and pepper. Mix well.

3. Pat dry the steaks with a paper towel. Season both sides of the steaks with salt and pepper.

4. Heat the olive oil in an oven-safe skillet over medium-high heat. Once the skillet is hot, add the steaks and sear for about 2-3 minutes on each side until browned.

5. Remove the skillet from heat and divide the blue cheese mixture evenly among the tops of the steaks, pressing it gently.

6. Place the skillet with the steaks in the preheated oven and cook for about 6-8 minutes for medium-rare steaks, or until desired doneness is reached.

7. While the steaks are cooking, prepare the red wine sauce. In a saucepan, heat the red wine and beef broth over medium heat. Allow the mixture to simmer and reduce by half, about 10-15 minutes.

8. In a separate small saucepan, melt the butter over medium heat. Stir in the flour and cook for about 1-2 minutes, stirring constantly, until the mixture becomes lightly golden.

9. Gradually whisk in the reduced red wine mixture into the flour and butter mixture until smooth. Cook for an additional 2-3 minutes, stirring constantly, until the sauce thickens. Season with salt and pepper to taste.

10. Once the steaks are done, remove them from the oven and let them rest for a few minutes.

8. Truss the chicken by tying the legs together and tucking the wing tips under. Here's a helpful video on how to truss a chicken.
9. Place the chicken on a rack in a roasting pan and roast in the oven for approximately 60-70 minutes, or until the juices run clear when you cut between a leg and thigh.
10. Check the chicken after 45 minutes. If you see that the skin is getting too brown, cover the chicken with aluminum foil and continue to roast.
11. Once the chicken is done, remove it from the oven and let it rest for 15 minutes before carving. This will ensure that the juices are evenly distributed and the chicken will be moist and tender.

text:
Recipe: Potato-Stuffed Grilled Bell Peppers

Ingredients:
- 4 medium-sized bell peppers (any color)
- 4 medium-sized potatoes, peeled and diced
- 1 small onion, finely chopped
- 2 cloves of garlic, minced
- 1/2 cup shredded cheddar cheese
- 2 tablespoons olive oil
- 1 teaspoon dried oregano
- 1 teaspoon dried thyme
- Salt and pepper, to taste

Instructions:

1. Preheat your grill to medium-high heat.

2. Cut off the tops of the bell peppers, remove the seeds and white pith, and set aside. Make sure the peppers can stand upright without tipping over.

3. In a large pot, boil the diced potatoes until tender, around 10 minutes. Drain and set aside.

4. In a medium-sized skillet, heat the olive oil over medium heat. Add the chopped onion and minced garlic, and cook until softened and fragrant, around 3-4 minutes.

5. Add the boiled potatoes to the skillet with the onion and garlic mixture. Mash the potatoes with a fork or a potato masher, leaving some chunks for texture.

6. Stir in the dried oregano, dried thyme, shredded cheddar cheese, salt, and pepper into the potato mixture until well combined.

7. Stuff each bell pepper with the potato mixture, filling it to the top but not overpacking it.

8. Place the stuffed peppers on the preheated grill and cook for 10-15 minutes, or until the peppers are charred and tender.

9. Carefully remove the peppers from the grill using tongs or a spatula and let them cool slightly before serving.

10. Serve the potato-stuffed grilled bell peppers as a delicious side dish or main course. Enjoy!

Note: You can add other ingredients to the potato mixture, such as cooked bacon, cooked ground meat, or vegetables, according to your taste and preference.

- 1/3 cup kosher salt

Instructions:

1. Pat dry the turkey with kitchen paper towels.

3. Place the turkey on a tray or large dish and cover loosely with a plastic wrap. Refrigerate for at least 24 - 48 hours for the salt to penetrate and season the meat. This process is called dry-brining.

8. Place the turkey on a rack in a large roasting pan, breast side up.

9. Cook for about 2.5 - 3 hours. The actual roasting time depends on the size of the turkey. The turkey is done when a meat thermometer inserted in the thickest part of the thigh (without touching the bone) reads 165°F (74°C).

10. When the turkey is done, remove it from the oven and let it rest for at least 20 minutes before carving. This allows the juices to redistribute throughout the turkey, resulting in a more moist and flavorful bird.

We evaluate Vessel-CAPTCHA on a dataset of retinal fundus images and achieve superior performance compared to state-of-the-art vessel segmentation methods. We present a method for segmenting neuron membranes in 2D electron microscopy
imagery. This segmentation task has been a bottleneck to reconstruction efforts
of the brain's synaptic circuits. One common problem is the misclassification
of blurry membrane fragments as cell interior, which leads to merging of two
adjacent neuron sections into one via the blurry membrane region. Human
annotators can easily avoid such errors by implicitly performing gap
completion, taking into account the continuity of membranes.
  Drawing inspiration from these human strategies, we formulate the
segmentation task as an edge labeling problem on a graph with local topological
constraints. We derive an integer linear program (ILP) that enforces membrane
continuity, i.e. the absence of gaps. The cost function of the ILP is the
pixel-wise deviation of the segmentation from a priori membrane probabilities
derived from the data.
  Based on membrane probability maps obtained using random forest classifiers
and convolutional neural networks, our method improves the neuron boundary
segmentation accuracy compared to a variety of standard segmentation
approaches. Our method successfully performs gap completion and leads to fewer
topological errors. The method could potentially also be incorporated into
other image segmentation pipelines with known topological constraints.

example of a complicated aggregation system with several levels of structures
is peptide/protein self-assembly. The problem of protein aggregation is
important for the understanding and treatment of neurodegenerative diseases and
also for the development of bio-macromolecules as new materials. We write the
effective Hamiltonian in terms of interaction energies between protein
monomers, protein and solvent, as well as between protein filaments. The grand
partition function can be expressed in terms of a Zimm-Bragg-like transfer
matrix, which is calculated exactly and all thermodynamic properties can be
obtained. We start with two-state and three-state descriptions of protein
monomers using Potts models that can be generalized to include q-states, for

lattice systems, corresponding to the ordered structures observed in some real
fibrils. We have obtained results on nucleation processes and phase diagrams,
in which a protein property such as the sheet content of aggregates is

- 1 tablespoon of minced garlic

- Fresh parsley for garnishing

text:
Ingredients:

- 4 veal shanks
- 2 tablespoons olive oil
- 1 onion, chopped
- 1 carrot, chopped
- 1 celery stalk, chopped
- 4 cloves garlic, minced
- 1 cup dry white wine
- 2 cups beef broth
- 1 can (16 oz) crushed tomatoes
- 1 tablespoon chopped fresh thyme
- 1 tablespoon chopped fresh rosemary
- Salt and pepper to taste
- 2 tablespoons fresh chopped parsley (for garnishing)

Instructions:

1. Preheat your oven to 325°F (165°C) for a slow cook.

2. Pat dry the veal shanks with a clean kitchen towel to remove any excess moisture. Season each shank on all sides with salt and pepper.

3. In a large dutch oven or oven-safe pot, heat the olive oil over medium-high heat. Add the veal shanks and sear each side until they are a nice golden brown. Be sure not to crowd the pot; you may need to do this in batches depending on the size of your pot. Remove the shanks from the pot and set them aside.

4. In the same pot, add the chopped onions, carrots, and celery. Sauté for a few minutes until the vegetables start to soften. Add garlic and sauté for another minute.

5. Pour in the white wine, stirring and scraping the bottom of the pot to loosen any browned bits. Let it simmer for a few minutes until the wine has reduced by half.

6. Add the beef broth, crushed tomatoes, thyme, and rosemary. Bring the mixture to a boil.

7. Return the veal shanks to the pot, making sure they are covered at least halfway with the liquid. If necessary, add more broth. 

8. Cover the pot and transfer it to the preheated oven. Let it cook for about 2 to 2.5 hours, or until the meat is very tender and almost falling off the bone.

9. Once cooked, remove the pot from the oven. Skim off any excess fat from the top of the cooking liquid if necessary.

10. Serve the veal shanks hot, garnished with fresh chopped parsley. 

Braised Veal Shanks is a hearty dish that pairs perfectly with mashed potatoes, risotto, or polenta and a glass of red wine. Enjoy!

Preheat the oven to 220°C. Lay out the sheets of puff pastry. They will defrost while you prepare the chicken. Cut the chicken breast into long strips. You will need half a large chicken breast or half a medium chicken breast plus the tenderloin from the other half. Sprinkle the stock powder over the chicken. I use an organic vegetable stock but use whatever you have. I have tried soy sauce but it makes the chicken too wet. Dry ingredients are better and light flavours don't overpower the asparagus. Beat an egg lightly and then brush some eggwash along the cut in the middle of the sheet of pastry. With a sheet in front of you with the cut going left to right (not up and down), take the edge near you and fold it over the chicken and asparagus. Use the folded edge to shove the filling nearer to you until it is tucked around the filling quite tightly. Now roll up the pastry to the eggwash and make sure the cut edge stays on the bottom of the roll. Brush the top with egg and sprinkle plenty of sesame seeds on top. Cut into 6 pieces. Repeat for the other 9 strips to give you 60 little bites.
