I
The August day you wake to takes you by surprise.
Its bitterness. Black sullen clouds. Brackish downpour.
A drift-net of wetness enmeshes the rented cottage,
towels and children’s swimwear sodden on the line.
Dry-gulleted drains gulp down neat rain.
Drops bounce from a leaking gutter with hard,
uncompromising slaps: and, like resignation
in the face of death, you contemplate winter
with something close to tenderness, the sprint
from fuel shed to back door, the leisurely
ascent of peat smoke, even the suburban haze
of boiler flues when thermostats are set.
You warm to those thoughts as you sit there,
brainstorming ways to keep the family amused,
plans abandoned for barefoot games on dry sand.
Handcraft shops? Slot-machine arcades? Hotel grills?
In truth - manipulating toast crumbs backwards,
forwards at the unsteady table’s edge - you’d prefer
to return to your bed as if with some mild
ailment, pampered by duvet, whiskey, cloves.
II
Let it rain.
Let the clouds discharge their contents like reserve tanks.
Let the worms burrow their way to the topsoil
from whatever dank Sargasso they were spawned in.
Let dampness rot the coffin-boards of the summer house.
Let the shrubs lose their foothold in the wind,
the nettles lose their edge, the drenched rat
with slicked-back hair scuttle to its sewage pipe.
Let the tropical expanses of the rhubarb leaves
serve as an artificial pond, a reservoir.
Let the downpour’s impact on the toolshed be akin
to the dull applause on an archive recording of a love duet.
Let the bricklayers at the building site wrap
pathetic sheets of polythene around doomed foundations.
Let the limb ripped from the tree’s socket
hover fleetingly in the air, an olive branch.
Let a rainbow’s fantail unfurl like a bird of paradise.
Let a covenant be sealed, its wording watertight.
Let the floods recede.
Let there be light.
III after Giacomo Leopardi
The storm runs out of wind; nature, which
abhors a silence, fills the vacancy with birdsong.
Deserting the airless, low-ceilinged coop,
the hen repeats herself ad infinitum. Replenished
like the rain-barrels, hearts grow sanguine.
Hammering resumes. Humming. Gossip. Croons.
Sun strides down lanes that grass has repossessed,
takes a shine to the brasses at the hotel where,
by the window she thrust open, the chambermaid
is marvelling at the cleansed freshness, calm.
Balm of mind and body. Will we ever feel
more reconciled to life than now, ever
know a moment more conducive to new hopes,
eager beginnings, auspicious starts?
How easily pleased we are. Rescind
the threat of torment for the briefest
second and we blot out dark nights of the soul
when lightning flashes fanned by wind
ignited fire and brimstone visions.
Sorrow is perennial; happiness, a rare
bloom, perfumes the air - so that we breathe
with the ease of a camphor-scented chest
from which congestion has just lifted.
Lack of woe equates with rapture then,
though not till death will pain take full leave
of our senses, grant us permanent relief.

Norwood Russell Hanson (August 17, 1924 – April 18, 1967) was an American philosopher of science. Hanson was a pioneer in advancing the argument that observation is theory-laden — that observation language and theory language are deeply interwoven — and that historical and contemporary comprehension are similarly deeply interwoven. His single most central intellectual concern was the comprehension and development of a logic of discovery. Work
Hanson's best-known work is Patterns of Discovery (1958), in which he argues that what we see and perceive is not what our senses receive, but is instead filtered sensory information, where the filter is our existing preconceptions – a concept later called a 'thematic framework.' He cited optical illusions such as the famous old Parisienne woman (Patterns of Discovery, p. 11), which can be seen in different ways. Hanson drew a distinction between 'seeing as' and 'seeing that' which became a key idea in evolving theories of perception and meaning. He wanted to formulate a logic explaining how scientific discoveries take place. He used Charles Sanders Peirce's notion of abduction for this.

- 1 cup organic sugar
- ¼ cup vegan margarine
- 2 tablespoons almond milk
- ¼ cup dark rum
- ½ teaspoon vanilla extract

Instructions:

1. Preheat your oven to 350°F (175°C) and grease a 9-inch round cake pan

2. To prepare the cake, in a large bowl, combine the flour, sugar, cocoa powder, baking soda, and salt.

3. In a separate bowl, stir together the almond milk and vinegar. Let stand for a few minutes until curdled.

5. Pour the wet ingredients into the flour mixture and stir until just mixed. Don't overmix.

6. Pour the batter into the prepared pan, spreading evenly.

7. Bake for about 30-35 minutes, or until a toothpick inserted into the center comes out clean.

8. While the cake is baking, prepare the sticky rum glaze. In a small saucepan, combine the sugar, margarine, and almond milk. Bring to a simmer and cook, stirring, until the sugar has completely dissolved.

9. Remove the saucepan from the heat and stir in the rum and vanilla.

10. Once the cake is done, remove it from the oven and immediately poke several holes in the top with a skewer or toothpick.

11. Pour the hot sticky rum glaze over the hot cake, making sure it seeps into the holes. 

12. Let the cake cool before removing it from the pan. The glaze will form a sticky, sweet crust on the top of the cake as it cools.

prompt: Write the body of a Wikipedia article titled "Crosswind stabilization".
text:
Crosswind stabilization is a feature used in some aircraft to help maintain stability and control during flight in the presence of crosswinds.

A crosswind is a wind that blows across the direction of flight, as opposed to a headwind or tailwind, which blows directly into or away from the direction of flight. Crosswinds can cause an aircraft to roll or yaw, making it difficult to maintain a steady course.

Crosswind stabilization systems work by using a combination of sensors, computers, and control surfaces to detect and counteract the effects of crosswinds. These systems typically use a combination of gyroscopes, accelerometers, and pressure sensors to measure the orientation and speed of the aircraft, as well as the direction and speed of the crosswind.

Based on this data, the computer controller of the crosswind stabilization system calculates the appropriate control surface deflections to counteract the crosswind. For example, if a crosswind is blowing from the left side of the aircraft, the computer may command the ailerons to deflect up on the left wing and down on the right wing, which will cause the aircraft to roll into the crosswind and maintain a steady course.

There are several types of crosswind stabilization systems used in aircraft, including:

1. Mechanical crosswind stabilization: This system uses a mechanical linkage to connect the control surfaces to the rudder pedals, so that when the pilot presses the rudder pedal to correct for a crosswind, the control surfaces will also deflect to help stabilize the aircraft.
2. Electro-mechanical crosswind stabilization: This system uses a combination of mechanical and electrical components to provide crosswind stabilization. It typically consists of a mechanical linkage between the control surfaces and the rudder pedals, along with an electrical servo motor that adjusts the position of the control surfaces based on input from the computer controller.
3. Fly-by-wire crosswind stabilization: This system uses an all-electric system to provide crosswind stabilization. It replaces the mechanical linkage between the control surfaces and the rudder pedals with an electronic flight control system (EFCS) that uses sensors and actuators to control the position of the control surfaces.

- 1 1/2 cups granulated sugar
- 7 large eggs
- 1 teaspoon pure vanilla extract

Instructions:

1. Preheat your oven to 375°F (190°C) and position a rack in the middle of the oven.

10. Before serving, dust the top of the cake with confectioners’ sugar, if desired, and cut into slices. Serve with fresh berries, if you like.

In contrast, DatasetGAN leverages Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to efficiently generate high-quality labeled datasets.

Our approach consists of two main components: a generator network that produces synthetic data, and a discriminator network that evaluates the generated data and provides feedback to the generator. The generator is trained to produce data that is indistinguishable from real-world data, while the discriminator is trained to accurately classify the generated data. Through this adversarial process, the generator improves over time, generating increasingly realistic and diverse data that can be used for a variety of tasks.

We evaluate DatasetGAN on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate its effectiveness in generating high-quality labeled data. In particular, we show that DatasetGAN can generate datasets that are comparable in quality to those obtained through manual annotation, while reducing the annotation effort by up to 95%. Furthermore, we demonstrate the versatility of DatasetGAN by applying it to a variety of tasks, including image classification, object detection, and natural language processing.

Our results have significant implications for the field of machine learning, as they demonstrate a novel and efficient way to generate large-scale labeled datasets with minimal human effort. This has the potential to greatly accelerate the development of machine learning models and reduce the cost and time required for dataset creation. prompt: Write the body of a Wikipedia article titled "Reterritorialization".
text:
Reterritorialization refers to the process in which elements or concepts detached from their original geographical, cultural, or socio-political context are restored or restructured within a new context or territory. The term is used primarily in the fields of social and political theory, cultural analysis, and geography, and is often contrasted with "deterritorialization," which refers to the loss or removal of physical, cultural, or social attributes from a specific place.

Origins

The concept of reterritorialization was first introduced by Gilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari in their two-volume work "Capitalism and Schizophrenia," addressing it as a counterpoint to deterritorialization. They suggest that every act of deterritorialization creates spaces for potential reterritorialization, as social and cultural entities naturally tend to restructure themselves into new forms and orders. Nevertheless, they noted that reterritorialization often leads to fresh deterritorializations, thus placing both processes in a relationship of constant flux.

Applications and Examples

Examples of reterritorialization can be found in the cultural sphere, where the process often takes place when elements of a global culture are adopted and adapted by a local culture, thus giving them new forms and meanings. A well-known example is the global spread of US American fast food chains. While globally promoting a standardized menu, they often adjust their products to local tastes and preferences, effectively reterritorializing such quintessentially American elements like the hamburger in new cultural contexts.

Economic and socio-political reterritorialization often occurs through globalisation where multinational corporations or global institutions enact local initiatives or incorporate local resources and labour in their global production chains. Here, reterritorialization refers to the embedding of these global processes into specific local contexts, often shaping local economic structures.

Consequences

The consequences of reterritorialization can be both positive and negative. It may allow local cultures to retain their identity and resist cultural homogenization, but it may also contribute to the erasure of local cultural specificities. Critics have also pointed out that reterritorialization, especially in its economic form, can lead to new forms of inequality and exploitation.

Moreover, the complex interplay of deterritorialization and reterritorialization is increasingly seen as intricately linked to issues such as migration and displacement, technological change, and environmental challenges.

prompt: Write a recipe for "Simple Chocolate Strawberry Shortcake".
text:
Ingredients:

For the Shortcakes:
- 2 cups all-purpose flour 
- 1/3 cup unsweetened cocoa powder
- 1/2 cup granulated sugar 
- 1 tablespoon baking powder 
- 1/2 teaspoon salt 
- 1/2 cup unsalted butter, cold and cut into cubes 
- 2/3 cup whole milk 
- 1 teaspoon vanilla extract

For the Topping:
- 1/2 cup heavy cream 
- 1 tablespoon powdered sugar 
- 1 teaspoon vanilla extract
- 2 cups fresh strawberries, hulled and sliced 
- 1/4 cup granulated sugar 
- Chocolate shavings (optional)

Instructions:

1. Preheat your oven to 425°F (220°C) and line a cookie sheet with parchment paper.

2. In a large bowl, combine the flour, cocoa powder, granulated sugar, baking powder, and salt. 

3. Add the cold cubed butter to the flour mixture. Use a pastry cutter or your fingers to cut the butter into the flour until the mixture resembles coarse crumbs.

4. Pour in the milk and vanilla extract. Stir until just combined. Do not overmix.

5. On a lightly floured surface, gently knead the dough a few times until it comes together. Pat the dough into a 1-inch thick rectangle.

6. Using a round biscuit cutter, cut out shortcakes from the dough and place them on the prepared cookie sheet.

7. Bake for about 15 minutes, or until a toothpick inserted into the center of the shortcakes comes out clean.

8. While the shortcakes are cooling, prepare your strawberry topping. In a separate bowl, mix the sliced strawberries with the 1/4 cup of granulated sugar. Let them sit for at least 10 minutes to draw out the juices.

9. For the whipped cream, beat the heavy cream, powdered sugar, and vanilla extract in a chilled bowl until soft peaks form.

10. Once the shortcakes are cool, cut them in half horizontally. Spoon a layer of strawberries onto the bottom half, add a dollop of whipped cream, then place the top half of the shortcake on top. 

11. Serve each shortcake with more strawberries and whipped cream on top. Sprinkle with some chocolate shavings, if desired.

Enjoy these simple yet decadent chocolate strawberry shortcakes. Perfect for a sweet summer treat or a special occasion dessert.

prompt: Write a recipe for "Pan de Muertos (Day of the Dead Bread) Recipe".

Ingredients:
- 4 cups all-purpose flour
- 1/2 cup sugar
- 1/2 teaspoon salt
- 1 tablespoon active dry yeast
- 1/2 cup warm water
- 1/2 cup warm milk
- 1/2 cup unsalted butter, melted
- 4 eggs
- 1 tablespoon orange zest
- 1 tablespoon orange juice
- 1 teaspoon anise seeds
- A pinch of ground cinnamon
- 1 egg yolk
- Sugar for dusting

Instructions:

5. Transfer the dough onto a lightly floured surface and knead for about 10 minutes until it becomes smooth and elastic.
6. Place the dough into a greased bowl, cover it with a towel, and let it rise in a warm place for about 1 hour or until it doubles in size.
7. Preheat your oven to 350°F (175°C).
8. Once the dough has risen, punch it down to release any air bubbles. Divide the dough into smaller portions and shape them into round balls.
9. Place the shaped dough onto a baking sheet lined with parchment paper. Use your fingers to create bone and skull shapes on top of the balls of dough.
10. In a small bowl, whisk the egg yolk with a tablespoon of water. Brush this mixture over the bread dough.
11. Sprinkle sugar over the bread dough to give it a nice crust.
12. Bake the Day of the Dead bread in the preheated oven for approximately 25-30 minutes or until it becomes golden brown.

Ingredients:
- 1 (16.5 oz) refrigerated sugar cookie dough
- 1/2 cup fresh strawberries, diced
- 1/4 cup white sugar
- 1 teaspoon ground cinnamon
- Powdered sugar, for dusting

Instructions:
1. Preheat oven to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C). 
2. Roll out the cookie dough on a lightly floured surface into a 1/4 inch thick circle. 
3. In a small bowl, mix together the diced strawberries, white sugar, and ground cinnamon. 
4. Spread the strawberry mixture over the cookie dough, leaving a 1 inch border around the edge. 
5. Roll the dough tightly from one of the shorter sides, then cut the roll into 1 inch thick slices. 
6. Place the slices cut side up in a lightly greased 9x9 inch baking dish. 
7. Bake in the preheated oven for 20 to 25 minutes, or until the edges are lightly golden. 
8. Let the rolls cool for a few minutes before dusting them with powdered sugar. 
9. Serve warm with a dollop of whipped cream or vanilla ice cream, if desired. Enjoy!

image segmentation and hence 3D navigation for robot-assisted Minimally
Invasive Surgeries (MISs). However, current DCNNs usually use down sampling
layers for increasing the receptive field and gaining abstract semantic
information. These down sampling layers decrease the spatial dimension of
feature maps, which can be detrimental to image segmentation. Atrous

The Video Relay Service is being piloted by the Royal National Institute for Deaf People (RNID), but the organisation says unless the service is provided at the same rate as voice calls it will be beyond most people's pockets. The RNID is urging telecoms regulator, Ofcom, to reduce the cost of the service from the current £7.00 per minute and make it the same as ordinary phone calls. The service works by putting a deaf person in visual contact with a BSL interpreter via a webcam or video phone, and the interpreter then relays the deaf person's conversation using a telephone and translates the other person's response into sign language.
For many deaf people, especially those born deaf, BSL is a first and preferred means of communication.
Until now, the only alternative has been to use textphones which means having to type a message and have it relayed via an operator. "In the past, I've used textphones but they have problems," said Robert Currington who is taking part in the pilot. "I communicate in BSL; my written English is not very good and it takes me longer to think in English and type my message." "I sometimes find it difficult to understand the reply." The RNID says the UK is lagging behind other countries which are already making relay services available at the cost of an ordinary phone call. "There are no technical or economic reasons for not providing equivalent access to services for deaf people," said RNID technology director, Guido Gybels. "In the US and Australia, sign language relay services have already been made universally available at the same cost as a voice call. For Love Of The Game

Maybe I'm looking at this film through rose colored glasses. Sam Raimi is one of my favorite directors, a real talent with visual ingenuity and a penchant for silliness. With last holiday's bleak A SIMPLE PLAN, Raimi gave up his EVIL DEAD past and churned out the most satisfying dramatic thriller of last year. He is certainly growing by leaps and bounds as a storyteller, and his latest film, FOR LOVE OF THE GAME, is another surprise for those of us who are fans. A truly elegant, dashingly romantic, white-knuckled look at baseball and matters of the human heart, GAME represents what a true Hollywood soap opera should be, effective.

Kevin Costner plays Billy Chapel, an aging pitcher for the Detroit Tigers heading for the mound for may be his last time ever. The team owner has sold the organization to a corporation and they have plans to trade Billy. His arm continues to fail him more every time he steps up to thrown. And to top it all off, Billy must deal with his tempestuous relationship with Jane, a woman he met by a broken down car on the side of the road five years ago and has yet to fully commit to. With all these thoughts swirling inside Billy's head, he unknowingly begins pitching a perfect game. Unable to keep his mind clear, Billy thinks back on his life during the game and considers the mistakes he has made and the people he has met.

Told mostly in flashback, LOVE OF THE GAME is first and foremost a baseball movie. While being knocked for his recent professional choices (yeah, I liked THE POSTMAN, say what you will) Kevin Costner seems to have been crowned king of the baseball flicks. Ron Shelton's BULL DURHAM is pure genius, the best baseball film ever. FIELD OF DREAMS is more like GAME, both share a strong heartbeat and retaining a smart enthusiasm for the sport. Costner has been the glue that held both films together. He's always been a good actor, only reaching brilliance once (DURHAM). He has the rare charm the many actors forget to consider. While not technically proficient, Costner knows screen charisma well. GAME gives us a desperate Costner performance, one which lets the actor take his guard down for once. His Billy Chapel is a man used to success, yet unsure how to use it to his advantage. A man who can hardly imagine himself consumed by anything but baseball. It's a great performance from Costner. My only hope is that public opinion doesn't tarnish the acting for the paying crowd.

Kelly Preston has the more troublesome task of shining brighter than Costner. A working actress for sometime now, this new film feels like the first time Preston is really acting. I enjoyed her supporting work in 1998's underrated JACK FROST, and GAME finally puts her front and center. She bounces effortlessly of Costner, and the two - while skittish at first - melt into a nice chemistry that packs more emotion than I expected. The loopy John C. Reilly (BOOGIE NIGHTS) and Jena Malone (STEPMOM) are also quite pleasant in small roles.

Working with even more restraint than his SIMPLE PLAN, Raimi brings to the table his gift for camera placement and visual tenacity. The baseball scenes in GAME are very romantic, the title doesn't lie. A self-professed fanatic of baseball, Raimi's love of the game shows in each shot. With noted cinematographer John Bailey, the two create a pristine looking film. The stadium scenes are both frightening cinematic and realistic at the same time. The look of the film might not register with many people, but I couldn't help but to admire such attention to detail.

Screenwriter Dana Stevens made quite an impression with her spare and warm CITY OF ANGELS remake. What she brings to GAME is the feeling of courtship that I enjoyed in Costner's last film MESSAGE IN A BOTTLE. Costner and Preston really show the genesis of a relationship, warts and all. The structure of flashback that Stevens uses to tell the story isn't as unfortunate as it sounds. It's all a rather nice mix of familiar baseball melodrama and a hearty dose of Hollywood soap opera. Stevens proves once again that she has a wonderful ear for romantic entanglements.

Call me a sucker for the obvious, but FOR LOVE OF THE GAME really worked for me. I really was moved by the story and enjoyed all the nuances and quirks. This classy film might not have a hero with a chainsaw for a hand, a crispy scientist with a reliance on synthetic skin, or a quickdrawing Sharon Stone. What it does have is strong emotional resonance. A audience film that the mainstream will love and the arthouse will abhor. I'll take that any day.-------- 10/10

In this paper, we explore the concept of first-order reducts of unary structures and introduce a novel dichotomy for these structures. First-order reducts are structures that can be obtained from a given structure by forgetting some of the relations or functions that define it. Unary structures, on the other hand, are structures in which every relation or function involves only one element.

Our dichotomy shows that first-order reducts of unary structures can be divided into two distinct categories: those that are "locally decidable" and those that are not. Locally decidable structures are those in which every first-order sentence that is true in the structure can be decided by considering only a finite number of elements. In other words, the truth of a first-order sentence in a locally decidable structure depends only on the values of a finite number of elements.

We demonstrate the applicability of our dichotomy by providing examples of first-order reducts of unary structures that are locally decidable, as well as examples of those that are not. We also explore the implications of our results for the study of first-order reducts and their relationship to other areas of mathematical logic, such as model theory and proof theory.

Our work provides a new perspective on the study of first-order reducts of unary structures, and represents a significant contribution to the field of mathematical logic. Our results have important implications for the study of the complexity of logical reasoning and decision procedures in artificial intelligence, and have the potential to inform the development of more efficient algorithms for solving logical reasoning tasks.

Ingredients:

- 1 teaspoon baking soda
- 1/2 teaspoon baking powder
- 1 cup unsalted butter (softened)

- 1/2 teaspoon almond extract
- Colored sugar for decoration (optional)

text:
Title: Generator evaluator-selector net for panoptic image segmentation and splitting unfamiliar objects into parts

Abstract: Panoptic image segmentation is a crucial task in object detection and recognition. In this study, we develop a generator evaluator-selector net for panoptic image segmentation. We investigate on the problem of generating new object instances from scratch in the training set by using generative adversarial network (GAN) in contrast to other methods that generate by reusing existing instances. Our proposed method has three modules: Generator evaluator, label generator, and network selector. The generator evaluator generates new object instances in the image, the label generator predicts object masks, and the network extracts relevant parts of the images for label generator inputs. Consequently, our method achieves an impressive performance on several segmentation tasks while being able to split unfamiliar objects into more specific and accurate parts. Our study showcases the effectiveness of our proposed method in generating new object instances and improving performance in panoptic image segmentation.

text:
While it's definitely not my intention to spoil anyone's fun, it's worth addressing some misconceptions about daily marijuana use. Often, we find people comparing smoking weed to drinking alcohol with weed emerging as the less harmful option. However, it's important to note that abusing any substance on a daily basis is harmful, and weed is not an exception to this.

Firstly, chronic marijuana use has been linked to mental health problems, including anxiety, depression, and in rare cases, psychosis. Regular, heavy users are more likely to have lower life satisfaction, poorer mental health, poorer physical health, and more relationship issues. Also, smoking marijuana often can result in breathing issues. Although it doesn't harm the lungs as much as tobacco, marijuana smoke still produces tar, which can lead to bronchitis and lung complications over time.

Secondly, you may have heard the term 'marijuana use disorder,' which directly links to addiction. The National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA) says that people who begin using marijuana before the age of 18 are four to seven times more likely to develop a marijuana use disorder than adults. Sure, not everyone using weed every day becomes addicted, but the risk of addiction is high with daily usage.

Thirdly, just like alcohol, marijuana can alter judgment and coordination, leading to poor decisions, like driving under the influence, which, needless to say, can potentially be life-threatening. 

Now, none of this means that marijuana doesn't have medical benefits for patients suffering from chronic disorders and illnesses. However, using it recreationally every day puts an individual at notable risk for the above issues, just as drinking alcohol every day does.

Both substances, in moderation, can fit into an adult’s lifestyle without significant problems. But daily and heavy use of either is damaging in physical, psychological, and social aspects. We need to advocate for responsible use rather than picking a 'lesser evil' between weed and alcohol. In the end, abuse is abuse, irrespective of the substance.

Ingredients:

- 200g spaghetti
- 2 pieces of chicken breasts
- 2 tablespoons olive oil
- salt and pepper to taste

- 2 cloves garlic, minced

- 1 teaspoon sugar
- 2 tablespoon of unsalted butter
- 1 small finely chopped onion
- Shaved Parmesan cheese for garnish

Instructions

1. Heat a large pot of salted water until it boils, add the spaghetti and cook according to the package instructions until al dente. Once cooked, drain and set aside.

2. Meanwhile, season the chicken breasts with salt and pepper on both sides. Heat 1 tablespoon of olive oil in a large skillet over medium heat. text:
Ingredients for Toasted Almond Semifreddo:

1. 1 cup of almonds
2. 1 cup of granulated sugar
3. 1/2 cup of honey
4. 1/2 teaspoon of pure vanilla extract
5. 4 large eggs, separated
6. 1 1/4 cups of heavy cream.
7. A pinch of salt.

Steps:

1. Preheat the oven to 350°F (175°C). Allowing the almonds to spread out in a single layer on a baking sheet. Toast them in the oven for approximately 10 minutes, or until they're fragrant and slightly browned.

2. Let the almonds cool, then coarsely chop them. Artificially separate approximately half of the almonds and set them aside for garnish.

3. Set up a medium heatproof bowl over a pot of boiling water (making sure that the bowl doesn't touch the water), and add the egg yolks, sugar, honey, and salt to the bowl. Whisk these ingredients together until they're thoroughly combined. 

4. Continue whisking the mixture until it's creamy, and warm to the touch, for about 5 to 7 minutes.

5. Remove the bowl from the heat, and whisk in the vanilla extract. Keep whisking the mixture until it cools down to room temperature.

6. In a different bowl, whisk your egg whites until peaks form that are stiff but not dry. Gently fold this into your now cooled yolk mixture.

7. Whip your heavy cream in another bowl, again aiming for soft peaks. Fold this as gently as possible into your previous mixture.

8. Fold in the cooled, chopped almonds (remembering to save some for garnish).

9. Pour this final mixture into a prepared 9x5 loaf pan lined with plastic wrap. Make sure to smooth out the top of your mixture.

10. Cover the loaf pan with plastic wrap, and then let it freeze for a minimum of 6 hours. However, for the best results, let it freeze overnight.

11. When you're ready to serve, gently remove the semifreddo from the pan by lifting the plastic wrap. Cut the semifreddo into slices, top with the remaining toasted almonds, and serve immediately. Enjoy your delicious Toasted Almond Semifreddo!

text:
Peanut Butter Surprise Cupcakes

Ingredients:
- 1 3/4 cups all-purpose flour
- 1 1/2 teaspoons baking powder
- 1/2 teaspoon salt
- 1/2 cup unsalted butter, softened
- 1 cup granulated sugar
- 2 large eggs
- 1 teaspoon vanilla extract
- 3/4 cup milk
- 1/2 cup creamy peanut butter
- 24 small chocolate candies (e.g. peanut butter cups)
- Optional: frosting, decorative sprinkles

Instructions:

1. Preheat the oven to 350°F (175°C). Line a muffin tin with cupcake liners.

2. In a medium bowl, whisk together the flour, baking powder, and salt. Set aside.

3. In a large bowl, cream together the softened butter and sugar until light and fluffy. This can be done using an electric mixer or by hand using a wooden spoon.

4. Add the eggs, one at a time, mixing well after each addition. Stir in the vanilla extract.

5. Gradually add the flour mixture to the butter mixture, alternating with the milk. Begin and end with the flour mixture, mixing just until combined. Be careful not to overmix, as this can result in tough cupcakes.

6. Gently fold in the creamy peanut butter until incorporated into the batter.

7. Fill each cupcake liner about halfway full with the batter. Place a small chocolate candy (e.g. peanut butter cup) into the center of each cupcake, pressing it down slightly.

8. Spoon additional batter over the top of each candy, covering it completely. The cupcake liners should be about 2/3 full.

9. Bake in the preheated oven for 18-20 minutes, or until a toothpick inserted into the center of a cupcake comes out clean.

10. Remove the cupcakes from the oven and allow them to cool in the muffin tin for a few minutes. Transfer the cupcakes to a wire rack to cool completely.

11. Once cooled, frost the cupcakes with your favorite frosting, if desired, and decorate with sprinkles.

12. Serve and enjoy the delicious surprise of peanut butter hidden inside each cupcake!

Note: You can store these cupcakes in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days.

text:
Breaded Pork Cutlets with Lemon Aioli Recipe

Ingredients:
- 4 pork cutlets
- 1 cup breadcrumbs
- ½ cup all-purpose flour
- 2 eggs, beaten
- Salt and pepper, to taste
- Vegetable oil, for frying
- Lemon wedges, for serving

For Lemon Aioli:
- ½ cup mayonnaise
- 1 tablespoon lemon juice
- 1 garlic clove, minced
- Salt and pepper, to taste

Instructions:

1. Preheat the oven to 250°F (120°C) to keep the cooked cutlets warm.

2. In a shallow bowl, combine the breadcrumbs, salt, and pepper. In another shallow bowl, place the flour. In a third shallow bowl, beat the eggs.

3. Pat the pork cutlets dry with paper towels and season them with salt and pepper.

4. Dredge each cutlet in flour, shaking off any excess. Dip the floured cutlets into the beaten eggs, allowing any excess to drip off. Finally, coat the cutlets with the breadcrumb mixture, pressing gently to adhere the breadcrumbs.

5. Heat vegetable oil in a large pan over medium heat. Place the breaded cutlets in the hot oil, being careful not to crowd the pan. Fry the pork cutlets for about 3-4 minutes on each side until they are golden brown and cooked through.

6. Remove the cutlets from the pan and transfer them to a baking dish lined with a wire rack. Place the cooked cutlets in the preheated oven to keep them warm while you prepare the lemon aioli.

7. For the lemon aioli, in a small bowl, whisk together the mayonnaise, lemon juice, minced garlic, salt, and pepper. Adjust the seasoning according to taste.

8. Serve the breaded pork cutlets with lemon aioli drizzled on top and wedges of lemon on the side. These cutlets pair well with a side of roasted potatoes or a fresh green salad.

Enjoy your delicious Breaded Pork Cutlets with Lemon Aioli!

Vanillekipferl are traditional German cookies that are soft and packed with vanilla flavor. Here is a recipe you can try at home:

Ingredients:
- 2 3/4 cups all-purpose flour
- 1 teaspoon baking powder
- 1/2 teaspoon salt
- 1 cup unsalted butter, at room temperature
- 3/4 cup granulated sugar
- 1 egg
- 1 teaspoon vanilla extract
- 1/2 cup powdered sugar
- 1/2 cup chopped almonds (optional)

Instructions:
1. Preheat oven to 350°F (175°C). Line a baking sheet with parchment paper.
2. In a medium sized bowl, whisk together the flour, baking powder and salt.
3. In a large bowl, beat the butter and sugar together until light and fluffy. Add in the egg and vanilla extract and beat until combined.
4. Gradually add the flour mixture to the butter mixture and beat until fully incorporated.
5. If you are using almonds, fold them into the dough now.
6. Using an ice cream scoop or spoon, form balls of dough and place them onto the prepared baking sheet. Leave about 2 inches of space between each ball.
7. Flatten the balls slightly with the back of a spoon.
8. Bake for 12-15 minutes or until the edges are lightly golden.
9. Remove from the oven and allow to cool on the baking sheet for 5 minutes before transferring to a wire rack to cool completely.
10. Once the cookies have cooled, dust them with powdered sugar.

Enjoy your delicious Vanillekipferl!

A new European directive could put software writers at risk of legal action, warns former programmer and technology analyst Bill Thompson.
If it gets its way, the Dutch government will conclude its presidency of the European Union by pushing through a controversial measure that has been rejected by the European Parliament, lacks majority support from national governments and will leave millions of European citizens in legal limbo and facing the possibility of court cases against them. If the new law was about border controls, defence or even the new constitution, then our TV screens would be full of experts agonising over the impact on our daily lives. Sadly for those who will be directly affected, the controversy concerns the patenting of computer programs, a topic that may excite the bloggers, campaigning groups and technical press but does not obsess Middle Britain. After all, how much fuss can you generate about the Directive on the Patentability of Computer-Implemented Inventions, and the way it amends Article 52 of the 1973 European Patent Convention? Yet if the new directive is nodded through at the next meeting of one of the EU's ministerial councils, as seems likely, it will allow programs to be patented in Europe just as they are in the US. Many observers of the computing scene, including myself, think the results will be disastrous for small companies, innovative programmers and the free and open source software movement. It will let large companies patent all sorts of ideas and give legal force to those who want to limit their competitors' use of really obvious ideas.
In the US you cannot build a system that stores customer credit card details so that they can pay without having to re-enter them unless Amazon lets you, because they hold the patent on "one-click" online purchase. It is a small invention, but Amazon made it to the patent office first and now owns it.
We are relatively free from this sort of thing over here, but perhaps not for long. The new proposals go back to 2002, although argument about patentability of software and computer-implemented inventions has been going on since at least the mid-1980s. They have come to a head now after a year in which proposals were made, endorsed by the Council of Ministers, radically modified by the European Parliament and then re-presented in their original form. Some national governments seem to be aware of the problems. Poland has rejected the proposal and Germany's main political parties have opposed it, but there is not enough opposition to guarantee their rejection. Early in December the British government held a consultation meeting with those who had commented on the proposals. Science Minister Lord Sainsbury went along to listen and outline the UK position, but according to those present, it was embarrassing to see how little the minister and his officials actually understood the issues concerned.
The draft Directive is being put through the council as what is called an "A" item and can only be approved or rejected. No discussion or amendment is allowed. So why should we be worried? First, there is the abuse of the democratic process involved in disregarding the views of the parliament and abandoning all of their carefully argued amendments. This goes to the heart of the European project, and even those who do not care about software or patents should be worried. If coders are treated like this today, who is to say that it will not be you tomorrow?
More directly, once software patents are granted then any programmer will have to worry that the code they are writing is infringing someone else's patent. This is not about stealing software, as code is already protected by copyright. Patents are not copyright, but something much stronger. A patent gives the owner the right to stop anyone else using their invention, even if the other person invented it separately. I have never, to my shame, managed to read Lord Byron's Childe Harold's Pilgrimage. If it was pointed out that one of my articles contained a substantial chunk of the poem then I could defend myself in court by claiming that I had simply made it up and it was coincidence. The same does not hold for a patent. If I sit down this afternoon and write a brilliant graphics compression routine and it happens to be the same as the LZW algorithm used in GIF files, then I am in trouble under patent law, at least in the US. Coincidence is no defence. The proposed directive is supported by many of the major software companies, but this is hardly surprising since most of them are US-based and they have already had to cope with a legal environment that allows patents. They have legal departments and, more crucially, patents of their own which they can trade or cross-license with other patent holders.
Even this system breaks down, of course, as Microsoft found out last year when they initially lost a case brought by Eolas which claimed that Internet Explorer (and other browsers) infringed an Eolas patent. That one was eventually thrown out, but only after months of uncertainty and millions of dollars. But small companies, and the free and open software movement do not have any patents to trade. Much of the really useful software we use every day, programs like the Apache web server, the GNU/Linux operating system and the fearsomely popular Firefox browser, is developed outside company structures by people who do not have legal departments to check for patent infringements. The damage to software will not happen overnight, of course. If the directive goes through it has to be written into national laws and then there will be a steady stream of legal actions against small companies and open source products. Eventually someone will decide to attack Linux directly, probably with some secret funding from one or two large players. The new directive will limit innovation by forcing programmers to spend time checking for patent infringements or simply avoiding working in potentially competitive areas. And it will damage Europe's computer industry. We can only hope that the Council of Ministers has the integrity and strength to reject this bad law.
Bill Thompson is a regular commentator on the BBC World Service programme Go Digital.

In the outbreak of the Civil War, Overton served in the Parliamentary army. He was appointed as the Governor of Hull in 1643, and later advanced to the rank of Major-General in 1644. His strong Calvinist faith shaped his political principles, becoming a prominent leader in the Puritan movement.

After his release, Overton lived a relatively quiet life in seclusion. He died in December 1678 and was survived by his wife and eight children. - 1/2 cup unsalted butter, melted

- 2 tablespoons fresh sage, chopped

- 1 lemon, halved
- 1 onion, quartered

- Salt and pepper to taste

- 1/2 cup chopped celery

- 1/2 teaspoon cayenne pepper
- 1/2 teaspoon paprika

- Steamed rice for serving

9. Serve the crawfish étouffée over steamed rice. Enjoy hot.

I hear from the Mussulman mosque the muezzin calling;
I see the worshippers within, (nor form, nor sermon, argument, nor

I hear the Egyptian harp of many strings,
The primitive chants of the Nile boatmen;
The sacred imperial hymns of China,
To the delicate sounds of the king, (the stricken wood and stone;)
Or to Hindu flutes, and the fretting twang of the vina,           120
A band of bayaderes.

To organs huge, and bands, I hear as from vast concourses of voices,

The passionate Agnus Dei, or Gloria in Excelsis.
Composers! mighty maestros!

To you a new bard, carolling free in the west,

Fill me with all the voices of the universe,

Come, for I have found the clue I sought so long,                 150

Nor German organ majestic--nor vast concourse of voices--nor layers
of harmonies;
Nor strophes of husbands and wives--nor sound of marching soldiers,
Nor flutes, nor harps, nor the bugle-calls of camps;              160

Poems, bridging the way from Life to Death, vaguely wafted in night
air, uncaught, unwritten,
Which, let us go forth in the bold day, and write.

prompt: Write a recipe for "Challah, Braided ".
text:
Ingredients:
- 4 cups all-purpose flour
- 1/4 cup granulated sugar
- 2 teaspoons active dry yeast
- 1/2 cup warm water (110°F)
- 1/2 cup vegetable oil
- 3 large eggs
- 1 teaspoon salt
- 1 egg yolk, beaten with 1 tablespoon water (for egg wash)
- Sesame seeds or poppy seeds for topping (optional)

Instructions:
1. In a small bowl, dissolve the yeast in warm water and let it sit for 5 minutes until frothy.

2. In a large mixing bowl, combine flour, sugar, and salt. Make a well in the center and pour in the yeast mixture, vegetable oil, and eggs. Mix until everything is well combined.

3. Transfer the dough onto a floured surface and knead for about 5-7 minutes until smooth and elastic. Add more flour if the dough is too sticky.

4. Place the dough in a greased bowl, cover with a clean kitchen towel, and let it rise in a warm place for about 1-2 hours or until doubled in size.

5. Once the dough has risen, punch it down gently to release any air bubbles. Divide the dough into three equal parts.

6. Roll each portion into a long rope, about 18 inches in length. Place the ropes side by side on a greased baking sheet.

7. Starting from the middle, braid the ropes, bringing the left rope over the middle rope, then the right rope over the new middle rope, and so on until the end. Pinch the ends together and tuck them under the loaf.

8. Cover the loaf with a clean towel and let it rise for another 30-45 minutes.

9. Preheat the oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush the braided challah with the egg wash and sprinkle with sesame seeds or poppy seeds if desired.

10. Bake for 25-30 minutes or until the challah is golden brown and sounds hollow when tapped on the bottom. If the top starts to brown too quickly, cover it loosely with aluminum foil.

11. Remove the challah from the oven and let it cool on a wire rack before slicing and serving.

Enjoy your homemade braided challah! It's perfect for sandwiches, French toast, or simply enjoyed with butter or jam.

text:
Ingredients:

1. 4 oz. cream cheese, softened
2. 1/3 cup granulated sugar
3. 1 cup heavy cream
4. 1/2 tsp. pure vanilla extract
5. 2 large egg yolks
6. 2 tbsp. brown sugar
7. Berries for garnish 

Instructions:

1. Preheat your oven to 325°F (165°C). 
2. In a large bowl, beat the softened cream cheese with an electric mixer on medium speed until it becomes creamy. This should take about 2 minutes.
3. Gradually add the granulated sugar into the cream cheese while continuing to beat on medium. Beat the mixture until it is well combined. 
4. Add the heavy cream and the pure vanilla extract to the cream cheese mixture. Mix until the mixture is smooth and combined.
5. Add in the egg yolks one at a time, beating well after each addition.

rotating about a vertical axis and driven by a vertically invariant horizontal
body-force. This system admits vertically invariant solutions that satisfy the

Ingredients:

For the Donuts:
- 1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
- 1/2 cup raw cane sugar
- 1 teaspoon baking powder
- 1/2 teaspoon baking soda
- 1/4 teaspoon salt
- 1 teaspoon cinnamon
- 2 ripe bananas, mashed
- 1/4 cup non-dairy milk
- 1/4 cup bourbon
- 1 teaspoon apple cider vinegar
- 1/3 cup coconut oil, melted
- 1 teaspoon pure vanilla extract

For the Cashew Cream Cheese Frosting:
- 1 cup cashews, soaked overnight then drained
- 3 tablespoons lemon juice
- 2 tablespoons maple syrup
- 1 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
- Pinch of salt
- 2-4 tablespoons non-dairy milk

Instructions:

1. Preheat your oven to 350°F (175°C). Grease a donut baking pan.
2. In a large bowl, mix together flour, sugar, baking powder, baking soda, salt, and cinnamon.
3. In another bowl, combine the mashed bananas, non-dairy milk, bourbon, apple cider vinegar, melted coconut oil, and vanilla extract. Stir until all ingredients are well combined.
4. Gradually add the wet banana mixture to the dry ingredients. Stir until just combined, being careful not to over mix.
5. Spoon the batter into the prepared donut pan, filling each one about 3/4 of the way full.
6. Bake for 12-15 minutes, or until a toothpick inserted into a donut comes out clean. Allow the donuts to cool in the pan for a few minutes, then transfer them to a wire rack to cool completely.
7. While the donuts are cooling, prepare the Cashew Cream Cheese Frosting. In a blender or food processor, combine the soaked and drained cashews, lemon juice, maple syrup, vanilla extract, salt, and 2 tablespoons of non-dairy milk. Blend until completely smooth, adding additional milk if needed for a smoother consistency.
8. Once the donuts are completely cool, frost them with the Cashew Cream Cheese Frosting.
9. Enjoy your Vegan Baked Banana-Bourbon Donuts with Cashew Cream Cheese Frosting.

- The frosting can be made ahead of time and stored in the fridge until ready to use. 
- The donuts are best enjoyed the day they are made.
- Remember to soak your cashews

text:
In moments of stillness, I feel it creep
A slow and gentle melancholy, a soft embrace
It's not a sadness, not a sorrow, not a tear
But a quiet introspection, a looking inward, dear

It's the feeling of a breeze on a summer eve
The sound of crickets, the rustle of leaves

Sometimes I feel it in the morning light
As the sun rises, and the world takes flight
The dew on the grass, the birds in the trees
A new day dawns, and all things are possible, it seems

It's the feeling of a warm cup in my hands
A sip of coffee, a moment to stand
And watch the world awaken, to feel alive
A time to reflect, to let the world thrive

It's the calm before the storm, the still before the fray
A moment to gather my thoughts, to find my way
To look within, to listen to my heart
A time to remember, to feel the start

Sometimes it comes in the silence of the night
As the stars twinkle, and the world is quiet and bright
A time to dream, to hope, to wish and to pray
A time to let go, to let the world sway

It's the feeling of a gentle touch
A comforting embrace, a loving clutch
A time to feel connected, to feel alive
A moment to know, that I am not alone, I realize

Sometimes it's the stillness that helps me find
My place in the world, my peace of mind
A time to slow down, to take a breath
A moment to know, that all is well, beneath

So I'll cherish these moments of quiet and calm
For in them, I find my peace, my balance, my psalm
As life rushes on, and the world spins round
I'll hold on to these moments, profound.

In the moon-fade and the sun’s puppy breath,
in the crow’s plummeting cry,
in my broken foot and arthritic joints,
memory calls me
to the earth’s opening, the graves dug, again, and again
I, always I am left
to turn away
into a bat’s wing-brush of air.
That never changes . . .
not this morning, not here
where I’ve just found
in the back of my truck, under the rubber mat,
in a teacup’s worth of dirt,
where it seems no seed could possibly be
a corn kernel split to pale leaves and string-roots.
It’s a strange leap but I make it
and bend to these small harvests
because somewhere in North Carolina there was a house
and in it, my room and my bed,
bare boards and the blood stains of a man
that in each slant rain’s worried whispers puddles to the cries of a slave,
murdered in 1863 trying to escape.
Somewhere there was a child who slept
on the living room’s red-vinyl couch
who still matters
especially now that I can’t remember when the creek
that bounded our family farm led to an ocean
or when a boxcar’s weather-wasted letters spelling Illinois
meant somewhere there was an Illinois.
It’s still 1976--
the day after I’ve been seen playing tennis
with a black boy, and it seems I will always
be held at gunpoint and beaten
as if the right punch would chunk out his name.
--------
No, it’s 1969--
The year my mother becomes a wax paste,
or so she looks to the child I was,
and she drips into the pink satin
and I learned the funereal smell of carnations.
That year the moon was still made of green cheese.
That year men first bagged and labeled that moon.
There are no years, only the past
and I still don’t know why Odell Horne
pulled a shotgun on my brother
or how the body contains so much blood.
I still don’t know why Donna Hill went to Myrtle Beach
and three days later came back dead.
For ten years I lived with Louise Stegall,
the lover of my father, one of her four men, all buried--
suicide, murder, drink, again murder.
It was after the second one that she sat stock still
and silent, four years in the asylum.
Now she walks the road all day,
picking up Cracker Jack trinkets
to give to children
brave enough to approach her.
When I was nine, the starling pecked outside her windowa whole week.
Somebody’s gonna die, she said
and made me hug Uncle Robert’s neck
as if I couldn’t know he’d be gone in two hours,
as if I hadn’t learned anything about people
and their vanishing.
The last time I saw her she wouldn’t look at me,
jerked her sweatshirt’s hood across
her face and stepped into the ditch,
as though there are some things even she won’t tell,
as though I’ve never known it’s dirt and dust after all--
the earth’s sink and the worms’ castings.
--------
With the wet leaves thick on my steps,
the evening sky bruised dull gray to black,
when I’ve spilt salt and as the saying goes the sorrow and tears,
and the stove is cold so salt won’t burn,
tell me my pocket of charms can counter any spell.
Tell me again the reason for my grandfather’s fingers
afloat in the Mason jar on the fireplace mantel
between the snuff tin and the bowl of circus peanuts.
What about the teeth in the dresser bureau,
the sliver of back bone I wear around my neck?
Again the washed-out photo in the family album,
Pacific wind lifting the small waves onto Coral Beach,
clicking the palm trees’ fronds.
Again my father’s rakish grin,
his bayonet catching a scratch of sun,
his left foot propped on the stripped and bloodied body.
Behind him, a stack of Japanese.
--------
Let me believe in anything.
Doesn’t the grizzled chicken dig up hoodoo hands?
Won’t the blue door frame, the basket of acorns protect me;
what about the knife in a pail of water?
When giving me the dead’s slippered feet
room to room,
why not also synchronicity’s proof,
a wish and the tilted ears of angels?
I want to believe in the power of rosemary
knuckled along the fence
even as the stars order themselves
to an unalterable and essential law.
I want the wind-whipped leaves to settle
and the flattened scrub to right itself,
want the loose tin in the neighbor’s shed
to finish its message.
When this season in its scoured exactitude shifts closer,
give me Devil’s Blue Boletus through the piled leaves,
the slender green of Earth Tongue,
phosphorescent Honey Tuft dispatched by the dead.
Their voices coming nearer, almost deciphered.
Whatever lies you have
there in that nail-clipping of time,
give them to me.

prompt: Write a recipe for "Pumpkin Spice Creme Brulee".
text:
Pumpkin Spice Creme Brulee Recipe:

Ingredients:
- 1 cup pumpkin puree
- 1 cup heavy cream
- 1/2 cup granulated sugar
- 4 large egg yolks
- 1 teaspoon vanilla extract
- 1 teaspoon pumpkin pie spice
- 1/4 teaspoon salt
- Extra sugar for caramelizing the top

Instructions:
1. Preheat your oven to 325°F (162°C). Place 4 ramekins in a baking dish and set aside.

2. In a medium saucepan, combine the heavy cream, pumpkin puree, pumpkin pie spice, and salt. Heat over medium heat until it almost reaches a simmer. Remove from heat and let it sit for a few minutes to infuse the flavors.

3. In a separate bowl, whisk the egg yolks and sugar until well combined. Slowly pour the heated cream mixture into the egg yolks, whisking constantly to prevent curdling.

4. Stir in the vanilla extract until fully incorporated. Divide the mixture evenly among the ramekins placed in the baking dish.

5. Carefully pour hot water into the baking dish, taking care not to let any water get into the ramekins, until it reaches halfway up the sides of the ramekins. This water bath will help the custard to cook evenly and prevent cracking.

6. Place the baking dish with the ramekins in the preheated oven and bake for approximately 35-40 minutes, or until the custard is set around the edges, but the center still has a slight jiggle.

7. Remove the ramekins from the water bath and let them cool for about 10 minutes. Then cover and refrigerate for at least 2 hours to allow the custard to fully set.

8. Before serving, sprinkle a thin and even layer of sugar on top of each custard. Use a culinary torch to caramelize the sugar until it forms a crispy and golden brown crust. If you don't have a torch, you can also use the broiler in your oven, but monitor closely to avoid burning.

9. Allow the caramelized layer to harden for a few minutes before serving. Enjoy your Pumpkin Spice Creme Brulee with a spoon and savor the rich, creamy pumpkin flavor with a satisfying crunch of caramelized sugar on top.

text:
Title: Broken Glass Jello

Preparation Time: 30 minutes
Setting Time: 4 hours
Serving: 10-12

Ingredients:
- 4 boxes of flavored gelatin (different colors)
- 4 cups of boiling water
- 2 cups of cold water
- 1 cup of sweetened condensed milk
- Cooking spray

Instructions:

1. Prepare a 9x13-inch glass dish by spraying it with cooking spray. This will ensure easy removal of the jello later on.

2. Choose four different flavors of gelatin and start by dissolving one box of gelatin in one cup of boiling water. Stir the mixture until the gelatin is fully dissolved.

3. Add ½ cup of cold water to the gelatin mixture and stir well. Allow the mixture to cool slightly.

4. Pour the gelatin mixture into the prepared glass dish and refrigerate for about 1 hour or until the gelatin is set but not fully firm.

5. Repeat steps 2-4 with the remaining three flavors of gelatin, using a different color for each box.

6. Once all four layers of gelatin have set, it's time to make the broken glass effect. Take a sharp knife and cut the entire dish of set gelatin into small, irregular shapes. Be creative and break the layers apart. The result should resemble a beautiful and colorful mosaic.

7. In a separate bowl, combine the sweetened condensed milk with 1 cup of boiling water. Stir until well mixed.

8. Allow the sweetened condensed milk mixture to cool to room temperature before pouring it over the broken gelatin pieces in the dish.

9. Return the dish to the refrigerator and let it set for at least 3 hours or until the milk layer is fully set.

10. Once the Broken Glass Jello has set, it is ready to be served. Cut it into squares or simply scoop it out with a spoon.

11. Enjoy this delightful and visually appealing dessert! The combination of different flavors and textures makes it a favorite among kids and adults alike.

Note: Broken Glass Jello can be prepared a day ahead of time. Keep it refrigerated until serving for the best taste and appearance.

prompt: Write a recipe for "Coconut Shrimp Summer Rolls".
text:
Coconut Shrimp Summer Rolls Recipe:

Ingredients:
- 8 rice paper wrappers
- 16 medium shrimp, peeled and deveined
- 1 cup sweetened shredded coconut
- 1 cup panko breadcrumbs
- 2 eggs, beaten
- 1 cup flour
- Salt and pepper to taste
- 2 cups mixed salad greens
- 1 cucumber, julienned
- 1 carrot, julienned
- 1/4 cup fresh mint leaves
- 1/4 cup fresh cilantro leaves
- Peanut sauce or sweet chili sauce for dipping

Instructions:
1. Preheat the oven to 400°F (200°C) and line a baking sheet with parchment paper.
2. In separate bowls, place flour, beaten eggs, and a mixture of shredded coconut, panko breadcrumbs, salt, and pepper.
3. Dip each shrimp into the flour, shaking off any excess. Then, dip it into the beaten eggs, allowing any excess to drip off. Finally, coat the shrimp in the coconut-panko mixture, pressing lightly to adhere.
4. Place the coated shrimp onto the prepared baking sheet and bake for 12-15 minutes or until the shrimp turn golden brown and crispy.
5. While the shrimp are baking, prepare the other ingredients for the summer rolls. Julienne the cucumber and carrot, and wash and dry the salad greens, mint leaves, and cilantro leaves.
6. Fill a large shallow bowl with warm water. Dip one rice paper wrapper into the water for a few seconds until it becomes pliable. Carefully transfer the wrapper onto a clean work surface.
7. Arrange 2-3 pieces of shrimp on the bottom third of the rice paper wrapper. Top with a small handful of mixed salad greens, cucumber and carrot slices, and a few fresh mint and cilantro leaves.
8. Fold the sides of the wrapper over the filling and roll it up tightly, similar to rolling a burrito. Repeat this process with the remaining ingredients.
9. Serve the coconut shrimp summer rolls with peanut sauce or sweet chili sauce for dipping. Enjoy immediately!

Note: You can also add additional fillings like avocado slices, bell peppers, or rice noodles to customize the summer rolls according to your taste.

In this paper, we propose a new approach to estimating equations for high-dimensional models, which are models that involve a large number of variables and/or parameters. Our proposed approach, called higher order estimating equations (HOEE), addresses this problem by exploiting the structure of the model to efficiently estimate the parameters. We demonstrate the effectiveness of HOEE through simulations and real-world applications, including image and text processing, recommender systems, and bioinformatics. Our results show that HOEE significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency, and is able to handle models that are too complex for traditional methods.

text:
Carbapenem-resistant enterobacteriaceae (CRE) are a group of bacteria that are resistant to carbapenem antibiotics, a class of widely used antibiotics to treat serious infections. These bacteria are part of the normal flora of the human intestine and are usually harmless. However, in some cases, they can cause severe infections, particularly in people with weakened immune systems, such as those undergoing chemotherapy or with HIV/AIDS.

CREs are a growing concern due to their increasing prevalence and the limited number of effective antibiotics available to treat them. They are resistant to a range of antibiotics, including carbapenems, fluoroquinolones, and aminoglycosides. This makes them difficult to treat and can lead to higher mortality rates in patients.

The spread of CREs is often associated with hospitals, where they can be transmitted to patients through contaminated equipment, surfaces, or healthcare workers. They can also be acquired by patients who have traveled to countries with high rates of CRE infections.

Prevention of CRE infections involves good hygiene practices, such as regular hand washing, as well as proper infection control measures in healthcare settings. Antibiotic stewardship, or the responsible use of antibiotics, is also important in reducing the spread of antibiotic-resistant bacteria.

When CRE infections do occur, it is important to identify the specific strain of bacteria and determine the most effective treatment options. This may involve using alternative antibiotics or combination therapies. In some cases, surgical removal of infected tissue may be necessary.

Efforts are being made to develop new antibiotics and alternative treatment strategies for CRE infections. However, this process is time-consuming and expensive, and there is no guarantee that new therapies will be effective against all strains of CREs. It is, therefore, important to continue to implement prevention measures and promote responsible use of antibiotics to reduce the spread of CRE and other antibiotic-resistant bacteria.

The algorithm stops when the labels converge. We validate the effectiveness of our interactive LPCN method by comparing it with state-of-the-art methods on several benchmark datasets. From a young age, many girls are indoctrinally led to believe that their role in the family is that of a caregiver, someone who's expected to sustain the familial harmony by occasionally compromising her own needs or desires. These lessons often come from seemingly harmless comments, like telling girls they will be mothers one day who will have to put their children before themselves, or portraying the woman's role in the family as synonymous with selflessness.

Now, I can't argue against the necessity of teaching children about compromise and empathy. After all, these are the keystones of any healthy relationship. But is it not problematic if these lessons disproportionately target girls, teaching them that sacrifice is an inherent part of their future?

We rarely teach boys about familial sacrifices to the same extent. Why is it that we cultivate this sense of obligation primarily in girls, potentially influencing them to accept unfulfilling roles or relationships in the future out of a sense of duty? Besides continuing gender stereotypes, this imbalanced messaging might inadvertently contribute to the further conditioning of women's roles as secondary or subordinate.

There is, of course, nothing wrong with women—or anyone—choosing to prioritize their family, to be a stay-at-home parent, etc. But the choice keyword here is "choosing." If, from an early age, we impress upon girls that these sacrifices are expected, we rob them of agency and decision. Instead, shouldn't we be teaching all children, regardless of gender, about responsibilities, compromise, and altruism equally?

I wanted to start this discussion to understand what other members of this community think about this issue. 

Are there better ways we can convey the message of familial responsibility without burdening young girls with the expectation of sacrifice? And how can we make sure this message reaches boys in equal measure? Would love to hear your thoughts on this.

Title: One-stage Shape Instantiation from a Single 2D Image to 3D Point Cloud

Abstract:

Point cloud generation from 2D images has significant potential in diverse applications such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), robotics, and autonomous driving. Traditional methods have relied on object detection and segmentation, followed by shape estimation and point cloud instantiation. However, these methods are often time-consuming and computationally expensive, and may also suffer from occlusions and variations in lighting conditions. In this paper, we propose a novel one-stage approach that directly generates 3D point clouds from a single 2D image in a single deep learning pipeline. We introduce a novel shape instantiation network that learns the geometry of shapes from a 2D image, and integrates it with a 3D point cloud generation network. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on various shapes using an extensive set of 2D images and show competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods. Our work enables real-time point cloud generation from a single 2D image, which paves the way for practical applications in AR, VR, and robotics.

Frosted Brownie Cookies Recipe

Ingredients:
-1 cup of packed flour
-1/2 cup of unsweetened cocoa powder
-1/2 teaspoon of baking powder
-1/4 teaspoon of salt
-2 large eggs
-1 cup of granulated sugar
-1/2 cup of vegetable oil
-2 teaspoons of vanilla extract
-1 cup of semi-sweet chocolate chips

Frosting:

-1/2 cup of unsalted butter, softened
-4 cups of powdered sugar
-1 teaspoon of vanilla extract
-1/4 cup of milk

Instructions:

1. Preheat the oven to 350 degrees Fahrenheit. 
2. Line two baking sheets with parchment paper. 
3. In a medium-sized bowl, whisk together the flour, cocoa powder, baking powder, and salt. 
4. In a separate, larger bowl, beat the eggs and sugar until light and fluffy. 
5. Add the oil and vanilla to the egg mixture, and beat until fully combined.
6. Gradually add the dry ingredients to the wet ingredients, stirring until well mixed. 
7. Fold in the chocolate chips.
8. Using an ice cream scoop or spoon, scoop the dough onto the prepared baking sheets, leaving about 2 inches of space between each cookie. 
9. Bake for 12-15 minutes, or until the cookies are firm around the edges. 
10. Allow the cookies to cool on the baking sheets for 5 minutes before transferring them to wire racks to cool completely. 
11. While the cookies are cooling, make the frosting by beating the cream cheese and butter in a large bowl until smooth. 
12. Add the powdered sugar, vanilla extract, and milk to the frosting, and beat until fully combined.

I understand and appreciate the stringent policies that many animal shelters are implementing in order to ensure their animals are going to secure, loving homes. I know these are crucial checks which serve to avoid cases of returning the pet due to bad matching or unforeseen issues. Half of the time, potential adopters who are ready and willing to provide a loving home are turned away because they don't meet some overly rigid criteria. For instance, I’ve heard of individuals being rejected because they work regular, 9-5 jobs (even though plenty of dog owners maintain this kind of schedule without issue), or because they live in an apartment (despite the fact that many dogs can thrive in smaller spaces).

What matters to a dog's well-being is not the presence of a fence but rather the commitment of the owner to meet the exercise needs of the dog.

A related that issue that really concerns me is the fact that some shelters inflate the costs of adoption fees to an almost prohibitive extent. Fees are necessary, I understand that, for spaying/neutering, vaccinations, etc. But when the costs run into several hundreds of dollars, it detracts potential adopters who can offer a kind and loving home, but may not be financially affluent.

We all agree that there's an unfortunate number of dogs in shelters that need homes. The problem dogs face isn't a lack of people wanting to adopt them; it's unfortunately the red tape and high costs that discourage potential adopters. 

I strongly feel we need to review and reconsider these adoption requirements and costs to make adoption more inclusive and accessible, focusing more on the quality of care prospective owners can provide rather than their living situation or financial standing.

To think of to-day, and the ages continued henceforward!
Have you guess'd you yourself would not continue?
Have you dreaded these earth-beetles?
Have you fear'd the future would be nothing to you?
Is to-day nothing? Is the beginningless past nothing?
If the future is nothing, they are just as surely nothing.
To think that the sun rose in the east! that men and women were
flexible, real, alive! that everything was alive!
To think that you and I did not see, feel, think, nor bear our part!
To think that we are now here, and bear our part!                  10
Not a day passes--not a minute or second, without an accouchement!
Not a day passes--not a minute or second, without a corpse!
The dull nights go over, and the dull days also,
The soreness of lying so much in bed goes over,
The physician, after long putting off, gives the silent and terrible
look for an answer,
The children come hurried and weeping, and the brothers and sisters
are sent for,
Medicines stand unused on the shelf--(the camphor-smell has long
pervaded the rooms,)
The faithful hand of the living does not desert the hand of the
dying,
The twitching lips press lightly on the forehead of the dying,
The breath ceases, and the pulse of the heart ceases,              20
The corpse stretches on the bed, and the living look upon it,
It is palpable as the living are palpable.
The living look upon the corpse with their eye-sight,
But without eye-sight lingers a different living, and looks curiously
on the corpse.
To think the thought of Death, merged in the thought of materials!
To think that the rivers will flow, and the snow fall, and fruits
ripen, and act upon others as upon us now--yet not act upon us!
To think of all these wonders of city and country, and others taking
great interest in them--and we taking no interest in them!
To think how eager we are in building our houses!
To think others shall be just as eager, and we quite indifferent!
(I see one building the house that serves him a few years, or seventy
or eighty years at most,                                     30
I see one building the house that serves him longer than that.)
Slow-moving and black lines creep over the whole earth--they never
cease--they are the burial lines,
He that was President was buried, and he that is now President shall
surely be buried.
A reminiscence of the vulgar fate,
A frequent sample of the life and death of workmen,
Each after his kind:
Cold dash of waves at the ferry-wharf--posh and ice in the river,
half-frozen mud in the streets, a gray, discouraged sky
overhead, the short, last daylight of Twelfth-month,
A hearse and stages--other vehicles give place--the funeral of an old
Broadway stage-driver, the cortege mostly drivers.
Steady the trot to the cemetery, duly rattles the death-bell, the
gate is pass'd, the new-dug grave is halted at, the living
alight, the hearse uncloses,
The coffin is pass'd out, lower'd and settled, the whip is laid on
the coffin, the earth is swiftly shovel'd in,                40
The mound above is flatted with the spades--silence,
A minute--no one moves or speaks--it is done,
He is decently put away--is there anything more?
He was a good fellow, free-mouth'd, quick-temper'd, not bad-looking,
able to take his own part, witty, sensitive to a slight, ready
with life or death for a friend, fond of women, gambled, ate
hearty, drank hearty, had known what it was to be flush, grew
low-spirited toward the last, sicken'd, was help'd by a
contribution, died, aged forty-one years--and that was his
funeral.
Thumb extended, finger uplifted, apron, cape, gloves, strap, wet-
weather clothes, whip carefully chosen, boss, spotter, starter,
hostler, somebody loafing on you, you loafing on somebody,
headway, man before and man behind, good day's work, bad day's
work, pet stock, mean stock, first out, last out, turning-in at
night;
To think that these are so much and so nigh to other drivers--and he
there takes no interest in them!
The markets, the government, the working-man's wages--to think what
account they are through our nights and days!
To think that other working-men will make just as great account of
them--yet we make little or no account!
The vulgar and the refined--what you call sin, and what you call
goodness--to think how wide a difference!
To think the difference will still continue to others, yet we lie
beyond the difference.                                       50
To think how much pleasure there is!
Have you pleasure from looking at the sky? have you pleasure from
poems?
Do you enjoy yourself in the city? or engaged in business? or
planning a nomination and election? or with your wife and
family?
Or with your mother and sisters? or in womanly housework? or the
beautiful maternal cares?
--These also flow onward to others--you and I flow onward,
But in due time, you and I shall take less interest in them.
Your farm, profits, crops,--to think how engross'd you are!
To think there will still be farms, profits, crops--yet for you, of
what avail?
What will be, will be well--for what is, is well,
To take interest is well, and not to take interest shall be well.  60
The sky continues beautiful,
The pleasure of men with women shall never be sated, nor the pleasure
of women with men, nor the pleasure from poems,
The domestic joys, the daily housework or business, the building of
houses--these are not phantasms--they have weight, form,
location;
Farms, profits, crops, markets, wages, government, are none of them
phantasms,
The difference between sin and goodness is no delusion,
The earth is not an echo--man and his life, and all the things of his
life, are well-consider'd.
You are not thrown to the winds--you gather certainly and safely
around yourself;
Yourself! Yourself! Yourself, forever and ever!
It is not to diffuse you that you were born of your mother and
father--it is to identify you;
It is not that you should be undecided, but that you should be
decided;                                                     70

You are henceforth secure, whatever comes or goes.
The threads that were spun are gather'd, the weft crosses the warp,

The preparations have every one been justified,
The orchestra have sufficiently tuned their instruments--the baton
has given the signal.
The guest that was coming--he waited long, for reasons--he is now
housed,
He is one of those who are beautiful and happy--he is one of those

The law of the past cannot be eluded,
The law of the present and future cannot be eluded,
The law of the living cannot be eluded--it is eternal,             80

The law of heroes and good-doers cannot be eluded,

can be eluded.
Slow moving and black lines go ceaselessly over the earth,

Atlantic side, and they on the Pacific, and they between, and
all through the Mississippi country, and all over the earth.

good-doers are well,
The known leaders and inventors, and the rich owners and pious and
distinguish'd, may be well,
But there is more account than that--there is strict account of all.
The interminable hordes of the ignorant and wicked are not nothing,
The barbarians of Africa and Asia are not nothing,                 90
The common people of Europe are not nothing--the American aborigines
are not nothing,
The infected in the immigrant hospital are not nothing--the murderer
or mean person is not nothing,
The perpetual successions of shallow people are not nothing as they
go,
The lowest prostitute is not nothing--the mocker of religion is not
nothing as he goes.
Of and in all these things,
I have dream'd that we are not to be changed so much, nor the law of
us changed,
I have dream'd that heroes and good-doers shall be under the present
and past law,
And that murderers, drunkards, liars, shall be under the present and

If maggots and rats ended us, then Alarum! for we are betray'd!

The past and the present indicate that it is good.
How beautiful and perfect are the animals!

What is called good is perfect, and what is called bad is just as

That the exquisite scheme is for it, and the nebulous float is for
