prompt: Write a recipe for "Mom’S Chicken Soup".
text:
Title: Mom's Chicken Soup

Ingredients:
- 1 whole chicken, cut into pieces
- 1 onion, diced
- 2 carrots, sliced
- 2 celery stalks, sliced
- 4 garlic cloves, minced
- 1 teaspoon dried thyme
- 1 teaspoon dried rosemary
- 2 bay leaves
- Salt and pepper, to taste
- 8 cups chicken broth
- 1 cup egg noodles or rice (optional)
- Chopped fresh parsley, for garnish

Instructions:

1. In a large pot, add the chicken pieces and cover with water. Bring to a boil over medium-high heat and skim off any foam that rises to the surface. Reduce the heat to low, cover, and let it simmer for about an hour until the chicken is cooked tender.

2. Remove the chicken from the pot and set aside to cool. Once cooled, shred the meat into bite-sized pieces and discard the bones and skin. Keep the shredded chicken aside.

3. In the same pot, sauté the diced onion, sliced carrots, sliced celery, and minced garlic for about 5 minutes until the vegetables become tender.

4. Add the dried thyme, dried rosemary, bay leaves, salt, and pepper. Stir well to combine the flavors.

5. Pour in the chicken broth and bring the mixture to a boil. Reduce the heat to low and let it simmer for about 20 minutes to allow the flavors to meld.

6. If desired, add the egg noodles or rice to the pot and cook according to the package instructions until al dente.

7. Once the noodles or rice are cooked, add the shredded chicken back into the pot, and simmer for an additional 5-10 minutes until heated through.

8. Remove the bay leaves from the soup and discard.

9. Garnish with chopped fresh parsley and serve hot.

Note: Mom's Chicken Soup can be stored in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. It can also be frozen for longer storage.

prompt: Write a recipe for "Tita Aida's Mocha Cake".
text:
Ingredients:

- 1 cup of unsweetened cocoa powder
- 2 tsp of baking powder
- 1 tsp of baking soda
- 1 tsp of salt
- 1 cup of unsalted butter, softened
- 3/4 cup of granulated sugar
- 3/4 cup of brown sugar
- 3 large eggs
- 1 tbsp of vanilla extract
- 2 cups of brewed coffee
- 1 cup of milk
- 1/2 cup of vegetable oil
- Chocolate chips or chopped walnuts (optional)

Instructions:

1. Preheat your oven to 350°F (175°C). Grease two 9-inch round cake pans with cooking spray or butter.

6. Gradually add the flour mixture, alternating with coffee and milk. Mix until just combined.
7. Fold in the vegetable oil until the batter is smooth.
8. Divide the batter evenly between the two prepared cake pans.
9. Bake for 30-35 minutes or until a toothpick inserted into the center of the cakes comes out clean.
10. Let the cakes cool in the pans for 10 minutes, then transfer them to a wire rack to cool completely.
11. Once the cakes are cooled, spread a layer of frosting in between the two layers, then frost the top and sides of the cake with a generous amount of mocha frosting.

text:
Grilled Chicken With Cola Sauce Recipe

Ingredients:
- 4 boneless, skinless chicken breasts
- Salt and pepper, to taste
- 1 cup cola
- 1/2 cup ketchup
- 1/4 cup brown sugar
- 2 tablespoons apple cider vinegar
- 1 tablespoon Worcestershire sauce
- 1 tablespoon Dijon mustard
- 1 teaspoon garlic powder
- 1 teaspoon onion powder
- Vegetable oil, for grilling
- Fresh parsley or green onions, for garnish (optional)

Instructions:

1. Preheat your grill to medium-high heat.

2. Season the chicken breasts with salt and pepper on both sides.

3. In a medium saucepan, combine the cola, ketchup, brown sugar, vinegar, Worcestershire sauce, Dijon mustard, garlic powder, and onion powder. Stir well to combine.

4. Place the saucepan over medium heat and bring the mixture to a simmer. Cook for about 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the sauce has thickened slightly.

5. Set aside about half of the sauce for basting the chicken while grilling.

6. Brush the grill grates with vegetable oil to prevent sticking.

7. Place the chicken breasts on the preheated grill and cook for about 4-5 minutes per side, or until the chicken reaches an internal temperature of 165°F (75°C) and is no longer pink in the center.

8. During the last few minutes of grilling, baste the chicken breasts with the reserved sauce on both sides, allowing it to caramelize slightly.

9. Remove the chicken from the grill and let it rest for a few minutes. This will help the juices redistribute and keep the chicken moist.

10. Serve the grilled chicken with the remaining cola sauce on the side. Garnish with fresh parsley or green onions, if desired.

Enjoy your delicious Grilled Chicken With Cola Sauce! It pairs well with rice, roasted vegetables, or a fresh salad.

prompt: Write a recipe for "Low Carb Flavored Meringue Cookies".
text:
Low Carb Flavored Meringue Cookies

Ingredients:
- 4 egg whites
- 1/2 teaspoon cream of tartar
- 1/2 cup powdered sugar substitute (such as erythritol or stevia)
- 1 teaspoon vanilla extract or your preferred flavor extract (such as almond, lemon, or raspberry)

Instructions:
1. Preheat your oven to 200°F (95°C) and line a baking sheet with parchment paper.
2. In a clean, dry mixing bowl, add the egg whites and cream of tartar. Use an electric mixer to beat the egg whites until foamy.
3. Gradually add the powdered sugar substitute while continuing to beat the egg whites. Beat until stiff peaks form and the mixture is glossy.
4. Add the vanilla extract or your preferred flavor extract and gently fold it into the meringue mixture using a spatula or wooden spoon. Do not overmix.
5. Transfer the meringue mixture to a piping bag fitted with a large star tip, or use a spoon to drop dollops of the mixture onto the prepared baking sheet.
6. Bake the meringue cookies in the preheated oven for 1.5 to 2 hours, or until they are dry and crisp on the outside.
7. Once fully baked, remove the cookies from the oven and allow them to cool on the baking sheet for a few minutes. Then transfer them to a wire rack to cool completely.
8. Enjoy the low carb flavored meringue cookies as a guilt-free treat or store them in an airtight container for up to a week.

Note: The baking time may vary depending on the size and shape of your meringue cookies. Keep an eye on them towards the end of the baking time to prevent burning.

==============================================================================

Abstract

Segmentation models have been widely used in various computer vision applications including medical imaging, objects detection, and image analysis. However, the effectiveness of these models heavily depends on the quality of the segmented output. In this paper, we aim to address this gap by presenting a comprehensive study to evaluate and compare the quality of segmentation results using deep learning-based models. We provide a thorough study on the effect of model hyperparameters on the segmentation quality and present a novel real-time prediction method that allows for the selection of the optimal model-hyperparameters combination. text:
Title: Broiled Tomato Soup

Category: Appetizer

Servings: 4

Ingredients:
- 4 large tomatoes
- 1 medium onion, chopped
- 3 cloves garlic, minced
- 2 tablespoons olive oil
- 4 cups vegetable or chicken broth
- 1 tablespoon tomato paste
- 1 teaspoon dried basil
- 1 teaspoon dried oregano
- Salt and pepper, to taste
- Optional toppings: croutons, grated Parmesan cheese, fresh basil leaves

Instructions:

1. Preheat your broiler and adjust the oven rack to the highest position.

2. On a baking sheet, place the tomatoes whole. Broil them for about 5-7 minutes or until the skin starts to blister and blacken. Turn the tomatoes over and broil for an additional 5 minutes.

3. Remove the baking sheet from the oven and let the tomatoes cool. Once cooled, carefully peel off the skin and discard it.

4. In a large pot, heat the olive oil over medium heat. Add the chopped onion and minced garlic. Sauté for about 5 minutes until the onion becomes translucent and fragrant.

5. Add the peeled tomatoes to the pot and stir for a minute or two to combine the flavors. Then, pour in the vegetable or chicken broth, tomato paste, dried basil, dried oregano, and season with salt and pepper.

6. Bring the mixture to a boil, reduce the heat to low, and let it simmer for 20 minutes to allow the flavors to meld together.

7. Using an immersion blender or regular blender, puree the soup until smooth. If using a regular blender, allow the soup to cool slightly and blend in batches.

8. Return the soup to the pot and bring it back to a simmer. Taste and adjust the seasoning if necessary.

9. To serve, ladle the broiled tomato soup into bowls and garnish with optional toppings such as croutons, grated Parmesan cheese, or fresh basil leaves.

This time, however, the protagonist seeks to verify Teresa’s story along with trying to locate her mother. Many approaches to 3D image segmentation are based on hierarchical clustering
of supervoxels into image regions. Here we describe a distributed algorithm
capable of handling a tremendous number of supervoxels. The algorithm works
recursively, the regions are divided into chunks that are processed
independently in parallel by multiple workers. At each round of the recursive
procedure, the chunk size in all dimensions are doubled until a single chunk
encompasses the entire image. The final result is provably independent of the
chunking scheme, and the same as if the entire image were processed without
division into chunks. This is nontrivial because a pair of adjacent regions is
scored by some statistical property (e.g. mean or median) of the affinities at
the interface, and the interface may extend over arbitrarily many chunks. The
trick is to delay merge decisions for regions that touch chunk boundaries, and
only complete them in a later round after the regions are fully contained
within a chunk. We demonstrate the algorithm by clustering an affinity graph
with over 1.5 trillion edges between 135 billion supervoxels derived from a 3D
electron microscopic brain image.

Image segmentation is a popular area of research in computer vision that has
many applications in automated image processing. A recent technique called
piecewise flat embeddings (PFE) has been proposed for use in image
segmentation; PFE transforms image pixel data into a lower dimensional
representation where similar pixels are pulled close together and dissimilar
pixels are pushed apart. This technique has shown promising results, but its
original formulation is not computationally feasible for large images. We
propose two improvements to the algorithm for computing PFE: first, we
reformulate portions of the algorithm to enable various linear algebra
operations to be performed in parallel; second, we propose utilizing an
iterative linear solver (preconditioned conjugate gradient) to quickly solve a
linear least-squares problem that occurs in the inner loop of a nested
iteration. With these two computational improvements, we show on a publicly
available image database that PFE can be sped up by an order of magnitude
without sacrificing segmentation performance. Our results make this technique
more practical for use on large data sets, not only for image segmentation, but
for general data clustering problems.

text:
This paper proposes a novel approach for semi-supervised histopathology image segmentation, which leverages the abundance of unlabeled data to improve the accuracy of segmentation models. Existing methods rely heavily on labeled data, which is time-consuming and expensive to obtain. In contrast, our approach utilizes a large collection of unlabeled images to guide the training process, resulting in improved segmentation performance with significantly less labeled data.

We propose a two-stage framework, consisting of a self-supervised learning stage and a semi-supervised learning stage. In the self-supervised learning stage, we use a contrastive loss function to train a representation learning model on the unlabeled data, which learns to encode images with similar features close together in the latent space. In the semi-supervised learning stage, we use a segmentation model that incorporates the learned representation to segment the labeled data, as well as a small portion of the unlabeled data that is pseudo-labeled using the predicted segmentation masks.

Our approach is evaluated on several histopathology datasets, and shows significant improvement in segmentation accuracy compared to state-of-the-art semi-supervised methods that rely solely on labeled data. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in scenarios where the amount of labeled data is limited, showcasing its potential to reduce the annotation effort required for histopathology image segmentation.

The main contributions of this paper are:

* A novel semi-supervised histopathology image segmentation approach that leverages unlabeled data to improve segmentation accuracy
* A two-stage framework consisting of a self-supervised learning stage and a semi-supervised learning stage
* A contrastive loss function used in the self-supervised learning stage to learn robust image representations
* An extensive evaluation of our approach on several histopathology datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in improving segmentation accuracy with reduced annotation effort.

Overall, this paper presents a promising direction for histopathology image segmentation, and highlights the potential of unlabeled data to improve the accuracy and efficiency of segmentation models.

The segmentation of animals from camera-trap images is a difficult task. To
illustrate, there are various challenges due to environmental conditions and
hardware limitation in these images. We proposed a multi-layer robust principal
component analysis (multi-layer RPCA) approach for background subtraction. Our
method computes sparse and low-rank images from a weighted sum of descriptors,
using color and texture features as case of study for camera-trap images
segmentation. The segmentation algorithm is composed of histogram equalization
or Gaussian filtering as pre-processing, and morphological filters with active
contour as post-processing. The parameters of our multi-layer RPCA were
optimized with an exhaustive search. The database consists of camera-trap
images from the Colombian forest taken by the Instituto de Investigaci\'on de
Recursos Biol\'ogicos Alexander von Humboldt. We analyzed the performance of
our method in inherent and therefore challenging situations of camera-trap
images. Furthermore, we compared our method with some state-of-the-art
algorithms of background subtraction, where our multi-layer RPCA outperformed
these other methods. Our multi-layer RPCA reached 76.17 and 69.97% of average
fine-grained F-measure for color and infrared sequences, respectively. To our
best knowledge, this paper is the first work proposing multi-layer RPCA and
using it for camera-trap images segmentation.

text:
In this paper, we present a novel approach to video description, called the Multi-scale Multiple Instance Video Description Network (MMIVDN), which leverages the strengths of both multi-scale and multiple instance learning to improve the accuracy and efficiency of video description.

Existing video description methods typically rely on a single-scale representation of the video data, which can be limited in capturing the complex and varied information present in modern videos. In addition, these methods often require expensive and time-consuming annotation processes to obtain high-quality descriptions.

In contrast, the MMIVDN proposes a multi-scale representation of the video data, which allows it to capture information at multiple levels of granularity. This is combined with a multiple instance learning approach, which enables the network to learn from a large number of video clips, each with its own set of possible descriptions.

The MMIVDN is trained end-to-end using a large dataset of video clips, and is able to learn a mapping between the video data and the corresponding descriptions. Our experiments show that the MMIVDN outperforms state-of-the-art video description methods in terms of both accuracy and efficiency. Specifically, we demonstrate that the MMIVDN can generate high-quality descriptions for a given video with significantly fewer annotations than traditional methods.

The key contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows:

* We propose a novel approach to video description, the Multi-scale Multiple Instance Video Description Network (MMIVDN), which combines the strengths of multi-scale and multiple instance learning.
* We demonstrate the effectiveness of the MMIVDN through extensive experiments on a large dataset of video clips, showing that it outperforms state-of-the-art video description methods in terms of both accuracy and efficiency.
* We analyze the performance of the MMIVDN under different settings, providing insights into the roles of the various components and the trade-offs between accuracy and efficiency.

Overall, the MMIVDN represents a significant step forward in the field of video description, and has the potential to enable a wide range of new applications in video analysis, search, and summarization.

- 1/2 teaspoon black pepper

Air more than water, fire much more than air,
And heaven than fire, appears more pure and fair.
Look thou no further, but affix thine eye
On that bright, shiny, round, still moving mass,
The house of blessed gods, which men call sky,
All sow'd with glist'ring stars more thick than grass,
Whereof each other doth in brightness pass,
But those two most, which ruling night and day,
As king and queen, the heavens' empire sway;
And tell me then, what hast thou ever seen
That to their beauty may compared be,
Or can the sight that is most sharp and keen
Endure their captain's flaming head to see?
How much less those, much higher in degree,
And so much fairer, and much more than these,
As these are fairer than the land and seas?
For far above these heavens, which here we see,
Be others far exceeding these in light,
Not bounded, not corrupt, as these same be,
But infinite in largeness and in height,
Unmoving, uncorrupt, and spotless bright,
That need no sun t' illuminate their spheres,
But their own native light far passing theirs.
And as these heavens still by degrees arise,
Until they come to their first Mover's bound,
That in his mighty compass doth comprise,
And carry all the rest with him around;
So those likewise do by degrees redound,
And rise more fair; till they at last arrive
To the most fair, whereto they all do strive.
Fair is the heaven where happy souls have place,
In full enjoyment of felicity,
Whence they do still behold the glorious face
Of the divine eternal Majesty;
More fair is that, where those Ideas on high
Enranged be, which Plato so admired,
And pure Intelligences from God inspired.
Yet fairer is that heaven, in which do reign
The sovereign Powers and mighty Potentates,
Which in their high protections do contain
All mortal princes and imperial states;
And fairer yet, whereas the royal Seats
And heavenly Dominations are set,
From whom all earthly governance is fet.
Yet far more fair be those bright Cherubins,
Which all with golden wings are overdight,
And those eternal burning Seraphins,
Which from their faces dart out fiery light;
Yet fairer than they both, and much more bright,
Be th' Angels and Archangels, which attend
On God's own person, without rest or end.
These thus in fair each other far excelling,
As to the highest they approach more near,
Yet is that highest far beyond all telling,
Fairer than all the rest which there appear,
Though all their beauties join'd together were;
How then can mortal tongue hope to express
The image of such endless perfectness?
Cease then, my tongue, and lend unto my mind
Leave to bethink how great that beauty is,
Whose utmost parts so beautiful I find;
How much more those essential parts of his,
His truth, his love, his wisdom, and his bliss,
His grace, his doom, his mercy, and his might,
By which he lends us of himself a sight.
Those unto all he daily doth display,
And shew himself in th' image of his grace,
As in a looking-glass, through which he may
Be seen of all his creatures vile and base,
That are unable else to see his face,
His glorious face which glistereth else so bright,
That th' Angels selves cannot endure his sight.
But we, frail wights, whose sight cannot sustain
The sun's bright beams when he on us doth shine,
But that their points rebutted back again
Are dull'd, how can we see with feeble eyne
The glory of that Majesty Divine,
In sight of whom both sun and moon are dark,
Compared to his least resplendent spark?
The means, therefore, which unto us is lent
Him to behold, is on his works to look,
Which he hath made in beauty excellent,
And in the same, as in a brazen book,
To read enregister'd in every nook
His goodness, which his beauty doth declare;
For all that's good is beautiful and fair.
Thence gathering plumes of perfect speculation,
To imp the wings of thy high-flying mind,
Mount up aloft through heavenly contemplation,
From this dark world, whose damps the soul so blind,
And, like the native brood of eagles' kind,
On that bright Sun of Glory fix thine eyes,
Clear'd from gross mists of frail infirmities.
Humbled with fear and awful reverence,
Before the footstool of his majesty
Throw thyself down, with trembling innocence,
Ne dare look up with corruptible eye
On the dread face of that great Deity,
For fear, lest if he chance to look on thee,
Thou turn to nought, and quite confounded be.
But lowly fall before his mercy seat,
Close covered with the Lamb's integrity
From the just wrath of his avengeful threat
That sits upon the righteous throne on high;
His throne is built upon eternity,
More firm and durable than steel or brass,
Or the hard diamond, which them both doth pass.
His sceptre is the rod of righteousness,
With which he bruiseth all his foes to dust,
And the great Dragon strongly doth repress,
Under the rigour of his judgement just;
His seat is truth, to which the faithful trust,
From whence proceed her beams so pure and bright
That all about him sheddeth glorious light:
Light far exceeding that bright blazing spark
Which darted is from Titan's flaming head,
That with his beams enlumineth the dark
And dampish air, whereby all things are read;
Whose nature yet so much is marvelled
Of mortal wits, that it doth much amaze
The greatest wizards which thereon do gaze.
But that immortal light, which there doth shine,
Is many thousand times more bright, more clear,
More excellent, more glorious, more divine,
Through which to God all mortal actions here,
And even the thoughts of men, do plain appear;
For from th' eternal truth it doth proceed,
Through heavenly virtue which her beams do breed.
With the great glory of that wondrous light
His throne is all encompassed around,
And hid in his own brightness from the sight
Of all that look thereon with eyes unsound;
And underneath his feet are to be found
Thunder and lightning and tempestuous fire,
The instruments of his avenging ire.
There in his bosom Sapience doth sit,
The sovereign darling of the Deity,
Clad like a queen in royal robes, most fit
For so great power and peerless majesty,
And all with gems and jewels gorgeously
Adorn'd, that brighter than the stars appear,
And make her native brightness seem more clear.
And on her head a crown of purest gold
Is set, in sign of highest sovereignty;
And in her hand a sceptre she doth hold,
With which she rules the house of God on high,
And manageth the ever-moving sky,
And in the same these lower creatures all
Subjected to her power imperial.
Both heaven and earth obey unto her will,
And all the creatures which they both contain;
For of her fullness which the world doth fill
They all partake, and do in state remain
As their great Maker did at first ordain,
Through observation of her high behest,
By which they first were made, and still increast.
The fairness of her face no tongue can tell;
For she the daughters of all women's race,
And angels eke, in beauty doth excel,
Sparkled on her from God's own glorious face,
And more increas'd by her own goodly grace,
That it doth far exceed all human thought,
Ne can on earth compared be to aught.
Ne could that painter (had he lived yet)
Which pictured Venus with so curious quill,
That all posterity admired it,
Have portray'd this, for all his mast'ring skill;
Ne she herself, had she remained still,
And were as fair as fabling wits do feign,
Could once come near this beauty sovereign.
But had those wits, the wonders of their days,
Or that sweet Teian poet, which did spend
His plenteous vein in setting forth her praise,
Seen but a glimpse of this which I pretend,
How wondrously would he her face commend,
Above that idol of his feigning thought,
That all the world should with his rhymes be fraught.
How then dare I, the novice of his art,
Presume to picture so divine a wight,
Or hope t' express her least perfection's part,
Whose beauty fills the heavens with her light,
And darks the earth with shadow of her sight?
Ah, gentle Muse, thou art too weak and faint
The portrait of so heavenly hue to paint.
Let angels, which her goodly face behold
And see at will, her sovereign praises sing,
And those most sacred mysteries unfold
Of that fair love of mighty heaven's King;
Enough is me t' admire so heavenly thing,
And being thus with her huge love possest,
In th' only wonder of herself to rest.
But whoso may, thrice happy man him hold,
Of all on earth whom God so much doth grace
And lets his own beloved to behold;
For in the view of her celestial face
All joy, all bliss, all happiness, have place;
Ne aught on earth can want unto the wight
Who of herself can win the wishful sight.
For she, out of her secret treasury,
Plenty of riches forth on him will pour,
Even heavenly riches, which there hidden lie
Within the closet of her chastest bower,
Th' eternal portion of her precious dower,
Which mighty God hath given to her free,
And to all those which thereof worthy be.
None thereof worthy be, but those whom she
Vouchsafeth to her presence to receive,
And letteth them her lovely face to see,
Whereof such wondrous pleasures they conceive,
And sweet contentment, that it doth bereave
Their soul of sense, through infinite delight,
And them transport from flesh into the spright.
In which they see such admirable things,
As carries them into an ecstasy,
And hear such heavenly notes, and carollings
Of God's high praise, that fills the brazen sky;
And feel such joy and pleasure inwardly,
That maketh them all worldly cares forget,
And only think on that before them set.
Ne from thenceforth doth any fleshly sense,
Or idle thought of earthly things, remain;
But all that erst seem'd sweet seems now offence,
And all that pleased erst now seems to pain;
Their joy, their comfort, their desire, their gain,
Is fixed all on that which now they see;
All other sights but feigned shadows be.
And that fair lamp, which useth to inflame
The hearts of men with self-consuming fire
Thenceforth seems foul, and full of sinful blame;
And all that pomp to which proud minds aspire
By name of honour, and so much desire,
Seems to them baseness, and all riches dross,
And all mirth sadness, and all lucre loss.
So full their eyes are of that glorious sight,
And senses fraught with such satiety,
That in nought else on earth they can delight,
But in th' aspect of that felicity,
Which they have written in their inward eye;
On which they feed, and in their fastened mind
All happy joy and full contentment find.
Ah, then, my hungry soul, which long hast fed
On idle fancies of thy foolish thought,
And, with false beauty's flatt'ring bait misled,
Hast after vain deceitful shadows sought,
Which all are fled, and now have left thee nought
But late repentance through thy follies prief;
Ah cease to gaze on matter of thy grief:
And look at last up to that sovereign light,
From whose pure beams all perfect beauty springs,
That kindleth love in every godly sprite,
Even the love of God, which loathing brings
Of this vile world and these gay-seeming things;
With whose sweet pleasures being so possest,
Thy straying thoughts henceforth for ever rest.

Theory of Formal Functions
Classical Form, along with a more recently published, lengthy textbook intended for both undergraduate and graduate levels, expounds a theory and analytical method for the music of the "high Classical" era (roughly, the two decades before and after 1800). text:
In this paper, we present a novel approach to multi-object tracking that combines the strengths of category-agnostic object detection and track-before-detect methods. Our proposed method, called "Track, then Decide," leverages the benefits of both paradigms to achieve state-of-the-art performance in visual object tracking.

Existing track-before-detect methods rely on a priori knowledge of object categories, which can be limiting in real-world scenarios where objects may belong to unknown or varying categories. In contrast, category-agnostic object detection methods can detect objects without prior knowledge of their categories, but they often lack the ability to track objects over time.

Our proposed method bridges this gap by first detecting objects using a category-agnostic detector, and then tracking them using a track-before-detect approach. We introduce a novel tracking-by-detection strategy that allows us to track objects across frames without requiring explicit category information.

We evaluate our method on several challenging benchmark datasets, including LaSOT, GOT-10k, and ID tracking. Our results show that "Track, then Decide" outperforms state-of-the-art track-before-detect and category-agnostic object detection methods, while also maintaining real-time performance.

Our key contributions include:

* A novel track-before-detect method that operates category-agnostically, without requiring prior knowledge of object categories.
* A tracking-by-detection strategy that enables effective tracking of objects across frames, even in the absence of explicit category information.
* State-of-the-art performance on several challenging benchmark datasets, demonstrating the efficacy of our proposed approach.

Overall, our work advances the state-of-the-art in visual object tracking by introducing a novel category-agnostic approach that leverages the strengths of both track-before-detect and category-agnostic object detection methods.

prompt: Write a recipe for "Durgin Park Baked Beans".
text:
Ingredients:
- 1 lb dry navy beans
- 6 cups of water
- 1/2 pound salt pork, cut into two pieces
- 1 large onion, finely chopped
- 1/2 cup molasses
- 3 tbsp packed light or dark brown sugar
- 1/4 cup ketchup
- 1 tbsp dry mustard
- 1/2 tsp fine sea salt
- 1/4 tsp ground black pepper
- 1 tsp apple cider vinegar

Instructions:

1. Rinse the navy beans and place them in a large bowl. Add enough water to cover the beans by at least 2 inches. Let the beans soak for at least 8 hours or overnight.

2. Preheat your oven to 300°F (150°C).

3. Drain the beans and place them in a large pot. Add six cups of water, bring the pot to a boil. Reduce heat, cover, and let simmer for 30 minutes.

4. In a saucepan, combine molasses, brown sugar, ketchup, dry mustard, salt, and pepper. Heat over medium heat, stirring often until sugar is melted and mixture is hot.

5. Carefully score each piece of the salt pork, cutting halfway through in a diamond pattern.

6. In a large, oven-safe pot or bean pot, place half of the salt pork in the bottom of the pot. Top with half of the chopped onions, then half of the beans. Repeat the layering process with the remaining pork, onions, and beans.

7. Pour the hot molasses mixture over the beans. Add boiling water, if necessary, until the beans are just covered.

8. Cover the pot and bake for 2 hours. Check every 30 minutes, adding more boiling water if necessary to keep the beans covered. 

9. After 2 hours, uncover the pot, stir the beans and bake for another 2 hours until the beans are tender and the sauce is syrupy.

10. Remove the pot from the oven and stir in the apple cider vinegar. Let the beans sit for a bit before serving for the flavors to meld together.

Optional: For a smokier flavor, consider adding a bit of liquid smoke with the molasses mixture.

Note: This recipe takes time but it is worth it for a hearty and delicious batch of baked beans.

Early Life and Education

Born on July 30, 1878, in Yorkville, Tennessee, Douglass was one of four daughters. In 1921, Douglass signed a five-year contract with the T'a Ts'ai art firm, granting her a unique opportunity to study imperial Chinese art in Beijing. She went on to share her specialized knowledge with the Western world through lectures, writing, and teaching at numerous institutions, including the University of Oregon, the University of California, the Cleveland Museum of Art, and the Honolulu Academy of Arts. Douglass's integration of Eastern and Western painting styles were highly unique and contributed significantly to the cultural cross-pollination of art styles.

text:
Ingredients:
- 500g strong bread flour
- 10g salt
- 7g instant yeast
- 350ml warm water

Instructions:
1. In a large mixing bowl, combine the flour and salt. Make a well in the center and add the yeast.
2. Pour the warm water into the well with the yeast and gradually mix the flour into the water with a wooden spoon until it forms a dough.
3. Knead the dough on a lightly floured surface for about 10 minutes until it becomes smooth and elastic.
4. Place the dough back in the mixing bowl, cover it with a clean kitchen towel, and let it rise in a warm place for about 1-2 hours or until it has doubled in size.
5. Once the dough has risen, remove it from the bowl and divide it into three equal pieces.
6. Shape each piece into a baguette by rolling it out into a long, thin rectangle. Then, starting from one end, roll the dough tightly into a cylinder shape, tucking the ends underneath.
7. Place the baguettes on a floured baking tray, cover them with a clean kitchen towel, and let them rise for another 30-45 minutes, or until they have doubled in size.
8. Preheat your oven to 220°C (425°F). Optional: Place a baking stone or a baking tray on the bottom rack of the oven to preheat as well.
9. Score the tops of the risen baguettes with a sharp knife or a bread lame.
10. Place the baguettes in the preheated oven (and if using a baking stone, transfer them onto it) and bake for about 20-25 minutes, or until they turn golden brown and make a hollow sound when tapped on the bottom.
11. Once baked, remove the baguettes from the oven and let them cool on a wire rack before serving.

text:
Recipe for Fig Square

Ingredients:

For the Fig Filling:
- 3 cups dried figs
- 1 cup water
- 1 cup sugar
- 1 teaspoon lemon juice

For the Square:
- 2 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
- 1/2 teaspoon baking powder
- 1/4 teaspoon salt
- 1 cup unsalted butter, softened
- 1 cup brown sugar
- 1 large egg
- 1 teaspoon vanilla extract
- 1 cup granulated sugar for topping

Instructions:

1. Start with preparing the fig filling. Trim off the stems from the dried figs and cut them into small pieces. 

2. In a medium-size saucepan, combine the fig pieces, sugar, and water. It is advisable to stir it until the sugar dissolves and the mixture begins to boil.

3. Reduce the heat to low and simmer for about one to two hours, or until the figs become mushy and most of the liquid gets absorbed. Keep stirring occasionally to avoid the figs from sticking to the bottom of the pan.

4. Remove the saucepan from the stove and stir in the lemon juice. Set aside and allow the mixture to cool.

5. Meanwhile, preheat the oven to 350 degrees Fahrenheit (175 degrees Celsius) and line a 9x13 inch baking pan with parchment paper.

6. For preparing the fig square dough, in a large bowl, combine flour, baking powder, and salt and set it aside.

7. In another bowl, beat the butter and brown sugar using an electric mixer until fluffy. Then, add the egg and vanilla extract to the butter mixture and beat until combined.

8. Gradually add the flour mixture to butter mixture and mix on low speed until a dough forms.

9. Divide the dough into halves. Pat half of the dough evenly into the prepared baking pan. Spread the cooled fig filling over the dough.

10. Then, crumble the remaining dough over the fig filling to cover.

11. Sprinkle a generous amount of granulated sugar on top for added crunch. This is optional.

12. Bake for about 35-40 minutes or until the top of the squares is golden brown.

13. Remove from oven and allow to cool completely in the pan on a wire rack. Once cooled, use the parchment paper to lift the squares out of the pan and cut into individual pieces before serving. 

Enjoy your homemade Fig squares!

Title: Sauteed Calf's Liver with Onions, Balsamic Vinegar and Pancetta

Ingredients:
- 2 pounds calf’s liver, cut into 1/4-inch thick slices
- 1 large onion, thinly sliced
- 4 cloves garlic, minced
- 8 slices of Pancetta
- 3 tablespoons unsalted butter
- 1/4 cup balsamic vinegar
- Salt and pepper to taste
- 2 tablespoons chopped fresh parsley
- Olive oil for frying

Instructions:

1. Heat a large sauté pan over medium heat. Add 2 tablespoons of butter and pancetta. Cook the pancetta until it starts to crisp and brown.
   
2. Using a slotted spoon, remove the pancetta from the pan and set aside.

3. In the same pan, add sliced onions and cook them in the pancetta fat until they're soft and caramelized. This usually takes around 10 minutes. Then, add the minced garlic and cook for another minute.

4. Once the onions and garlic are caramelized, remove them from the pan and place them with the pancetta.

5. In the same pan, add a bit more butter and olive oil. When the butter melts, season the calf's liver with salt and pepper on each side. 

6. Add liver to the pan, let it cook for around 2-3 minutes on each side, until it's browned. 

7. Remove the liver from the pan and place it with the onions and pancetta. 

8. Deglaze the pan with balsamic vinegar, scraping the pan to get all the flavorful bits. 

9. Return the pancetta, onions, garlic and liver to the pan. 

10. Stir everything together until the liver is glazed with balsamic vinegar.

11. Serve hot, garnished with chopped parsley.

Tips:
Please ensure to not overcook the liver – it should be pink in the middle when you cut into it. Also, always choose liver from a trusted source to make sure you're getting a high-quality product. This dish pairs well with mashed potatoes or a fresh salad.

prompt: Write a recipe for "Raspberry-Chocolate Soufflés".
text:
Raspberry-Chocolate Soufflés Recipe

Ingredients:
- 1 cup fresh or frozen raspberries
- 1/4 cup granulated sugar
- 2 tablespoons cornstarch
- 1/4 cup water
- 1 cup semi-sweet chocolate chips
- 4 large eggs, separated
- 1/4 cup granulated sugar (for egg whites)
- 1/4 teaspoon cream of tartar
- Powdered sugar, for dusting

Instructions:

1. Preheat your oven to 375°F (190°C). Grease four 8-ounce ramekins with butter or cooking spray.

2. In a small saucepan, combine the raspberries, granulated sugar, cornstarch, and water. Cook over medium heat, stirring constantly, until the mixture thickens and the raspberries break down, about 5 minutes. Remove from heat and set aside to cool.

3. Place the chocolate chips in a microwave-safe bowl and melt in the microwave in 30-second intervals, stirring after each interval, until smooth and melted. Set aside to cool slightly.

4. In a large mixing bowl, beat the egg yolks with 1/4 cup granulated sugar until pale and creamy. Gradually stir in the melted chocolate until well combined.

5. In a separate clean mixing bowl, beat the egg whites and cream of tartar on high speed until soft peaks form. Gradually add the remaining 1/4 cup granulated sugar and continue to beat until stiff peaks form.

6. Gently fold one-third of the beaten egg whites into the chocolate mixture to lighten it. Then fold in the remaining egg whites until no streaks of white remain, being careful not to deflate the mixture.

7. Divide the chocolate soufflé batter evenly among the prepared ramekins. Spoon about 1 tablespoon of the raspberry mixture onto the center of each soufflé, creating a well.

8. Place the ramekins on a baking sheet and bake in the preheated oven for 12-15 minutes, or until risen and set on top but still slightly jiggly in the center.

9. Dust the soufflés with powdered sugar and serve immediately. The soufflés should be enjoyed right out of the oven as they will deflate quickly.

Note: You can also serve the soufflés with a dollop of whipped cream or a scoop of vanilla ice cream, if desired. Enjoy!

Recipe for “Mushrooms and Penne in Wine Sauce”

Ingredients:

- 400 gr Penne pasta
- 2 cups of fresh mushrooms, sliced
- 2 cloves of garlic, minced
- 1 medium size onion, chopped 
- 1 cup of dry white wine
- 1 tablespoon of olive oil
- Salt and pepper to taste
- 1 cup of heavy cream
- 1/2 cup of grated Parmesan cheese
- 2 tablespoons of fresh parsley, chopped 

Instructions:

1. Start by bringing a large pot of salted water to boil. Add the penne pasta and cook according to package instructions until al dente. Drain and set aside.

2. While the pasta is cooking, heat the olive oil in a large saucepan over medium heat. Add the onion and minced garlic. Cook until the onion is translucent and the garlic is fragrant, about 2-3 minutes.

4. Add the white wine to the pan. Let it simmer and reduce for about 5 minutes. This will allow the wine to reduce and concentrate its flavor.

5. Season the mixture with salt and pepper to taste.

6. Lower the heat and add the heavy cream to the pan. Stir well, making sure all the ingredients are well mixed.

7. Add the cooked penne pasta to the saucepan and mix it with the cream and mushroom mixture. Make sure the pasta is well coated with the sauce.

8. Sprinkle the grated Parmesan cheese over the pasta and stir until the cheese is melted and the sauce is creamy.

9. Remove the pan from the heat. Garnish the pasta with chopped parsley before serving.

10. Serve the Mushrooms and Penne in Wine Sauce immediately while it is still warm with a side of garlic bread or a fresh salad. Enjoy! 

Preparation time: Approximately 10 minutes.
Cooking time: Approximately 30 minutes. 
Serving size: 4 Portions.

text:
Title: Currant Scones

Prep Time: 15 minutes
Cook Time: 12-15 minutes
Total Time: 27-30 minutes
Yield: 8 scones

Ingredients:
- 2 cups all-purpose flour
- 1/4 cup granulated sugar
- 1 tablespoon baking powder
- 1/2 teaspoon salt
- 1/2 cup cold unsalted butter, cubed
- 1/2 cup currants
- 3/4 cup buttermilk
- 1 teaspoon vanilla extract
- 1 egg, lightly beaten
- 1 tablespoon milk
- Optional: powdered sugar, for dusting

Instructions:

1. Preheat your oven to 400°F (200°C). Line a baking sheet with parchment paper or silicone mat.

2. In a large mixing bowl, whisk together the flour, sugar, baking powder, and salt.

3. Add the cold cubed butter to the dry mixture. Use a pastry cutter or your fingertips to cut the butter into the flour until the mixture resembles coarse crumbs.

4. Stir in the currants.

5. Make a well in the center of the mixture and pour in the buttermilk and vanilla extract. Mix everything together until just combined. Be careful not to overmix as it can result in tough scones.

6. Turn the dough out onto a floured surface. Gently knead the dough a few times until it comes together.

7. Pat or roll the dough into a circle about 1-inch thick. Using a sharp knife or a biscuit cutter, cut out scones in your desired size and place them onto the prepared baking sheet, leaving some space between them.

8. In a small bowl, whisk together the beaten egg and milk. Brush the tops of the scones with the egg wash.

9. Bake in the preheated oven for 12 to 15 minutes, or until the scones are golden brown and cooked through.

10. Remove from the oven and let the scones cool on a wire rack.

11. Optional: Dust the cooled scones with powdered sugar for an extra touch.

12. Serve and enjoy the currant scones warm or at room temperature. They are perfect with a cup of tea or coffee. 

Note: These scones are best enjoyed fresh on the day they are made. However, you can store them in an airtight container for up to 3 days

Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

1. We introduce a novel approach to clothing co-parsing, which jointly performs image segmentation and labeling.
2. We propose a deep neural network architecture that integrates segmentation and labeling branches with a spatial-spectral feature fusion module.
3. We demonstrate the superiority of our approach over state-of-the-art methods in terms of parsing accuracy and efficiency.

Ingredients:

* 4 large artichokes, trimmed and quartered
* 2 tablespoons olive oil
* 1 onion, finely chopped
* 2 cloves garlic, minced
* 1 teaspoon dried thyme
* 1 teaspoon dried tarragon
* 1/2 cup white wine
* 1/2 cup chicken broth
* 1/4 cup chopped fresh parsley
* Salt and pepper, to taste
* 1/4 cup grated Parmesan cheese (optional)
* Crusty bread, for serving

5. Stir in the chopped fresh parsley and cook for an additional 2-3 minutes, until the parsley is wilted.
6. Taste and adjust the seasoning as needed. If using Parmesan cheese, sprinkle it over the top of the artichokes and serve.
7. Serve the Provençal Artichoke Ragout hot, with crusty bread on the side for sopping up the juices.

prompt: Write a recipe for "Pomegranate Salmon With Garlic Smashed Potatoes".
text:
Recipe for Pomegranate Salmon with Garlic Smashed Potatoes: 

Ingredients:
- 4 fresh salmon fillets 
- Salt and freshly ground black pepper, to taste 
- 2 tablespoons olive oil 
- 4 cloves garlic, minced 
- 2 cups baby potatoes, halved 
- 1/4 cup freshly squeezed pomegranate juice 
- 2 tablespoons honey 
- 2 tablespoons Dijon mustard 
- 2 tablespoons chopped fresh parsley 
- Lemon wedges, for serving 

Instructions:

1. Preheat the oven to 400°F (200°C).

2. Arrange the salmon fillets, skin side down, on a baking sheet lined with parchment paper. Season both sides of the salmon with salt and pepper.

3. In a small bowl, mix together the olive oil and minced garlic. Drizzle the mixture over the potatoes and toss to coat. Spread the potatoes in a single layer on a separate baking sheet.

4. Roast the potatoes for 25 minutes, or until they are tender and beginning to brown.

5. While the potatoes are roasting, whisk together the pomegranate juice, honey, and Dijon mustard in a small saucepan. Cook over medium heat, stirring occasionally, until the mixture has thickened and reduced by about half, approximately 10 minutes.

6. Remove the potatoes from the oven and use a spatula to gently press down on them to smash them. Return the potatoes to the oven and roast for an additional 5 minutes, or until they are golden brown.

7. Brush the pomegranate glaze all over the salmon fillets. Return the salmon and potatoes to the oven and roast for an additional 10 minutes, or until the salmon is cooked through.

8. Remove from oven and let it rest for couple of minutes, then garnish with fresh parsley and serve with lemon wedges. Enjoy!

Although significantly less predominant than other more modern antivirals, Adapromine remains a crucial treatment option in particular cases, especially in specific strains of influenza.

1. [[Chemical Structure and Properties]]

Adapromine, with its systematic name, 1-adamantyl bromide, is a member of the adamantane family of compounds. The molecular formula for Adapromine is C10H15Br, and it has a molar mass of around 225.13 g/mol. It is a clear, colorless liquid at room temperature, and its boiling point is approximately 106 degrees Celsius at 15 mmHg.

2. [[Mechanism of Action]]

Similar to other adamantanes, Adapromine blocks the M2 ion channel protein, which is encoded by influenza A virus. Blocking these channels prevents the virus from entering the host cell, effectively halting its replication process. Adapromine possesses the capacity to interfere and disrupt the life cycle of the virus, limiting its ability to infect cells and reproduce.

3. [[Indications and Usage]]

Adapromine is primarily administered for the treatment of influenza A virus infections. It may also be prescribed off-label for other viral infections resistant to more commonly used antiviral drugs. 

4. [[Synthesis]]

While the exact process of synthesising Adapromine is proprietary knowledge, it generally involves bromination of the adamantane structure, which is then purified to create the final product.

5. [[Adverse Effects and Contraindications]]

Adverse effects of Adapromine include but are not limited to gastrointestinal problems, nervous system disorders which include but are not limited to, dizziness and difficulty concentrating, and skin reactions such as rashes. Adapromine is contraindicated in patients with a known allergy to the drug or any of its components. It is also typically avoided in pregnant women due to the lack of substantial information on its safety.

6. [[Pharmacokinetics]]

Data on the pharmacokinetics of Adapromine is limited. Nonetheless, it is assumed that it follows regular hepatic metabolism, renal excretion, and has a half-life comparable to similar antiviral drugs.

Trend following is a trade idea that involves identifying and following the direction of market trends. This approach is based on the assumption that prices tend to move in trends and that these trends can be identified and followed to generate profits. Trend followers use various indicators and chart patterns to identify trends and then trade in the direction of those trends.

Mean reversion is a trade idea that is based on the assumption that asset prices tend to revert to their historical means over time. This approach involves identifying assets that are trading at extreme levels and then betting on a return to those means. For example, a trader who believes in mean reversion might buy a stock that has fallen sharply in price, expecting that it will eventually rise back to its historical average.

Statistical arbitrage is a trade idea that involves exploiting statistical relationships between different assets. This approach involves identifying two or more assets that have a historical relationship in terms of their price movements, and then taking advantage of any deviations from that relationship. For example, a trader who identifies a statistical relationship between the prices of two stocks might buy the underperforming stock and sell the outperforming stock, expecting that the relationship will return to normal.

Here I'm sitting in the gloom
Of my quiet attic room.
France goes rolling all around,
Fledged with forest May has crowned.

Thinking how the fighting started,
Wondering when we'll ever end it,
Back to hell with Kaiser sent it,
Gag the noise, pack up and go,
Clockwork soldiers in a row.
I've got better things to do
Than to waste my time on you.

Robert, when I drowse to-night,
Skirting lawns of sleep to chase
Shifting dreams in mazy light,
Somewhere then I'll see your face
Turning back to bid me follow
Where I wag my arms and hollo,
Over hedges hasting after
Crooked smile and baffling laughter,
Running tireless, floating, leaping,
Down your web-hung woods and valleys,
Where the glowworm stars are peeping,
Till I find you, quiet as stone
On a hill-top all alone,
Staring outward, gravely pondering
Jumbled leagues of hillock-wandering.
III
You and I have walked together
In the starving winter weather.
We've been glad because we knew
Time's too short and friends are few.
We've been sad because we missed
One whose yellow head was kissed
By the gods, who thought about him
Till they couldn't do without him.
Now he's here again; I've been
Soldier David dressed in green,
Standing in a wood that swings
To the madrigal he sings.
He's come back, all mirth and glory,
Like the prince in a fairy tory.
Winter called him far away;
Blossoms bring him home with May.
IV
Well, I know you'll swear it's true
That you found him decked in blue
Striding up through morning-land
With a cloud on either hand.
Out in Wales, you'll say, he marches
Arm-in-arm with aoks and larches;
Hides all night in hilly nooks,
Laughs at dawn in tumbling brooks.
Yet, it's certain, here he teaches
Outpost-schemes to groups of beeches.
And I'm sure, as here I stand,
That he shines through every land,
That he sings in every place
Where we're thinking of his face.

Robert, there's a war in France;
Everywhere men bang and blunder,
Sweat and swear and worship Chance,
Creep and blink through cannon thunder.
Rifles crack and bullets flick,
Sing and hum like hornet-swarms.

All the while I watch the spark

The mode of production is a concept in Marxist theory that refers to the way society organizes and carries out economic production. It encompasses the processes and relations through which the means of production, such as land, resources, and technology, are allocated and utilized to produce goods and services.

According to Marx, the mode of production is the foundation of society and determines its social, political, and cultural aspects. He identified several historical modes of production, each characterized by its specific set of relations of production and class structure. These modes of production are the primitive communal mode, the slave mode, the feudal mode, and the capitalist mode.

In the primitive communal mode, production and distribution were based on communal ownership and cooperation. There was no private property or class distinction, and economic surplus was shared among the community. This mode of production characterized early human societies, where agriculture and hunting were the primary means of subsistence.

With the rise of slavery, a new mode of production emerged. In the slave mode, a class of slaves provided the labor while another class of slave-owners controlled the means of production. The surplus produced by the slaves was appropriated by the slave-owners, leading to the development of class divisions and social inequality.

Feudalism, which emerged in Europe during the Middle Ages, represented another mode of production. Feudal society was organized around a hierarchical system of lords, vassals, and serfs. The landed aristocracy owned the land and controlled the means of production, while the serfs worked the land and provided labor in exchange for protection and the right to use the land. Surplus production was extracted by the feudal lords, maintaining a system of social hierarchy.

The current dominant mode of production in most capitalist societies is known as capitalism. In this mode, private individuals or corporations own and control the means of production, driven by the pursuit of profit. The proletariat, or working class, provides the labor and is alienated from the means of production, as they must sell their labor power in exchange for wages. Capitalist production is driven by competition and the constant accumulation of capital.

Marx argued that each mode of production contains the seeds of its own destruction. He predicted that capitalism would eventually give way to a socialist mode of production, in which the means of production would be collectively owned and controlled by the working class. Socialism aims to overcome the exploitation and alienation inherent in capitalist production by establishing a society based on cooperation, social equality, and democratic control over the means of production.

text:
Ingredients:

- 1 lb boneless skinless chicken breasts, thin cut
- 1 tablespoon vegetable oil
- 2 cloves garlic, minced
- 1 tablespoon fresh ginger, minced
- 2 cups sliced mushrooms
- 2 cups thinly sliced Napa cabbage
- 2 carrots, shredded
- 1 red bell pepper, sliced thinly
- 3 green onions, sliced
- 1/4 cup hoisin sauce
- 2 tablespoons soy sauce
- 1 teaspoon sesame oil
- Salt and ground black pepper to taste
- 4-6 mu shu pancakes or flour tortillas

Instructions:

1. Cut the chicken breasts into thin strips. Season with salt and black pepper.

2. Heat the vegetable oil over medium heat in a large skillet or wok. Add the ginger and garlic, and sauté until fragrant.

3. Add the chicken to the skillet. Cook for about 5-7 minutes, or until no longer pink. Remove the chicken from the skillet and set aside.

4. In the same skillet, add the sliced mushrooms, Napa cabbage, shredded carrots, bell pepper, and green onions. Cook for about 5 minutes, or until the vegetables are tender.

5. Return the cooked chicken back to the skillet.

6. In a small bowl, whisk together the hoisin sauce, soy sauce, and sesame oil. Pour this sauce over the chicken and vegetables in the skillet. Stir well to combine.

7. Lower the heat and let the mixture simmer for about 2-3 minutes, allowing the flavors to blend together.

8. Warm the mu shu pancakes or flour tortillas in a pan over medium heat or in the microwave.

9. To serve, spoon some of the mu shu chicken and vegetable mixture onto a pancake or tortilla. Roll it up like a burrito and enjoy. Repeat with the remaining mixture and pancakes or tortillas.

10. Serve your Mu Shu Chicken and Vegetables hot.

Optional: You can add additional hoisin sauce or plum sauce as per your liking while serving.

Law French is a dialect of the French language that was utilized in the English judicial system from the 11th until the 17th century, following the Norman conquest of England in 1066. The language became the standard legal parlance used by law courts and scholars, significantly influencing the English legal terms and framework. 

Its eventual decline was a result of the gradual anglicisation of the English courts, culminating in the 'Proceedings in Courts of Justice Act 1730', which mandated the use of English instead of Law French in all future court proceedings.

==History==

Law French originated from Norman French, which was brought to England by William the Conqueror in the 11th century. It became the formal language for legal proceedings due to the ruling class predominantly speaking French or Latin, while the native lower classes primarily spoke Old English.

The language further developed into several dialects - Parisian French, used in formal documents, and Law French, used in legal proceedings and texts. Law French retained many characteristics of Old Norman, such as grammatical rules and orthographic peculiarities, demonstrating a clear deviation from standard French.

==Usage==

Law French was the official language used for pleadings, indictments, legal treatises, laws, and official records, shaping the precise terminology and technicalities of the English law. It was not restricted to lawyers alone; nobles, clerks, and scholars were also expected to be conversant in Law French.

==Decline==

Despite the prohibitions against Law French in 1362 in the Pleading in English Act - which required court proceedings to be conducted in English - the law was largely ignored, with courts resorting to diglossia, having official proceedings in English but using Law French for informal discussions and legal texts.

The 'Proceedings in Courts of Justice Act 1730' eventually brought about the decline of Law French, ordering legal proceedings to occur in English. Despite this, some legal terms derived from Law French, such as "defendant" and "evidence", continue to be used in English-speaking legal systems today.

==Legacy==

Although primarily obsolete as a spoken language, Law French's influence on English law is still noticeable in the legal jargon used today. Many terms of art in English law, such as "attorney", "bailiff", "plaintiff", "tort", etc., derive from Law French. MudrockNet: Semantic Segmentation of Mudrock SEM Images through Deep Learning

Traditional methods of mudrock characterization rely on manualpicking and typing, which are time-consuming, expensive, and prone to errors. In this paper, we present MudrockNet, a deep learning-based approach for semantic segmentation of mudrock Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) images.

MudrockNet leverages a convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture to learn the features and patterns in mudrock SEM images and predict the mineralogy and texture of the rock. We trained the network using a large dataset of labeled SEM images, and evaluated its performance using a set of independent test images.

Our results demonstrate that MudrockNet achieves high accuracy in segmenting minerals and textures in mudrock SEM images. Specifically, it accurately identified and segmented quartz, feldspar, mica, and amphibole, which are the most common minerals in mudrocks. It also distinguished between different textures such as matrix, grain boundary, and pore space.

MudrockNet has the potential to revolutionize the way mudrocks are characterized, providing a rapid, accurate, and cost-effective method for understanding their mineralogy and texture. This approach can be applied to a wide range of applications, including Petroleum exploration and production, environmental monitoring, and geological carbon sequestration.

In this paper, we investigate the representation theory of group algebras under oriented involutions, with a particular focus on the role of group identities on symmetric units. We prove that any strongly symmetric group has a unique oriented involution, and that the unit group of the group algebra is isomorphic to the group of involutive automorphisms of the algebra.

We also study the relationship between oriented involutions and the symmetric units of the group algebra. We show that the symmetric units are precisely the elements of the group algebra that are fixed by some oriented involution, and that the set of all symmetric units forms a subalgebra that is isomorphic to the fixed-point subalgebra of the oriented involution.

Our results have important implications for the study of group algebras and their representations, and provide new insights into the structure and properties of symmetric groups. In particular, we show that the notion of strong symmetry is closely related to the existence of a rational point in the modular representation variety of the group, and that the absence of oriented involutions in a group algebra is closely related to the absence of rational points in the modular representation variety.

* A new algorithm that jointly optimizes resource allocation and statistical parameter tuning
* A robust optimization framework that incorporates statistical requirements as regularization terms
* Experimental evaluation of the algorithm using real-world scenarios, showing significant improvements in energy efficiency
* Insights into the trade-offs between energy efficiency and statistical accuracy
