Few-shot segmentation is the task of segmenting images into their constituent parts or objects using only a few training examples. This is a challenging problem, as traditional segmentation methods require large amounts of labeled data to learn to recognize different objects.

Our approach, GLCL, addresses this challenge by combining the strengths of two popular few-shot learning methods: global contrastive learning and local contrastive learning. Global contrastive learning involves learning a representation that captures the global structure of the data, such as the layout and pose of objects in an image, while local contrastive learning involves learning a representation that captures the local details of the data, such as the texture and color of objects.

By combining these two approaches, GLCL is able to learn a representation that captures both the global and local information in the data, leading to improved few-shot segmentation performance. We evaluate GLCL on several benchmark datasets and show that it outperforms state-of-the-art few-shot segmentation methods. We also perform ablation studies to analyze the contribution of the different components of GLCL and show that both global and local contrastive learning are important for its performance.

Our main contributions are:

* The proposal of a novel few-shot segmentation method called Global and Local Contrastive Learning (GLCL) that combines global and local contrastive learning.
* The demonstration of the effectiveness of GLCL on several benchmark datasets, outperforming state-of-the-art few-shot segmentation methods.
* The performance of ablation studies to analyze the contribution of the different components of GLCL, showing that both global and local contrastive learning are important for its performance.

Overall, this paper makes an important contribution to the field of few-shot segmentation by introducing a novel approach that combines the strengths of global and local contrastive learning, leading to improved performance in this challenging task.

He believes that the "phenomenal ability" of games such as The Sims and others to capture the interest of adolescent audiences is ripe for exploitation. Boring lessons drumming vocabulary into pupils couched in terms they do not understand has made many languages far harder to learn than they should be. "The way we often teach foreign languages right now is somewhat akin to learning to ride a bike by formally studying gravity," he said.
By contrast, said Mr Purushotma, learning via something like The Sims may mean students do not feel like they are studying at all. This was because The Sims does not rely solely on words to get information across to players. The incidental information about what a Sim was doing could reinforce what a player or student was supposed to be learning, said Mr Purushotma. By contrast many language lessons try to impart information about a tongue with little context. For instance, he said, in a version of The Sims adapted to teach German, if a player misunderstood what was meant by the word "energie" the actions of a tired Sim, stumbling then falling asleep, would illustrate the meaning. One of the drawbacks of The Sims, said Mr Purushotma, was the lack of spoken language to help people brush up on pronunciation. Before now, he said, educational software titles suffer by comparison with the slick graphics and rich worlds found in games. prompt: Write a recipe for "Asparagus With Prosciutto Di Parma, Pecorino Pepato, And Poached Eggs ".
text:
Ingredients:
- 1 bunch of asparagus spears
- 4 slices of Prosciutto di Parma
- 50g of Pecorino Pepato cheese
- 4 eggs
- 2 tablespoons of vinegar
- Salt and black pepper to taste

Instructions:
1. Start by preparing the asparagus. Trim the tough ends of the asparagus spears and peel the lower half of the stalks. Rinse them under cold water.

2. Fill a large saucepan with water and bring it to a boil. Add a pinch of salt and vinegar to the boiling water. The vinegar will help keep the egg whites together when poaching.

3. While the water is boiling, prepare a bowl with ice water. This will be used to shock the asparagus after it is cooked to preserve its bright green color.

4. Add the asparagus spears to the boiling water and cook for 3-5 minutes, depending on the thickness of the stalks. The asparagus should be cooked until it is tender yet still crisp. Test it by piercing a spear with a fork. Once cooked, remove the asparagus from the boiling water and immediately transfer it to the ice water to stop the cooking process. Let it sit in the ice water for a couple of minutes before draining and patting dry.

5. Wrap each asparagus spear with a slice of Prosciutto di Parma, starting from the bottom and working your way up. The salty flavor of the prosciutto pairs perfectly with the sweet and tender asparagus.

6. Grate the Pecorino Pepato cheese using a fine grater and set it aside.

7. Poach the eggs. Bring a medium-sized saucepan of water to a gentle simmer. Crack an egg into a small bowl or ramekin. Create a gentle whirlpool in the simmering water by stirring it with a spoon. Carefully slide the egg into the center of the whirlpool. Repeat with the remaining eggs.

8. Poach the eggs for about 3-4 minutes until the whites are set, but the yolk is still runny. Remove the poached eggs from the water using a slotted spoon and drain on a paper towel.

9. Place the wrapped asparagus spears on individual serving plates. Season with salt and black pepper to taste.

10. Top each asparagus with a poached egg. The creamy yolk will add richness to the dish.

11. Sprinkle the grated Pecorino Pepato cheese

text:
Recipe: Coquilles St. Jacques

Ingredients: 
- 12 large sea scallops 
- 1/4 cup unsalted butter 
- 1 shallot, finely chopped 
- 1/4 cup all-purpose flour 
- 1/2 cup dry white wine 
- 1 cup heavy cream 
- 1/4 cup grated Gruyere cheese 
- 1/4 cup grated Parmesan cheese 
- 1/4 cup bread crumbs 
- Freshly chopped parsley, for garnish 
- Salt and pepper to taste 

Instructions: 

1. Preheat your oven to 350°F (175°C).

2. Rinse the sea scallops thoroughly and pat them dry with a paper towel. Season both sides of the scallops with salt and pepper.

3. Heat a large skillet over medium-high heat and melt the butter. Add the chopped shallots and sauté until they become translucent, about 2-3 minutes.

4. Place the sea scallops in the skillet and sear them on each side until they develop a golden brown crust, about 2-3 minutes per side. Remove the scallops from the skillet and set them aside.

5. In the same skillet, add the flour and cook for a minute, stirring constantly. Pour in the white wine and bring the mixture to a gentle boil. Allow it to simmer for 2-3 minutes, until it thickens slightly.

6. Add the heavy cream to the skillet and whisk until the sauce is smooth and creamy. Season the sauce with salt and pepper to taste.

7. Grease a baking dish and arrange the seared scallops in a single layer. Pour the sauce over the scallops, ensuring they are completely covered.

8. In a small bowl, combine the grated Gruyere cheese, Parmesan cheese, and bread crumbs. Sprinkle this mixture evenly over the scallops and sauce.

9. Place the baking dish on the middle rack of the preheated oven and bake for about 15-20 minutes, or until the top is golden brown and the sauce is bubbly.

10. Once cooked, remove the dish from the oven and let it cool for a few minutes. Garnish with freshly chopped parsley before serving.

11. Serve the Coquilles St. Jacques as an appetizer or a main course. They pair well with crusty bread or a side of steamed vegetables.

Enjoy your delicious and elegant Coquilles St. Jacques!

This practice has been prevalent for centuries, but it gained significant attention in the late 20th century due to concerns regarding worker safety, environmental pollution, and social implications.

The ship breaking industry primarily operates in countries with lower labor costs and less stringent environmental regulations, such as Bangladesh, India, Pakistan, and China. These countries have become the preferred destinations for ship owners to dispose of their vessels, as they offer competitive rates and efficient processing methods.

The ship breaking process typically involves a variety of activities, including breaking apart the ship's superstructure, removing interior fixtures and fittings, and segregating different types of materials for recycling. The most valuable materials recovered from ships include steel, aluminum, copper, and various other non-ferrous metals. These materials are generally sold to scrap metal merchants who recycle them for use in various industries.

Ship breaking is a labor-intensive industry that employs thousands of workers, often from impoverished backgrounds. These workers face hazardous conditions, including exposure to toxic substances, heavy machinery accidents, and precarious working environments. The lack of proper safety equipment and inadequate training further exacerbate the risks faced by shipbreaking workers.

text:
Ingredients:

- 3 lbs chuck roast
- 1/4 cup apple cider vinegar
- 4 garlic cloves, minced
- 2 chipotle peppers in adobo sauce
- 1 tablespoon ground cumin
- 1 tablespoon dried oregano
- 1/2 teaspoon ground cloves
- 1 cup beef broth
- 1/4 cup lime juice
- 2 teaspoons sea salt
- 1 teaspoon black pepper
- 1 large onion, chopped
- 3 bay leaves
- Fresh cilantro for garnishing (optional)

Instructions:

1. Preheat your oven to 325 degrees Fahrenheit. 

2. In a blender, combine the apple cider vinegar, garlic cloves, chipotle peppers in adobo sauce, cumin, oregano, cloves, beef broth, lime juice, salt, and black pepper. Blend until the mixture is smooth.

3. Place the chuck roast in a large Dutch oven and pour the blended sauce over the top.

4. Add the chopped onion and bay leaves into the pot, evenly distributing them over and around the roast.

5. Cover the Dutch oven with a lid and place it in the preheated oven. 

6. Allow the roast to cook for about 3 hours, or until the beef is tender and can easily be pulled apart with a fork.

7. Once the beef is done, remove it from the oven and let it rest for about 10 minutes. 

8. Using two forks, shred the beef into bite-sized pieces, while still in the pot, allowing it to absorb the leftover juices and flavors.

9. Before serving, remove the bay leaves and garnish with fresh cilantro if desired. 

10. Your oven beef barbacoa can be served atop rice or (for a more traditional approach) inside tortillas, making a delicious barbacoa beef taco/burrito. Enjoy!

text:
Ingredients:

For Crepes:
- 1 cup all-purpose flour
- 2 tablespoons cocoa powder
- 1 tablespoon gingerbread spice
- 1 tablespoon granulated sugar
- Pinch of salt
- 1 3/4 cups full cream milk
- 2 large eggs
- 2 tablespoons melted butter
- 1 teaspoon vanilla extract

For Crepe Filling:
- 1 cup dark chocolate chips
- 1 cup whipped cream
- 1/2 cup gingerbread cookies crumbs
- Powdered sugar, for dusting

Instructions:

Making the Crepe Batter:
1. In a mixing bowl, combine the all-purpose flour, cocoa powder, gingerbread spice, granulated sugar, and a pinch of salt. Mix well until thoroughly combined.
2. In another bowl, whisk together the milk, eggs, melted butter, and vanilla extract. 
3. Gradually add the wet ingredients to the dry ingredients, whisking constantly until the batter is smooth and free of lumps.
4. Allow the batter to rest for at least 30 minutes in the refrigerator.

Making the Crepes:
1. Preheat a 9-inch non-stick skillet or crepe pan over medium heat.
2. Brush the pan lightly with some melted butter. Pour about 1/4 cup of the batter into the center of the pan. Immediately tilt and rotate the pan to spread the batter evenly over the bottom.
3. Cook until the top surface appears dry, about 1 minute. Flip the crepe with a spatula, and cook it on the other side for 15-20 seconds.
4. Transfer the cooked crepe to a warm plate and repeat with the remaining batter, making sure to re-butter the pan between each crepe.

Making the Crepe Filling:
1. Put the dark chocolate chips in a microwave-safe bowl, and heat them in the microwave in 20-second intervals until the chocolate is fully melted, stirring well after each interval.
2. Spread about a tablespoon of the melted chocolate onto one half of a crepe. 
3. Add a generous dollop of whipped cream on top of the chocolate, then sprinkle some gingerbread cookie crumbs. 
4. Fold the crepe in half, then in half again to create a triangle shape.
5. Repeat with the remaining crepes.

Final Preparation:
1. Before serving, dust the crepes with powdered sugar.
2. Enjoy these delicious spiced chocolate-gingerbread crepes while they are still warm

prompt: Write a recipe for "Mascarpone".
text:
Recipe: Homemade Mascarpone

Ingredients:
- 4 cups heavy cream
- 2 tablespoons fresh lemon juice

Instructions:
1. In a large saucepan, heat the heavy cream over medium heat until it reaches a temperature of around 190°F (88°C). Stir occasionally to prevent the cream from sticking to the bottom of the pan.

2. Once the cream has reached the desired temperature, remove it from the heat and add the fresh lemon juice. Stir gently to combine.

3. Let the mixture sit at room temperature for about 30 minutes. During this time, the acid from the lemon juice will cause the cream to thicken and curdle slightly.

4. Line a fine-mesh sieve or colander with a couple of layers of cheesecloth. Place the sieve over a large bowl to catch the liquid that will drain out of the cream.

5. Carefully pour the curdled cream into the sieve, allowing the liquid to drain out. Gather the corners of the cheesecloth and gently squeeze to remove any excess liquid.

6. Transfer the sieve with the cheesecloth and cream to the refrigerator. Let it sit and drain for at least 12 hours, or overnight.

7. After the draining process, check the consistency of the mascarpone. It should be thick and creamy. If it's still too loose, you can let it continue draining for a few more hours.

8. Once the mascarpone has reached the desired consistency, transfer it to an airtight container and store in the refrigerator. It will keep well for up to a week.

Notes:
- The quality of the cream will greatly affect the outcome of the mascarpone. Use fresh, high-quality heavy cream for best results.
- If you prefer a slightly tangier mascarpone, you can increase the amount of lemon juice to 3 tablespoons.
- Mascarpone can be used in both sweet and savory recipes, such as tiramisu, cheesecake, pasta sauces, and more.
- This homemade mascarpone has a richer and creamier flavor compared to store-bought versions.

Calmodulin (CaM) is a ubiquitous, multifunctional, calcium-binding protein found in all eukaryotic organisms. Its name derives from “CALcium MODULated proteIN." This protein plays a crucial role in the calcium signal transduction pathway, regulating a wide array of diverse cellular target proteins and cellular activities.

Calmodulin contains 148 amino acid residues and is roughly 16.7 kDa in size. It features two homologous globular domains, each of which can bind two calcium ions, allowing Calmodulin to bind up to four calcium ions. This ability to bind calcium ions allows Calmodulin to undergo a major conformational change, wherein it reshapes from a compact shape to a more elongated form. This structural change opens up new binding sites, enabling the protein to interact with and modulate many different targets.

Calmodulin regulates a variety of biochemical activities in the cell, including the activities of a number of enzymes, ion channels, and other proteins. This regulation is primarily driven by changes in the concentration of free calcium ions within the cell. Some of the targets of CaM control include protein kinases and phosphatases, nitric oxide synthase, phosphodiesterases, the inositol trisphosphate receptor, and myosin light-chain kinase. The regulation of these targets by CaM mediates processes such as inflammation, metabolism, muscle contraction, intracellular movement, short-term and long-term memory, nerve growth and the immune response.

Mutations or abnormalities in calmodulin function or expression can lead to a variety of diseases, including heart disease, cancer, and neurological disorders. Research into Calmodulin and its interactions with its target proteins is ongoing, with the hope that it might lead to therapeutic interventions for these and other conditions.

Calmodulin has been the subject of extensive studies due to its crucial role in regulating cell functions in response to changes in calcium concentration. Its ability to control various intracellular processes makes it a key player in maintaining homeostasis and conducting a diverse range of cellular activities. text:
Ben's Chocolate Ice Cream Recipe

Ingredients:
- 2 cups heavy cream
- 1 cup whole milk
- 3/4 cup granulated sugar
- 3 large egg yolks
- 1/2 cup unsweetened cocoa powder
- 1 teaspoon vanilla extract
- Pinch of salt

Instructions:

1. In a medium saucepan, combine heavy cream, whole milk, granulated sugar, and a pinch of salt. Heat the mixture over medium heat, stirring constantly until the sugar is completely dissolved.

2. In a separate bowl, whisk together the egg yolks until they are pale and slightly thickened.

3. Slowly pour the hot milk mixture into the egg yolk mixture, whisking constantly. Return the mixture to the saucepan and cook over medium heat, stirring constantly, for about 2-3 minutes, until the mixture thickens and coats the back of a spoon.

4. Remove the saucepan from the heat and whisk in the unsweetened cocoa powder and vanilla extract until well combined.

5. Pour the mixture into an ice cream maker and churn according to the manufacturer's instructions.

6. Once the ice cream has finished churning, transfer it to a freezer-safe container and freeze for at least 2 hours, or until it reaches your desired level of firmness.

7. Once the ice cream has reached your desired level of firmness, scoop it into bowls or cones and serve. Enjoy your Ben's Chocolate Ice Cream!

"Kagemusha" is one of those films which wasn't intended as a great success, yet it became that, winning the Golden Palm and giving Kurosawa back his much needed acclaim in Japan and re-establishing his reputation as the giant of Asian cinema.

Although Kurosawa himself thought of this film as a mere dress rehearsal,a preparation for "Ran", "Kagemusha" carries its own distinctive essence which makes it a work in the same category as its successor.The story deals around one of the greatest feudal lords and generals in Japan's history, Takeda Shingen, showing his unexpected and untimely demise. Although Shingen is the most powerful figure here, he is used as a monument around which everything revolves and not as the principal hero.

This film is full of sad and tragic moments, starting with Shingen's untimely death and culminating with the rebuking of his impersonator, Kagemusha. Nakadai plays the dual roles wonderfully. He is so emotionally involved in his part as Kagemusha that it seems almost uncanny. Thus we see why Kurosawa has chosen him as Mifune's successor. The other actors are also splendid and specially young Daisuke Ryu makes a startling appearance as Shingen's arch rival Oda Nobunaga.

The ending is very hard to watch, both the scene where Kagemusha is thrown out in the rain and the last scene which illustrates the death of the Takeda clan. What makes this film a pleasure to watch is the incredible cinematography and photography, specially in the incredible dream sequence where the ghost of Shingen chases Kagemusha through red clouds, as well as the hauntingly beautiful music and marvelous performances.

All in all, this is a great film that will grow on you the more you watch it. Although "Ran" is more spectacular and gripping, "Kagemusha" is more compelling because of its epic nature. 9/10

EA publishes blockbuster titles such as Fifa and John Madden, as well as video game versions of movies such as Harry Potter and the James Bond films. Nine of the 20 biggest-selling games in the UK last year were published by EA.
Gerhard Florin, EA's managing director for European publishing, said: "Doubling our industry in five years is not rocket science." He said it would take many years before EA could challenge Disney - which in 2004 reported revenues of $30bn (£16bn) - but it remained a goal for the company. "We will be able to bring more people into gaming because games will be more emotional." Mr Florin predicted that the next round of games console would give developers enough power to create real emotion.
"It's the subtleties, the eyes, the mouth - 5,000 polygons doesn't really sell the emotion.
"With PS3 and Xbox 2, we can go on the main character with 30,000 to 50,000 polygons," he said. "With that increased firepower, the Finding Nemo video game looks just like the movie, but it will be interactive." Mr Florin said that more than 50% of all EA's games were sold to adults and played by adults, but the perception remained that the video game industry was for children. "Our goal is to bring games to the masses which bring out emotions." EA said the video game industry was now bigger than the music industry. "Nobody queues for music anymore."
"You can't ignore an industry when people queue to buy a game at midnight because they are so desperate to play it," he said, referring to demand for titles for such as Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas and Halo 2.
Jan Bolz, EA's vice president of sales and marketing in Europe, said the firm was working to give video games a more central role in popular culture. He said the company was in advanced stages of discussions over a reality TV show in which viewers could control the actions of the characters as in its popular game The Sims. "One idea could be that you're controlling a family, telling them when to go to the kitchen and when to go to the bedroom, and with this mechanism you have gamers all over the world 'playing the show'," said Mr Bolz.
He also said EA was planning an international awards show "similar to the Oscars and the Grammys" which would combine video games, music and movies. Mr Bolz said video games firm had to work more closely with celebrities. "People will want to play video games if their heroes like Robbie Williams or Christina Aguilera are in them." Mr Florin said the challenge was to keep people playing in their 30s, 40s and 50s. "There's an indication that a 30 year old comes home from work and still wants to play games. prompt: Write a recipe for "Sugar Cookies for Decorating (and eating)".
text:
Sugar Cookies for Decorating (and Eating)

Ingredients:
- 2 3/4 cups all-purpose flour
- 1 teaspoon baking soda
- 1/2 teaspoon baking powder
- 1 cup unsalted butter, softened
- 1 1/2 cups white sugar
- 1 egg
- 1 teaspoon vanilla extract
- 1 tablespoon buttermilk


Instructions:

1. Preheat your oven to 375°F (190°C) and line a baking sheet with parchment paper.

2. In a medium-sized bowl, whisk together the flour, baking soda, and baking powder. Set aside.

3. In a large mixing bowl, cream together the softened butter and white sugar until light and fluffy. This can be done with a hand or stand mixer.

4. Beat in the egg and vanilla extract until well combined.

5. Stir in the buttermilk.

6. Gradually add the dry ingredients to the wet ingredients, mixing until just combined. Do not overmix.

7. Divide the dough into two equal portions and wrap each portion in plastic wrap. Chill in the refrigerator for at least 1 hour, or until firm.

8. On a lightly floured surface, roll out one portion of the chilled dough to a thickness of about 1/4 inch. Use cookie cutters to cut out desired shapes and carefully transfer them to the prepared baking sheet. Repeat with the remaining portion of dough.

9. Bake in the preheated oven for 8-10 minutes, or until the edges are lightly golden. Do not overbake.

10. Remove the cookies from the oven and let them cool on the baking sheet for a few minutes before transferring them to a wire rack to cool completely.

11. Once the cookies are completely cooled, they are ready to be decorated. Prepare your favorite icing or use royal icing, and decorate the cookies as desired. Let the icing dry before storing the cookies in an airtight container.

Enjoy your delicious sugar cookies, whether they're simply decorated or fully adorned with your creativity! Remember, they're not just for decorating; they're for eating too!

text:
In this paper, we propose a novel approach to semantic segmentation titled Segmenter, which leverages the Transformer architecture to improve performance and efficiency in this fundamental computer vision task. Traditional CNN-based segmentation models suffer from limited receptive fields, requiring awkwardly large models or expensive dilated convolutions to achieve adequate performance. In contrast, our Segmenter model demonstrates how Transformers, originally designed for natural language processing, can be applied to vision tasks, providing a more efficient and effective solution.

Our key innovation is the introduction of local and global attention mechanisms, which enable the model to simultaneously capture local details and long-range dependencies in the image. This is achieved through a novel multi-resolution encoder-decoder architecture, which incorporates both local and global attention mechanisms to effectively capture and integrate spatial information at multiple scales. We demonstrate the efficiency and versatility of Segmenter by training a single model on several benchmark datasets, achieving competitive performance on each while maintaining a smaller model size compared to state-of-the-art methods.

Extensive ablation studies and visualizations provide insight into the effectiveness of our design choices, highlighting the benefits of using local and global attention in semantic segmentation. Our findings establish Segmenter as a strong baseline for future research in this area, and demonstrate the potential of Transformer-based architectures for vision tasks beyond natural language processing.

text:
Psychotherapy discontinuation refers to the process of prematurely terminating or discontinuing psychotherapy before the agreed-upon treatment goals are achieved. This decision can be made by the client/patient or the therapist and can occur for various reasons.

There are several factors that may contribute to psychotherapy discontinuation. One common reason is lack of progress or dissatisfaction with the therapy process. Clients may feel that they are not seeing the desired results or that the therapy is not addressing their specific needs. In some cases, clients may also experience financial constraints or logistical difficulties, such as scheduling conflicts or transportation issues, which make it difficult to continue attending therapy sessions.

Another reason for psychotherapy discontinuation is the experience of negative side effects or discomfort during therapy. Some clients may find the therapeutic process emotionally challenging or may experience heightened distress as a result of discussing traumatic or difficult life experiences. This can lead to a decision to discontinue therapy in order to avoid further distress.

Additionally, interpersonal factors between the client and therapist can also play a role in psychotherapy discontinuation. A lack of rapport or a mismatch in therapy approach or style can make it difficult for the client to engage fully in the therapeutic process. Trust and a good working alliance between the client and therapist are essential for effective therapy, and the absence of these factors may lead to a decision to discontinue treatment.

While psychotherapy discontinuation may be a common occurrence, it is important to consider the potential consequences. Prematurely ending therapy can limit the opportunity for personal growth, healing, and resolution of psychological distress. Additionally, discontinuation can result in a sense of unfinished business and may lead to a relapse of symptoms or the re-emergence of unresolved issues.

Therapists play a crucial role in managing the process of psychotherapy discontinuation. It is important for therapists to regularly assess the progress and goals of therapy with their clients, and to have open discussions about any concerns or factors that may lead to discontinuation. Exploring and addressing these issues can potentially lead to a resolution and continuation of therapy.

In conclusion, psychotherapy discontinuation is a complex process influenced by a variety of factors. It can occur due to lack of progress, dissatisfaction, negative side effects, or interpersonal dynamics. However, it is important to consider the potential consequences of discontinuation and for therapists to actively engage in managing this process. By working collaboratively with clients, therapists can facilitate a smooth transition or address any concerns that may lead to discontinuation, ultimately increasing the likelihood of positive treatment outcomes.

Uncertainty estimation methods are expected to improve the understanding and
quality of computer-assisted methods used in medical applications (e.g.,
neurosurgical interventions, radiotherapy planning), where automated medical
image segmentation is crucial. In supervised machine learning, a common
practice to generate ground truth label data is to merge observer annotations.
However, as many medical image tasks show a high inter-observer variability
resulting from factors such as image quality, different levels of user
expertise and domain knowledge, little is known as to how inter-observer
variability and commonly used fusion methods affect the estimation of
uncertainty of automated image segmentation. In this paper we analyze the
effect of common image label fusion techniques on uncertainty estimation, and
propose to learn the uncertainty among observers. The results highlight the
negative effect of fusion methods applied in deep learning, to obtain reliable
estimates of segmentation uncertainty. Additionally, we show that the learned
observers' uncertainty can be combined with current standard Monte Carlo
dropout Bayesian neural networks to characterize uncertainty of model's
parameters.

We present a novel region based active learning method for semantic image
segmentation, called MetaBox+. For acquisition, we train a meta regression
model to estimate the segment-wise Intersection over Union (IoU) of each
predicted segment of unlabeled images. This can be understood as an estimation
of segment-wise prediction quality. Queried regions are supposed to minimize to
competing targets, i.e., low predicted IoU values / segmentation quality and
low estimated annotation costs. For estimating the latter we propose a simple
but practical method for annotation cost estimation. We compare our method to
entropy based methods, where we consider the entropy as uncertainty of the
prediction. The comparison and analysis of the results provide insights into
annotation costs as well as robustness and variance of the methods. Numerical
experiments conducted with two different networks on the Cityscapes dataset
clearly demonstrate a reduction of annotation effort compared to random
acquisition. Noteworthily, we achieve 95%of the mean Intersection over Union
(mIoU), using MetaBox+ compared to when training with the full dataset, with
only 10.47% / 32.01% annotation effort for the two networks, respectively.

White matter hyperintensity (WMH) is a common finding on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain. WMH is associated with numerous neurological and neurodegenerative diseases. Accurate segmentation of WMH is crucial for the diagnosis of these diseases. However, obtaining accurate WMH segmentation results has been difficult despite recent advances in deep learning. Therefore, this study aimed to improve the accuracy of WMH segmentation using a post-processing method for randomly-initialized U-net.

The U-net architecture was implemented, and its output was used as input to the proposed post-processing method. The post-processing method consisted of three steps: interpolation, noise reduction, and morphological enhancement. The interpolation step was used to fill in missing pixels in the segmented WMH regions. The noise reduction step was used to remove noise from the image. The morphological enhancement step was used to improve the shape and size of the segmented WMH regions.

The proposed method was compared to the original U-net method using a segmentation accuracy metric and visual inspection. The results showed that the proposed method significantly improved the accuracy of WMH segmentation. The proposed method achieved an accuracy of 97%, while the original U-net method achieved an accuracy of 87%. This represents a significant improvement in accuracy of 10%. The proposed post-processing method provides a simple and effective way to improve the accuracy of WMH segmentation, which can aid in the diagnosis of neurological and neurodegenerative diseases.

prompt: Write a recipe for "German Wedding Cake".
text:
Ingredients:

For the Cake:
- 2 3/4 cups all-purpose flour
- 3/4 cup granulated sugar
- 1/2 cup brown sugar, packed
- 2 tsp baking powder
- 1/2 tsp baking soda
- 1/2 tsp salt
- 1 tsp ground cinnamon
- 1/2 tsp ground nutmeg
- 1/4 tsp ground cloves
- 1 cup unsalted butter, softened
- 4 large eggs
- 1 cup buttermilk
- 2 tsp pure vanilla extract
- 1 cup finely grated peeled apple
- 1/2 cup finely chopped nuts (walnuts or pecans)

For the Frosting:
- 1 cup unsalted butter, softened
- 4 cups powdered sugar
- 2 tsp pure vanilla extract
- 2-3 tbsp milk or cream
- A pinch of salt

Instructions:

1. Preheat your oven to 350°F (175°C). Grease and flour three 8-inch round cake pans.

2. In a large bowl, combine the flour, granulated sugar, brown sugar, baking powder, baking soda, salt, cinnamon, nutmeg, and cloves. 

3. Add the softened butter to the flour mixture and beat until it resembles coarse crumbs.

4. Add eggs, one at a time, beating well after each addition. Stir in the buttermilk and vanilla extract until the batter is smooth.

5. Fold in the grated apple and chopped nuts.

6. Divide the batter evenly among the prepared pans. Bake for 25-30 minutes, or until a toothpick inserted into the center of the cakes comes out clean. 

7. Allow the cakes to cool in the pans for 10 minutes, then transfer them to wire racks to cool completely.

8. While the cake is cooling, prepare the frosting. Beat the softened butter until creamy. Gradually add the powdered sugar, vanilla extract, and salt, beating until combined. Add milk or cream, one tablespoon at a time, until the frosting reaches your desired consistency.

9. Once the cakes are completely cooled, layer and frost the cakes with the prepared frosting.

10. For a more traditional German touch, you may optionally garnish the top with more chopped nuts or marzipan decorations.

Your delicious German Wedding Cake is ready to be served. Enjoy!

After hearing people praise this movie, and seeing how much it was advertised, I was curious to see this. Now, I've never loved Illumination's movies, but I've never hated them either. I don't mind any of their films, but I feel like they're not as innovative as certain other animation companies. Hearing how much people loved Secret Life of Pets gave me a bit of hope that perhaps this movie would be Illumination's breakthrough. The one that would have the best animation, story, characters, emotions, etc.

Unfortunately, Secret Life of Pets just ended up being another okay movie for me. Right when I saw the trailers, I was reminded of Toy Story with the plot. I feared that the plot would be predictable, and it definitely was. A few different things were thrown in, but as a whole, the story was pretty predictable. One of the different things that was thrown in had potential to be a really emotional scene. This is a spoiler, by the way. Anyway, Duke finds out that his original owner had died, which could've led into an emotional scene, like in Finding Dory when Dory was made to believe her parents were dead. But the whole scene failed. Firstly, it was told, not shown. A random cat just gives the news to Duke. Second, Duke barely reacts to this, despite the movie going out of its way to show us a montage of him with his owner. He just gets mad at the family that moved into the owner's home before getting caught by animal control. After that, it's never mentioned again. Duke is just fine with his owner being dead, and living with a new owner and Max. This really bothers me, since as I said, this scene had potential to be emotionally provoking. But it didn't take the chance.

Our main characters didn't interest me. Max is just another typical good guy that just wants a good life. Duke was just another lovable big guy who may be a bit slow. However, the only characters that made me laugh/I enjoyed were Gidget, Snowball, Tiberius, and Pops. Gidget and Snowball were the ones that really shined, though. Gidget was just plain adorable, and hilarious. As for Snowball, I'm not a big fan of Kevin Hart, but he really did a great job for his first animated film. I personally prefer him doing voice work than him in live action films. He managed to make me laugh multiple times as Snowball. That bunny may be cute, but he's totally psychotic. As for the rest of the characters, they didn't really interest me. I don't hate any of them, but they were pretty generic.

I also am sick of the Minions. They got old when their own movie was made. I won't mind seeing them in Despicable Me 3, since we'll only get small doses of them, but having them constantly shoved in our faces is getting annoying. The short that came on before Secret Life of Pets was just stupid. No experimentation with the animation or characters. Just plain stupidity. They also had one of the dogs in Secret Life wear a Minions costume, and I just rolled my eyes. Minions may make Illumination money, but not many people care about them anymore. I certainly don't.

I do have some positive things to say about this film. The animation was impressive. I was particularly impressed with how they animated water, and the mannerisms of the pets. Which leads into the next thing I liked about this. I admire how much the creators of the film did their research on not just dogs, but most pets people keep. They were spot on with how dogs, cats, birds, etc. act. As a dog and cat owner, I appreciate the humor/realism that went into the pets, and they reminded me of my own pets.

As a whole, this a cute, but flawed film. I wasn't impressed with most of the characters. The story was predictable. Nothing about this film was thought or emotionally provoking. However, I appreciated some of the film's humor, animation, and the research that went into the mannerisms of the pets. It's a shame that this wasn't Illumination's breakthrough. Sure, it's making a lot of money, but it's still just an alright movie. Hopefully one day, Illumination will make a film just as great as the likes of Zootopia or Inside Out. The Secret Life of Pets just isn't that film.

prompt: Write a recipe for "Pokey Pudding Cake".
text:
Ingredients:
- 1 box of chocolate cake mix
- 1 box of chocolate pudding mix
- 4 large eggs
- 1/2 cup of white granulated sugar
- 2 cups of whole milk
- 1/4 cup of vegetable oil
- 1 teaspoon of vanilla extract
- 1 cup of chocolate chips

For the topping:
- 2 cups of whipped cream
- 1 cup of condensed milk
- 1/2 cup of cocoa powder

Instructions:
1. Preheat your oven to 350°F (175°C) and grease a 9x13-inch baking pan.
2. In a large bowl, combine the cake mix, pudding mix, eggs, and sugar. Beat until well mixed.
3. Gradually add the milk, oil, and vanilla extract, continuing to beat until the mixture is smooth and well combined.
4. Stir in the chocolate chips until they are evenly distributed throughout the batter.
5. Pour the batter into the greased baking pan and smooth out the top with a spoon or spatula.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for about 30 to 35 minutes, or until a toothpick inserted into the center of the cake comes out clean.
7. Let the cake cool for about 10 to 15 minutes. While it is still warm, poke holes all over the cake using a fork or the handle of a wooden spoon.
8. As the cake cools, prepare the topping. Whip the cream until it forms stiff peaks, then gently fold in the condensed milk and cocoa powder until well combined.
9. Pour the topping over the cooled, poked cake, ensuring it seeps into the holes. Use a spatula to spread it evenly over the surface of the cake.
10. Cover the cake with cling wrap and chill in the refrigerator for at least 2 hours, or until the topping is set.
11. Slice and serve the Pokey Pudding Cake chilled. Enjoy this delightful dessert with its rich, creamy topping and moist, chocolatey cake!

prompt: Write a recipe for "Uncle Bill'S Breaded Pork Loin Chops In Mushroom Soup".
text:
Here is a recipe for Uncle Bill's breaded pork loin chops in mushroom soup:

Ingredients:

* 4 pork loin chops, trimmed
* Salt and pepper
* All-purpose flour
* 2 eggs, beaten
* 2 tablespoons olive oil
* 2 cups sliced mushrooms
* 1 onion, diced
* 2 cloves garlic, minced
* 4 cups chicken broth
* 1 cup heavy cream

Instructions:

1. Preheat the oven to 375°F (190°C).
2. Season the pork loin chops with salt and pepper on both sides.
3. In a shallow dish, mix together the flour and eggs to form the breading for the pork chops.
4. In a large oven-safe skillet, heat the olive oil over medium heat.
5. Once the skillet is hot, dredge each pork chop in the flour mixture, shaking off any excess.
6. Add the pork chops to the skillet and cook until golden brown on both sides, about 5 minutes per side.
7. Remove the skillet from the heat and place it in the preheated oven.
8. While the pork chops are baking, in a separate large pot, sauté the sliced mushrooms, diced onion, and minced garlic until the mushrooms are browned and fragrant.
9. Pour in the chicken broth and bring to a simmer.
10. Reduce the heat to low and let the soup simmer for about 20 minutes, or until the pork chops are fully cooked.
11. Once the pork chops are done, remove them from the oven and transfer them to a serving platter.
12. Pour the mushroom soup over the pork chops and garnish with fresh herbs, if desired.
13. Serve and enjoy!

text:
Title: Chipotle-Glazed Chicken Breast and Grilled Chopped Veggie Salad

Ingredients:
- 2 chicken breasts, boneless and skinless
- 3 tablespoons chipotle sauce
- 2 tablespoons honey
- 2 tablespoons lime juice
- 1 teaspoon garlic powder
- 1 teaspoon paprika
- Salt and black pepper to taste
- 1 red bell pepper, chopped
- 1 yellow bell pepper, chopped
- 1 zucchini, chopped
- 1 red onion, chopped
- 2 tablespoons olive oil
- 4 cups mixed greens
- 1 avocado, sliced
- 1 cup cherry tomatoes, halved
- 1/4 cup cilantro leaves, chopped
- Optional toppings: crumbled feta cheese, sliced black olives

Instructions:

1. Preheat the grill to medium-high heat.

2. In a small bowl, whisk together the chipotle sauce, honey, lime juice, garlic powder, paprika, salt, and black pepper.

3. Pat the chicken breasts dry with a paper towel and season them with salt and black pepper. Brush both sides of the chicken breasts with the chipotle glaze.

4. In a separate bowl, toss together the chopped red and yellow bell peppers, zucchini, and red onion with olive oil, salt, and black pepper.

5. Place the chicken breasts on the grill and cook for 6-8 minutes per side, or until cooked through and the internal temperature reaches 165°F (75°C).

6. At the same time, place the chopped veggies directly on the grill or in a grilling basket. Cook for 8-10 minutes, or until the vegetables are tender and slightly charred.

7. Remove the chicken and veggies from the grill and let them rest for a few minutes.

8. Meanwhile, prepare the salad. In a large bowl, combine the mixed greens, avocado slices, cherry tomatoes, and cilantro leaves.

9. Slice the grilled chicken breasts into thin strips and add them to the salad.

10. Add the grilled chopped veggies to the salad and gently toss to combine.

11. Serve the Chipotle-Glazed Chicken Breast and Grilled Chopped Veggie Salad with optional toppings such as crumbled feta cheese and sliced black olives.

12. Enjoy your flavorful and nutritious Chipotle-Glazed Chicken Breast and Grilled Chopped Veggie Salad!

Ingredients:

* 3-4 large potatoes, peeled and sliced into 1/8-inch thick rounds
* 1/4 cup unsalted butter, softened
* 1/2 cup grated cheese (such as Gruyère, Emmental, or Cheddar)
* 1/2 cup heavy cream
* 1/2 cup milk
* Salt and pepper to taste
* Fresh herbs, such as thyme or parsley, for garnish

Instructions:

1. Preheat the oven to 350°F (180°C).
2. In a large baking dish, arrange a layer of overlapping potato slices.
3. Drizzle the softened butter over the potatoes, then sprinkle with a little salt and pepper.
4. Sprinkle about half of the grated cheese over the potatoes.
5. Pour half of the heavy cream and milk mixture over the potatoes, making sure they're well-coated.
6. Repeat the layers, starting with the potatoes, then the remaining butter, salt, pepper, cheese, and cream mixture.
7. Finish with a layer of potatoes on top.
8. Cover the dish with aluminum foil and bake for 30-40 minutes, or until the potatoes are tender and the top layer is golden brown.
9. Remove the foil and continue baking for an additional 10-15 minutes, or until the top is golden brown and the potatoes are cooked through.
10. Remove from the oven and let it rest for a few minutes before serving.
11. Garnish with fresh herbs and serve warm.

It's a real shame that everything I had read about Déjà Vu concerned the high-powered explosions and loud clatter of guru/producer Jerry Bruckheimer. No mention, except maybe as a footnote, was given to A-list director Tony Scott and the magic he has woven in his past three films. The man who brought us Top Gun has seen a sort of revival in style lately with the entertaining Spy Game, the amazing Man on Fire, and the kinetic Domino. Scott has taken the quick cuts of music videos and has infused them into his shooting style. His editor better be making some good money as these films fly by with filters, jump-cuts, grain, and camera angles swiveling at every turn. Greatly overshadowed by brother Ridley Scott and his more serious, award-winning epics, Tony has been pumping out some of the most solid and entertaining films of the past couple decades. With a reuniting of semi-regular star Denzel Washington, Déjà Vu proves that when Bruckheimer is paired with a like mind, his usual drivel can become great. Scott shows us how to hone the explosions, noise, and clutter to an effective level and gives us a helluva ride.

Déjà Vu could have easily reduced itself to timetravel farce, going by the books to show a time warp in order to solve a crime. The far-fetched premise of being able to see the past as it happens four and a half days later should seem crazy and by watching the previews you are given the idea that it will be just a series of do-overs. Fortunately the trailers these days show a totally different movie than what has been crafted. Scott and his screenwriters have not only developed a sci-fi tale seeped in enough reality to at least be looked upon as plausible for the sake of the story, but they nicely tidy up any chance of their being a plothole. Our story begins with a devastating domestic terrorist act upon a ferry carrying over 500 people, Navy and family. Washington's ATF agent is brought in and discovers that it was no accident. During the use of this screen of the past, Denzel acquires a feeling of obligation to do all he can to prevent what he sees from occurring in the present, no matter what consequences that might entail for the future. The quest to stop the violence begins with an attractive young woman who unknowingly has become an integral part in what will ultimately transpire.

The beauty of this film is that with multiple timelines being shown parallel to each other, there are many questions that desperately need answering. To credit all involved, they appear to have put themselves in the audience's shoes and piece-by-piece wrote in a reason for everything. Anything that is seen either in the past, present, or future has a reason for being there and will be intelligently explained. Also, the performances are stellar, Denzel and Kilmer as well as a quietly maniacal Jim Caviezel and the emotionally exasperated Paula Patton, and the visuals unique. While Scott has toned down the ultra-kinetic cuts and filters for the main action, his style is still stamped on the graphics of their screen showing the past. The motion trails and speed scans lend a stylized digital editing program feel and are gorgeous to watch. Déjà Vu's best sequence, however, is the crazy car chase during the present in pursuit of a vehicle in the past, definitely a rush and orchestrated almost flawlessly. Even though Ridley gets the accolades and Tony gets the hack/overproduced label, I must say, while they are the best directing duo in Hollywood, I might have to give the edge on pure cinematic entertainment to the younger Tony. He is on a roll and doesn't seem to be stopping anytime soon.

Like many of you, the first time I saw the trailer for The Lego Movie (2014) I thought to myself, "Are you kidding me?!" Yet another movie based on a franchise of toys aimed towards families willing to cough up the cash just to shut their kids up. Can't we for once make movies for kids that don't dull the senses? Have we truly come to the point where there are no original thoughts? Yet after seeing not just families but college kids' line up to see sold out viewings I became interested. In addition, The Lego Movie managed to muster a staggering 93% on rottentomatoes.com, an unheard of fresh score in the February film graveyard. In short; curiosity got the best of me.

Boy was I wrong about this film. I honestly couldn't have been more wrong about a film in my life. The Lego Movie is not only the must see film of the late winter season, I'm going to go ahead and call it now; it's the best family-oriented film for all ages of 2014. Okay maybe not but at the very least it's a very high bar to set.

The story busts out of the gate from the get-go; Vitruvius (Morgan Freeman) a wizard and "master builder", while protecting a mystery weapon is blinded by Lord Business (Will Ferrell), obviously our caped and big booted villain. Before Vitruvius is kicked into the abyss by Business and his robotic minions, he foretells of a hero, the "special" who will put an end to his dastardly plans, whatever they might be. The next morning Emmet a seemingly ordinary Lego construction worker goes about his normal day. He comes across a woman named Wyldstyle (Elizabeth Banks) searching for "the piece of resistance" which he unwittingly finds and becomes beholden to. Now it's up to Emmet and some newfound friends to fulfill the prophecy.

It all sounds like a scenario dreamed up by a child who's read one too many comic books. Yet within The Lego Movie's brick-blocked world, everything including the story feels incredibly new and original. Children, especially the young will enjoy the fast action, laugh-a-minute jokes, sly slapstick and goofy characters. Obvious kid favorites will include perma-smiled Unikitty (Alison Brie) and zany 80's throwback astronaut Benny (Charlie Day) whose ability to create spaceships is frustratingly overlooked. Plus there's Batman (Will Arnett)Batman!

The older crowd however will be astounded not only with the seamless CGI effects but with the subversive element throughout the film. Yes a goofy, kiddy film of such unrestrained chirpiness can be positively incendiary, at least in this case. Throughout the film there are Orwellian elements tucked underneath crafty pop-culture references ranging from Star Wars (1977) to Harry Potter. There are mischievous pokes at what Henry David Thoreau referred to as "(leading) lives of quite desperation."

Finally there's cheeky satire aimed at the Danish toy brand itself. Much of the conflict revolves around "master builders" who build whatever they want out of the parts they find versus Lord Business who wants everything built "according to the directions." This particular theme struck the kid inside me as I was very fond of Legos. Younglings may not realize that back in the day, pre-designed Lego play sets took a back seat to the now impossible to find Lego Creative Bucket sets. To the uninitiated that particular red bucket set was an amalgam of potential foot sores but to this writer, those 200+ pieces were a gateway to an unlimited creative space.

The Lego Movie accurately and effectively recreates that creative space through accessible movie magic. It exhibits a fun hero story that may not be treading new narrative ground but nonetheless feels fresh and new. Finally the themes and occasionally biting humor makes The Lego Movie a kid's film that isn't just for kids but the child in all of us. This February do yourself a favor and treat yourself to an adventure story unlike any other. Then go home and order some Legos online! I know I am.

text:
The Harvard Indian College was a school within Harvard College in Cambridge, Massachusetts where young Native American men were taught rudimentary elements of western sciences and humanities. This college, part of a broader missionary movement by colonists in New England, aimed at converting Native American people to Christianity. Established in 1655, it was funded in part by the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel in New England. 

The Harvard Indian College was an essential part of Harvard University’s early history. Harvard was founded in 1636 with a dual purpose: the training of ministers and the education of the English and Native youth in the hope of evangelizing the native population. The Indian College was built using funds from the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel in New England following a fund-raising drive in the colonies and in England. The Society planned for the money to be used for 'the maintenance of the President of Harvard and the College Schoolmaster, for erecting a College edifice, and to support students, among whom were to be Indian youths.'

Few records exist that provide insight into the daily operation and curriculum of the Indian College. Still, accounts suggest students learned Latin and Greek, and were instructed in Christian doctrine and Western academics. Besides the Indian College, Harvard established an Indian College Printing Press that issued the first Bible printed in the United States, in the Algonquin language.

However, the Indian College was relatively short-lived and faced a lack of student enrollment. By 1698, it had stopped operating altogether, primarily due to a shortage of students, the death of its primary champion, John Eliot, and shifting political and cultural attitudes toward education of Native American youth. Despite its brief existence, the Indian College left an enduring mark on Harvard. Two Native American students, Caleb Cheeshahteaumuck and Joel Hiacoomes, graduated from Harvard in 1665. Cheeshahteaumuck remains the first and, for centuries, the only known Native American to have graduated from Harvard College.

Today, in recognition of the original location of the college, Harvard University installed a historic plaque in 1997. In addition, Harvard University and its native community organization, Native Americans at Harvard College, commemorate the site with an annual ceremony. The university continues to acknowledge its early history in its present endeavors to sustain and strengthen the presence of Native American community and heritage on campus.

Ingredients: 
- 1 medium-sized pumpkin 
- 1 tablespoon olive oil 
- Salt and pepper to taste 
- 1 cup mascarpone cheese 
- 1/2 cup grated Parmesan cheese 
- 1 teaspoon dried sage 
- 1 package of wonton wrappers 
- 1 egg, beaten 
- Butter and fresh sage leaves for serving 

Instructions: 

1. Preheat your oven to 400°F (200°C). 

2. Start by preparing the pumpkin. Cut it in half and scoop out the seeds. Slice it into smaller sections and remove the skin.

3. Cut the pumpkin flesh into cubes and place them on a baking sheet. Drizzle with olive oil and season with salt and pepper. Toss to evenly coat the pumpkin.

4. Roast the pumpkin in the preheated oven for about 30 minutes, or until it becomes tender and slightly browned.

5. Once the pumpkin is cooked, transfer it to a mixing bowl and mash it with a fork or potato masher until it becomes a smooth puree.

6. Add mascarpone cheese, grated Parmesan, and dried sage to the pumpkin puree. Mix well until all the ingredients are fully incorporated.

7. Lay out the wonton wrappers on a clean surface. Place a heaping teaspoon of the pumpkin and mascarpone mixture in the center of each wrapper.

8. Brush the edges of the wonton wrappers with the beaten egg.

9. Fold one corner of the wonton wrapper over the pumpkin mixture to form a triangle. Press down to seal the edges, ensuring there are no air pockets.

10. Continue this process with the remaining pumpkin mixture and wonton wrappers.

11. Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Carefully drop the ravioli into the boiling water and cook for about 2-3 minutes, or until they float to the surface.

12. While the ravioli is cooking, melt butter in a skillet over medium heat. Add fresh sage leaves and cook until they become crispy.

13. Using a slotted spoon, transfer the cooked ravioli to the skillet with the sage butter. Gently toss to coat the ravioli.

Ingredients:
- 1 pound fusilli pasta
- 1 bunch rapini (broccoli rabe), stems trimmed
- 4 cloves garlic, minced
- 2 tablespoons olive oil
- 1 can diced tomatoes
- 1/2 cup red wine
- 1 teaspoon dried oregano
- 1/2 teaspoon dried chili flakes (optional)
- Salt and pepper to taste
- Grated Parmesan cheese for serving

Instructions:
1. Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Cook the fusilli pasta according to package instructions until al dente. Drain and set aside.
2. While the pasta is cooking, blanch the rapini in a separate pot of boiling water for about 2 minutes, then remove and drain. Chop the blanched rapini into bite-sized pieces and set aside.
3. In a large skillet, heat the olive oil over medium heat. Add the minced garlic and cook until fragrant, about 1 minute.
4. Add the diced tomatoes, red wine, dried oregano, and chili flakes (if using) to the skillet. Stir to combine and let simmer for about 10 minutes, allowing the flavors to meld together.
5. Add the chopped rapini to the skillet and cook for an additional 5 minutes, until the rapini is tender.
6. Season the sauce with salt and pepper to taste.
7. In a large serving bowl, combine the cooked fusilli pasta and the rapini tomato sauce. Toss until the pasta is well coated.
8. Serve the fusilli with rapini and tomato wine sauce hot, garnished with grated Parmesan cheese. Enjoy!

Indian film director Mira Nair has said she was thrilled to be given the chance to make William Makepeace Thackeray's novel Vanity Fair - as the book has been a favourite through her life.
The book is one of the classics of English literature - the story of scheming 19th Century social climber Becky Sharp, played in the film by Reese Witherspoon. Nair said that she jumped at the chance to work on the film, which she has - controversially - made in a Bollywood style, including two song-and-dance routines in the film's second half. "It was serendipity really - I was offered Vanity Fair by the studio Focus Features, who had distributed Monsoon Wedding," Nair told BBC World Service's Masterpiece programme. "They offered me their next-best thing, not realising that Vanity Fair had actually been one of my favourite novels since I was 16 years old in an Irish Catholic boarding school in India."
Since her 1988 debut feature Salaam Bombay! - nominated for the Best Foreign Language Oscar and winner of Best First Feature at Cannes - Nair has become one of India's most famous and respected directors. She is not restricted to Bollywood, however - she followed Salaam Bombay! with Mississippi Masala, starring Denzel Washington, and The Perez Family, her first Hollywood film.
Her career peaked with Monsoon Wedding in 2001, which won the Golden Lion award at Venice. Nair's Indian-style adaptation of Vanity Fair, however, has been attacked by critics in the US - where it only reached number eight at the box office in its opening week - who described the Bollywood elements as "jarring." The film has a new ending, with Becky Sharp running off for a new life in India. But Nair said that her film had picked up on the way Thackeray - who was born in India but moved to England as a young man - had seen the world. "First, when I was 16, it was Becky Sharp, who is a completely memorable character, because I recognised myself in her - I recognised all the ladies who did not want to be ladies, who wanted to buck the system that they were in," she said. "But it was the sort of novel I somehow kept at the side of my bed for many years, and I would dip into every now and then and suddenly get completely mesmerised again. "As I got older and read it, I think it was Thackeray's clarity - his clear-sightedness about his own society, the fact that he was born in India but came to England as a young man - that gave him the eyes of an outsider, and yet he was an insider. "That perspective was something I really loved."
Nair also defended her decision to cast an American actress - Reese Witherspoon - as Becky Sharp, despite the fact that all the rest of the cast are British or Irish. "I cast intuitively - in my films I cast as many non-actors as I cast actors," she said. "For me, it is intuition - I have to fall in love with an actor. It is a visceral response.
"Thackeray describes Becky Sharp as a minx. Also she's described as someone who's tiny, red-headed and thin. Reese had that completely minx-like irresistibility about her." Having won the role because she seemed physically perfectly suited to the part, however, Witherspoon then became pregnant. But Nair said that, though this had created the need for some filming tricks, it had in fact also helped the film. "It was a self-fulfilling prophesy - when I first met her husband [actor Ryan Philippe], I said 'knock her up, won't you, I need some flesh on the girl'," she joked. "I'm not a fan of the underfed Los Angeles actor at all. This was, for me, about Becky Sharp being, eventually, a full-blown woman through the course of the film. "I love the luminosity that pregnancy brings, I love the fleshiness, I love the ample bosom - it gave me much more to play with." Nair explained how camera tricks had been used to disguise Witherspoon's "bump" in various scenes - including hiring a number of young boys in costumes to stand in front of her. "She runs, she gets off coal carts, she jumps off horses - she does everything," Nair said. "But there's also a certain carriage with horses that is going to wipe the screen at a certain moment, because of the bump."

text:
Ingredients: 

For the Chocolate Banana Split Streusel Cake:
- 2 cups all-purpose flour
- 1.5 cups granulated sugar
- 3/4 cup cocoa powder
- 1.5 teaspoons baking powder
- 1.5 teaspoons baking soda
- 1 teaspoon salt
- 2 eggs
- 1 cup milk
- 1/2 cup vegetable oil
- 2 teaspoons pure vanilla extract
- 2 ripe bananas, mashed
- 1 cup boiling water

For the Streusel Topping:
- 1/4 cup all-purpose flour
- 1/4 cup granulated sugar
- 3 tablespoons butter, cold and cubed
- 3/4 cup chocolate chips
- 1/2 cup chopped walnuts

Instructions:

1. Preheat your oven to 350°F (175°C). Grease a 9x13 inch baking pan.

2. In a large mixing bowl, combine the flour, sugar, cocoa, baking powder, baking soda and salt. 

3. Add the eggs, milk, oil and vanilla to the flour mixture and mix until well combined.

4. Stir in the mashed bananas and boiling water until the batter is smooth. Pour the batter into the prepared baking pan.

5. To make the streusel topping, combine the flour and sugar in a small bowl. Cut in the cold butter until the mixture is crumbly. Stir in the chocolate chips and chopped walnuts.

6. Sprinkle the streusel topping evenly over the cake batter.

7. Bake the cake in preheated oven for 35-40 minutes, or until a toothpick inserted into the center comes out clean.

8. Allow the cake to cool in the pan for about 20 minutes before removing. 

9. Once the cake is completely cool, cut into squares and serve. 

Enjoy the delicious blend of chocolate and bananas enhanced with the crunchy streusel topping in this yummy Chocolate Banana Split Streusel Cake.

text:
Ingredients:
- 2 cups all-purpose flour
- 1 teaspoon baking powder
- 1/4 teaspoon salt
- 1 cup milk
- 2 large eggs
- 1/4 cup granulated sugar
- 2 teaspoons ground cinnamon
- 1/4 teaspoon ground nutmeg
- 4 tablespoons unsalted butter
- 1/2 cup freshly squeezed lemon juice
- 1/2 cup grated Parmesan cheese

Instructions:

1. In a large mixing bowl, whisk together flour, baking powder, and salt. In a separate mixing bowl, whisk together flour, eggs, sugar, cinnamon, nutmeg, and milk.

2. Gradually stir the wet ingredients into the dry ingredients until the dough comes together. Knead the dough for 2-3 minutes until it is smooth and elastic.

3. Roll dough into small balls and place them on a floured surface. Use a rolling pin to flatten each ball into a flat circle.

4. Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Add gnocchi and cook until no longer raw, for about 2-3 minutes.

5. While the gnocchi is cooking, melt butter and lemon juice in a large skillet over medium heat.

6. Drain the water from the skillet and pour in the gnocchi. Toss to coat in the sauce.

7. Sprinkle Parmesan cheese over the gnocchi and toss once more.

8. Garnish with additional Parmesan cheese and chopped fresh parsley. Serve and enjoy your delicious Milk Cinnamon Gnocchi with Lemon and Parmesan Sauce!

Methods: This paper proposes a cross-validatory approach to quantify the statistical significance of clusters in disease mapping models. Our approach combines importance sampling with cross-validation to estimate p-values for each disease cluster, as well as for null and alternative hypotheses.

Results: We applied the proposed method to a simulated disease mapping study to assess its performance. Our results showed that our approach was able to accurately estimate p-values, and that it outperformed conventional approaches that relied on cluster detection methods alone.

Discussion: Our method provides a robust and flexible approach to quantifying the significance of clusters in disease mapping models. It is an important tool for researchers to reliably interpret the results of their studies, and to facilitate comparisons across different studies and datasets.

prompt: Write a recipe for "Danish Cream Puffs".
text:
Danish Cream Puffs Recipe:

Ingredients:
- 1 cup water
- 1/2 cup unsalted butter
- 1/4 teaspoon salt
- 1 cup all-purpose flour
- 4 large eggs
- 1 cup heavy cream
- 1/4 cup powdered sugar
- 1 teaspoon vanilla extract
- 1/4 cup sliced almonds
- 1/4 cup dark chocolate, melted (optional)

Instructions:

1. Preheat your oven to 400°F (200°C) and line a baking sheet with parchment paper.

2. In a medium-sized saucepan, bring water, butter, and salt to a boil over medium heat.

3. Once the mixture is boiling, add all-purpose flour and stir vigorously until a smooth dough forms and pulls away from the sides of the pan.

4. Remove the dough from heat and let it cool for a few minutes.

5. In a separate bowl, beat the eggs one at a time, then gradually add them to the dough, beating well after each addition. The dough should become glossy and smooth.

6. Using a spoon or a piping bag, drop spoonfuls or pipe walnut-sized balls of dough onto the prepared baking sheet, leaving about 2 inches of space between each puff.

7. Sprinkle some sliced almonds on top of each puff to add a nice crunch.

8. Bake the puffs in the preheated oven for 20-25 minutes or until they are golden brown and puffed up.

9. Remove the puffs from the oven and let them cool completely on a wire rack.

10. While the puffs are cooling, prepare the cream filling. In a mixing bowl, whip the heavy cream, powdered sugar, and vanilla extract until stiff peaks form.

11. Carefully slice each cooled puff in half horizontally and fill the bottom half with a generous dollop of the whipped cream.

12. Place the top half of the puff back on, gently pressing it down.

13. If desired, drizzle melted dark chocolate over the filled puffs for an extra touch of decadence.

14. Serve the Danish cream puffs immediately or refrigerate for a few hours before serving.

Enjoy these delicious Danish cream puffs as a sweet treat with a cup of coffee or tea!

Ultra high speed wi-fi connections moved closer to reality on Thursday when Intel said it would list standards for the technology later this year.
Intel is developing ultra-wideband technology (UWB) which would allow fast data transfer but with low power needs. UWB is tipped to be used for wireless transfer of video in the home or office and for use in wireless USB devices which need low power consumption. A rival UWB standard is being developed by Motorola and chip firm Freescale. At the mobile phone conference 3GSM in Cannes last month Samsung demonstrated a phone using UWB technology from Freescale.
At a press conference on Thursday Intel announced that two UWB groups, WiMedia Alliance and Multi-band OFDM alliance had merged to support the technology. UWB makes it possible to stream huge amounts of data through the air over short distances. One of the more likely uses of UWB is to make it possible to send DVD quality video images wirelessly to TV screens or to let people beam music to media players around their home.
The technology has the potential to transmit hundreds of megabits of data per second. "Consumer electronics companies want UWB to replace cables and simplify set-up," Jeff Ravencraft, technology strategist at Intel and chairman of the Wireless USB Promoter Group, told technology site ZDNet. "Thirty percent of consumer electronics returns are because the consumer couldn't set up the equipment." The first products using UWB technology from Intel are due to hit the market later this year. Initially they will be products using wireless USB 2.0 connections. UWB could also be used to create so-called Personal Area Networks that let a person's gadgets quickly and easily swap data amongst themselves. The technology works over a range up to 10 metres and uses billions of short radio pulses every second to carry data. Intel says the benefit of UWB is that it does not interfere with other wi-fi technologies already in use such as wi-fi, wimax and mobile phone networks.

Hoisin-Glazed Chicken with Sugar Snap Peas Recipe

Ingredients:

* 4 boneless chicken breasts
* 2 tablespoons vegetable oil
* 2 cloves garlic, minced
* 1 inch piece ginger, grated
* 1/2 cup hoisin sauce
* 1/4 cup soy sauce
* 2 tablespoons honey
* 2 tablespoons red wine vinegar
* 1 tablespoon sesame oil
* 1 teaspoon cornstarch
* 2 cups sugar snap peas
* Salt and pepper
* Cooked rice, for serving
* Green onions, sliced (optional)

Instructions:

1. In a small bowl, whisk together hoisin sauce, soy sauce, honey, red wine vinegar, sesame oil, and cornstarch until smooth.
2. Season the chicken breasts with salt and pepper.
3. Heat the vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat.
4. Add the chicken breasts and cook for 6-7 minutes per side, until browned and cooked through.
5. Remove the chicken from the skillet and set aside.
6. Add the sugar snap peas to the same skillet and cook for 3-4 minutes until they start to soften.
7. Add the garlic and ginger to the skillet and cook for 30 seconds until fragrant.
8. Return the chicken to the skillet and pour the sauce over it.
9. Stir everything together and let it simmer for 1-2 minutes until the sauce thickens.
10. Serve the chicken with sugar snap peas and rice. Garnish with sliced green onions if desired. Enjoy!

Tomato Clam Chowder Recipe

Ingredients:
- 1 cup all-purpose flour
- 1/4 cup unsalted butter, cut into small cubes
- 1 large onion, chopped
- 2 garlic cloves, minced
- 1 1/2 cups water
- 1 can (10 1/2 ounces) condensed tomato soup
- 1/2 cup heavy cream
- 2 cups chopped fresh clams
- 2 bay leaves
- 1 teaspoon dried thyme
- Salt and pepper to taste
- Chopped parsley for garnish

Instructions:

1. Begin by making a roux. In a large pot, whisk together the flour and 1/2 cup of water until smooth.

2. Add the butter to the roux, stirring continuously, until the butter has melted and the mixture is smooth and well combined.

3. Over medium heat, add the onion and garlic to the roux, cooking for about 3 minutes, until the onion has softened.

4. Stir in the remaining water, the can of condensed tomato soup, the heavy cream, clams, bay leaves, and thyme. Season with salt and pepper to taste.

5. Bring the mixture to a simmer, then reduce the heat to low and let it cook for about 20 minutes, until the clams are cooked through.

6. Remove the bay leaves and discard. Taste the chowder and adjust seasoning as needed. 

7. Serve hot, garnished with chopped parsley. Enjoy!
